**SYNTHETIC CLINICAL NOTE – UNSTRUCTURED**

[Patient Name: [Deid: Name]]  
[MRN: [Deid: MRN]]  
[Date of Encounter: [DATE: 25551]]  
[Service: Thoracic Surgery / Oncology]  
[Author: [Deid: Name]]  

**HPI:**  
70-year-old male with a significant history of hypertension, tobacco use (~37 pack-years, quit at time of lung cancer diagnosis), peripheral vascular disease, chronic kidney disease (stage 3), and a remote history of femoral and renal bruits, presented initially for evaluation of an incidentally discovered right upper lobe pulmonary nodule on low-dose CT lung cancer screening. He denied hemoptysis, chronic cough, chest pain, or weight loss at initial presentation. No family history of lung cancer, but positive family history of GI malignancy. Occupational exposure notable for prior work as a roofer but no asbestos or other lung carcinogen exposures. 

**Diagnostic Workup:**  
Initial low-dose CT demonstrated an 11 mm pulmonary nodule in the right upper lobe. PET imaging revealed a 1.3 x 1.2 x 0.9 cm part-solid FDG-avid nodule in the RUL, SUV max 2.0, with no definitive evidence of nodal or distant metastatic disease and no extrathoracic focus of uptake. No evidence for multiple lung primaries or contralateral disease.  
Further diagnostic workup by bronchoscopy with robotic-assisted navigation and endobronchial ultrasound was performed. Multiple lymph node stations were biopsied. Pathology confirmed non-small cell lung carcinoma (adenocarcinoma, NOS) limited to the right upper lobe nodule. All mediastinal and hilar nodes sampled were negative for malignancy.

**Preoperative Assessment:**  
Patient was evaluated in pulmonary and anesthesia pre-op clinics and deemed fit for surgical intervention. Cardiac risk stratification included non-invasive testing for coronary calcification noted incidentally on prior scans but with no symptoms of angina or exertional dyspnea. Renal function was CKD 3b but well compensated, so perioperative management planned accordingly.  
Functional status: Able to ambulate independently; climbs 2 flights of stairs without limitation. ECOG PS 0.  
No significant cognitive impairment by Mini-Cog. PHQ-9 negative for depression. No significant anxiety at baseline but increased distress noted during cancer workup.

**Surgical Course:**  
Patient underwent right posterolateral thoracotomy with wedge resection of the right upper lobe lesion and mediastinal lymph node dissection per standard oncologic technique. No intraoperative complications.  
Postoperatively, chest tube placed and managed with suction, no evidence of persistent air leak or subcutaneous emphysema. Post-surgical pain controlled with scheduled acetaminophen and PRN oral Dilaudid, later transitioned with adjunctive non-opioid analgesia. OnQ pump placed for local incisional analgesia.  
Ambulation initiated on post-op day 0; patient progressed from dangling to walking in the hall and bathroom with standby assistance. No perioperative fevers, hypoxia, or hemodynamic instability. Telemetry discontinued as patient maintained stable sinus rhythm throughout.

**Hospital Course:**  
Pain was moderate on day 1 (rated 5/10, improved to 3/10 with medication). Initially hesitant to report pain, required education on importance of adequate pain control for recovery. Postoperative labs notable for stable Hgb/Hct, no leukocytosis, normal platelet count, and creatinine at baseline CKD stage.  
Pulmonary hygiene emphasized with incentive spirometry, pillow splinting, and education provided on lung re-expansion techniques. No evidence of pneumonia, atelectasis, or new infiltrate on post-op chest imaging.  
Diet advanced as tolerated; patient denied issues with swallowing or oral intake and maintained good hydration. Voiding without difficulty, but mild constipation requiring docusate-senna noted.

Skin integrity maintained, no areas of breakdown or erythema at incision site or pressure points; dressing remained clean/dry/intact with minimal old serosanguinous drainage noted and marked.  
SCDs discontinued per patient preference once fully ambulatory. Activity level increased daily; up to 3 full walks on POD1, sat up in chair for meals, and tolerated increased mobility without falls or dizziness.

No new adverse neurological or cardiac events. Renal function monitored and remained stable.

**Discharge Readiness:**  
By POD2, chest tube transitioned to water seal and eventually removed after confirmation of resolved air leak and minimal output. No further oxygen requirement; SpO2 >95% on room air. Pain remained well controlled with scheduled acetaminophen, no further need for opioids.  
Patient was eating and drinking well, ambulating independently, and able to self-care. Nursing goals of increased activity and pain control met. Provided with written and verbal instructions on wound care, chest tube site management (as appropriate), use of incentive spirometry, and warning signs for infection or respiratory symptoms.  
Discharge plan coordinated with spouse present, MyChart access enabled for further communication.

**Post-Discharge Clinical Status:**  
On follow-up, patient reported procedural pain continued to improve, no new respiratory complaints, and was adherent to pulmonary exercises as reinforced by the care team. Ongoing supportive care for anxiety related to cancer diagnosis and recovery process, addressed during visits with resources provided. No evidence of postoperative complications or readmission.

**Medication Reconciliation:**  
Discharge medications included:  
- Acetaminophen 1,000 mg PO q6hr scheduled  
- Amlodipine 10 mg PO daily  
- Mirtazapine 15 mg PO QHS  
- Trazodone 100 mg PO QHS  
- Sennosides-docusate (Senokot-S) PRN for constipation  
- PRN Dilaudid as needed for breakthrough pain (limited post-discharge use, most doses unused)

No NSAIDs prescribed due to underlying CKD. Home blood pressure log initiated. No new anticoagulation required.

**Education and Supportive Measures:**  
Patient received comprehensive education on smoking cessation, wound care, activity progression, and monitoring for symptoms of recurrence or complications. Provided with lung surgery recovery packet and instructions for follow-up imaging, oncology, and PCP appointments. Advance care planning discussed and will be revisited at subsequent visits.

**Functional Status at Discharge and Outpatient Follow-Up:**  
Patient ambulating independently, tolerating regular diet, maintaining self-care, and demonstrating understanding of all discharge instructions. No new neurologic deficits, cardiopulmonary or infectious concerns. Ongoing psychosocial support in place.

**[END OF NOTE]**

**Oncology Nurse Navigator Note**  
[DATE: 24990]  

[Deid: Name] here today for a follow-up (Virtual Visit) with [Deid: Name] and [Deid: Name] to discuss recent biopsy results and review next steps in care. Please refer to the detailed consultation note completed today by [Deid: Name].

**Subjective**  
Patient states, "I am feeling good." She remains asymptomatic. No complaints of cough, shortness of breath, chest pain, or hemoptysis. Denies fever, chills, unintentional weight loss, night sweats, new pain, dizziness, or syncope. She reports being able to walk 2 blocks and climb 20 steps without shortness of breath. No issues with daily activities. Appetite and sleep unchanged.

**History of Present Illness**  
68-year-old female with a history of Stage IIB (pT2aN1M0) squamous cell carcinoma of the left upper lobe of the lung, status post left upper lobectomy (complicated by intraoperative vascular injury and emergent thoracotomy), with prior partial adjuvant chemotherapy discontinued due to side effects. In routine surveillance, a new and enlarging right upper lobe pulmonary nodule was detected:

- [DATE: 24828]: 7 × 6 mm RUL nodule identified on CT chest.
- [DATE: 24934]: Enlarged to 1.4 × 1.1 × 1.1 cm on CT chest with contrast.
- [DATE: 24941]: PET/CT scan showing mild FDG avidity of the RUL nodule (max SUV 3.5); no other pulmonary masses or FDG-avid nodes; no evidence of metastatic disease.
- Due to emphysematous changes and superficial blebs, percutaneous biopsy was considered high risk. Referred for robotic bronchoscopy with ENB and EBUS-guided lymph node sampling.

[DATE: 24983]: Underwent robotic bronchoscopy with transbronchial FNA of RUL lesion and EBUS-guided FNA of mediastinal nodes. No procedural complications.

Pathology:
- RUL lesion: Non-small cell carcinoma, favor squamous cell carcinoma.
- Station 7 lymph node: Negative for malignancy.

Recent pulmonary function testing ([DATE: 24969]) showed FEV1 65% predicted (1.53 L), DLCO 56% predicted.

**Social History**  
- Lives with husband in [Deid: Name], MN; strong social support at home.
- Retired.
- Former smoker: 43 pack-year history, quit 2014.
- No illicit drug use. Alcohol rare/social.
- No recent travel or sick contacts.

**Family History**  
- Daughter with breast cancer.
- Father with Alzheimer’s disease.

**Current Medications**  
- Alendronate 70 mg weekly  
- Amlodipine 5 mg daily  
- Famotidine 20 mg  
- Hydrochlorothiazide 12.5 mg  
- Pramipexole 0.125 mg  
- Rosuvastatin 5 mg  

**Review of Systems**  
- General: No fevers, chills, or malaise.  
- Respiratory: No new cough, hemoptysis, or dyspnea.  
- Cardiac: No chest pain, palpitations.  
- GI/GU: No changes.  
- MSK: No new bone pain.  
- Neuro: No focal deficits, headaches, or visual changes.  

**Recent Relevant Results**  
**Imaging**  
- [DATE: 24934] CT Chest: Postoperative changes left; emphysematous changes both lungs; irregular, enlarging 1.4 cm RUL nodule with spiculated border, new since [DATE: 24710]. No new pulmonary nodules or lymphadenopathy.  
- [DATE: 24941] PET/CT: Mild FDG avidity in RUL nodule (SUV 3.5), no other FDG-avid lesions, no nodal or distant metastatic disease.  
- [DATE: 24969] PFTs: FEV1 65% predicted (1.53 L), DLCO 56% predicted.

**Pathology**  
- RUL transbronchial FNA: Non-small cell carcinoma, favor squamous cell.  
- Station 7 EBUS FNA: Benign lymphoid tissue, negative for malignancy.

**Labs** ([DATE: 24922])  
- CBC: WBC 5.3, Hgb 13.7, Plt 448  
- CMP: Creatinine 1.15, BUN 17, Glucose 111, Na 140, K 3.7, Cl 101, CO2 28, Ca 10.6  
- Liver: AST 23, ALT 60, Alk Phos 76, Total Bili 0.4, Albumin 4.5, Total protein 7.8

**Exam** (Video)  
- Well appearing, alert, no acute distress  
- Nonlabored breathing at rest  
- No obvious neck masses, trachea midline  
- Mood/affect appropriate, engaging in discussion

**Psycho-social/Spiritual**  
- Patient lives with spouse; strong support system expressed.  
- No reported financial or transportation barriers.  
- Expressed desire to discuss options thoroughly with family.

**Education Provided**  
Patient and spouse educated on the nature of the lung nodule and the results of the diagnostic workup. Discussed that this appears to represent a new early-stage primary lung cancer, with no involvement of mediastinal lymph nodes and no evidence of spread. Reviewed surgical and non-surgical treatment options in full, including the nature of lobectomy, potential risks and complications, prior surgical history, and available alternatives (including stereotactic body radiation). Ensured understanding of diagnosis, options, and community resources.

Patient verbalized understanding but expressed desire to discuss with her oncologist and family prior to making a decision regarding next steps. All questions answered to apparent satisfaction.

**Materials Provided:**  
- Educational materials on lung cancer diagnosis and treatment  
- Contact information for Cancer Care Coordination team  
- Encouraged to reach out with any further questions or concerns

**[Deid: Name], BSN, OCN**  
Oncology Nurse Navigator  
Thoracic Program  
[Deid: Name] Health Cancer Institute, [Deid: Location]  

"Here to care, to motivate and to inspire."

CHIEF COMPLAINT:  
Follow-up for recently diagnosed metastatic non-small cell lung cancer, adenocarcinoma subtype, right upper lobe. Review of ongoing symptoms and systemic treatment tolerance.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS:  
[Deid: Name] is a 57-year-old male with a recent history of enlarging hypermetabolic right upper lobe lung nodule, biopsy-confirmed as adenocarcinoma. He was initially evaluated after PET/CT revealed an enlarging, hypermetabolic nodule in the right upper lobe, measuring 2.1 x 1.8 cm, with an SUV max of 10.5 and no evidence of mediastinal nodal or extrathoracic disease at that time. He underwent right robotic assisted thoracoscopic wedge resection, thoracic lymphadenectomy, bullectomy, and thoracotomy. Final pathology revealed invasive adenocarcinoma, pT2aN0M0, with negative margins. Postoperatively, he recovered well with expected complications including persistent pleuritic right-sided chest pain, improving productive cough, and a persistent rash attributed to pre-existing dermatologic history.

He has since completed a course of adjuvant systemic therapy tailored for advanced NSCLC, starting approximately six weeks ago. Broad molecular profiling of his resection specimen was notable for a HER2 (ERBB2) mutation. No other actionable mutations were detected. PD-L1 expression was <1%. He was therefore initiated on platinum doublet chemotherapy for advanced disease; he is currently completing his fourth cycle of pemetrexed plus carboplatin.

He describes ongoing but manageable pain at the thoracotomy site, continued intermittent cough now with less sputum, and mild exertional fatigue. He denies hemoptysis, new or worsening shortness of breath, fevers, sweats, or weight loss. Appetite is stable, and he reports regular bowel movements and normal voiding.

Previous issues with a pruritic, erythematous rash of the torso and upper back have improved with topical steroids and antihistamines. No new rashes or dermatologic complaints today.

— Constitutional: Fatigue, well controlled. No fever or chills.

No known drug allergies.

- Hypertension

- History of recurrent viral respiratory infections

NEUROLOGIC: Alert, oriented, grossly nonfocal.

LABORATORY AND IMAGING REVIEW:

— Most recent chest CT [DATE: 20969]: Post-surgical changes in right upper lobe, no evidence of new or progressive disease. No new pulmonary nodules or lymphadenopathy.

[Deid: Name]

Primary Care Provider: [Deid: Name]  
Location: [Deid: Location]

---
**SUBJECTIVE**  
[Deid: Name] is a 66-year-old female who presented with a suspicious lung nodule in the left upper lobe identified on CT screening. She has a significant smoking history (current, 0.5-1 pack per day for >50 years, now attempting to quit; currently 1-2 cigarettes/day). Pulmonary history is notable for moderate COPD, managed with PRN albuterol and fluticasone-based inhalers. She has known coronary artery disease (distal LAD stenosis, on medical management) and a past history of hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and chronic kidney disease stage 3b. No previous history of lung cancer prior to most recent workup.

Initial evaluation with navigational bronchoscopy and EBUS yielded atypical cells in the left upper lobe nodule; lymph node samples from stations 7, 10L, and 4L were negative for malignancy. She underwent further workup, including a PET-CT and pulmonary function testing, which demonstrated she was an acceptable surgical candidate (FEV1 1.08 L, 51% predicted; DLCO 71% predicted).

After discussion at the multidisciplinary thoracic oncology tumor conference, due to radiographic progression and persistent high suspicion for early-stage non-small cell lung cancer, the patient elected to proceed with excisional biopsy and surgical management. Risks, benefits, and expectations for recovery were thoroughly discussed, and [Deid: Name] expressed clear understanding and consented to the recommended procedure.

On [DATE: 24215], [Deid: Name] underwent robotic-assisted left video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS) with wedge resection of the left upper lobe nodule and mediastinal lymph node dissection. Immediate post-op recovery was notable for mild discomfort at the incision site, and the patient was able to ambulate with assistance. Pain was well-controlled with scheduled Tylenol and occasional oxycodone. She reported some difficulty sleeping overnight due to the new hospital environment but was able to sit up, order meals, and participate in post-operative activities.

On the first post-operative day, she was stable on room air, breathing comfortably, and ordering breakfast. She had minimal incisional pain, which was well controlled, and mild soreness at the chest wall incision. Oxygenation remained stable. She reported no shortness of breath, nausea, or new cough. She tolerated a regular diet and was able to void independently. Bowel movements had not yet occurred but she was asymptomatic and had bowel regimen ordered. Husband was present to assist with discharge planning, which was anticipated for later that day pending chest tube removal.

---
**OBJECTIVE**  

**Vital Signs (POD#1, [DATE: 24216]):**  
BP: 139/69 mmHg  
Pulse: 82 bpm  
Temp: 97.6°F (36.4°C)  
Resp: 18/min  
Ht: 1.6 m (5'3")  
Wt: 82.7 kg (182 lb 4.8 oz)  
BMI: 32.29 kg/m²  
SpO2: 93% on room air

**Physical Exam:**  
General: Alert, pleasant, no acute distress. Cooperative.  
Head/Eyes/Ears/Nose/Throat: Normocephalic, atraumatic. Eyes and ears normal. Oropharynx clear.  
Neck: Supple, no lymphadenopathy.  
Lungs: Non-labored respirations. Breathing comfortably. Lungs clear to auscultation bilaterally.  
Cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm. No murmurs, rubs, or gallops. Peripheral pulses intact.  
Abdomen: Soft, non-tender, normoactive bowel sounds.  
Extremities: No cyanosis, clubbing, or edema.  
Neurologic: Alert and oriented x3. Cranial nerves II-XII grossly intact. No focal deficits. Gait normal with assistance.  
Wound: Thoracoscopic incisions clean, dry, and intact. Chest tube site with clean dressing. No erythema, swelling, or drainage.  
Skin: No rashes, warm and dry.

**Imaging:**  
Chest X-ray ([DATE: 24216]): Worsening subcutaneous emphysema. Trace left apical pneumothorax with chest tube in place. No significant consolidation or infiltrate. No new nodules or effusion.  
Chest tube: To water seal, serosanguinous output overnight 50cc, no air leak on repeat coughs.

**Laboratory Data:**  
(Baseline preop labs reviewed; unremarkable except for chronic stable CKD.)

**Inpatient Course:**  
- Chest tube clamp trial performed POD#1 with no signs of air leak; chest tube removed same day after confirmation of stable repeat imaging.  
- Pain managed with scheduled acetaminophen and PRN oxycodone.  
- Incentive spirometry encouraged, with patient demonstrating appropriate technique (inspiratory volumes 1000-1200cc).  
- Early ambulation as tolerated.  
- Diet advanced as tolerated; bowel regimen in place.  
- Wound care with clean, dry dressings; no evidence of infection.

**Pathology:**  
Final Surgical Pathology (left upper lobe wedge, [DATE: 24216]):  
- Minimally invasive adenocarcinoma with acinar pattern (0.4 cm invasive focus, in setting of 1.5 cm area of chronic inflammation/fibrosis).  
- No visceral pleural invasion.  
- Margins negative.  
- No spread through airspaces.  
- No lymph nodes identified in specimen; separately resected mediastinal nodes (stations 9L, 8L, 7, 5, 11L) all benign and negative for metastatic carcinoma.  
- Background lung with emphysematous changes, respiratory bronchiolitis, and patchy smoking-related fibrosis.  
- Pathologic Stage IA1 (T1miN0M0; AJCC 8th Edition).

---
**POST-DISCHARGE COURSE**

Patient was discharged home on post-op day 1. During early recovery, she reported mild, expected left chest wall soreness, improved with ice and Tylenol. No fevers, chills, or infectious symptoms. She denied dyspnea or cough, used incentive spirometer as instructed, and increased her activity daily. Incisions continued to heal well without erythema, discharge, or dehiscence. Husband present at home to assist with recovery.

At follow-up, suture removal was uneventful. On exam, chest wall incisions had approximation with incomplete healing at chest tube entry, managed with steri-strips. Lungs were clear with no abnormal breath sounds; O2 saturation >95% on room air. No edema, no neurological deficits, no new complaints. CXR reviewed with pulmonology, demonstrating post-surgical changes without concerning findings for recurrence.

Pathology was reviewed in detail at the multidisciplinary lung tumor conference, with consensus supporting observation and surveillance for this stage, given absence of high-risk pathological features and clear surgical margins.

---
**SURVEILLANCE**

At most recent oncology follow-up, [Deid: Name] was 6 months post wedge resection, doing well with no pulmonary symptoms. Surveillance chest CT demonstrated post-surgical changes without evidence of new or recurrent lung nodules or mediastinal adenopathy.

---

**Medications**  
- Albuterol HFA inhaler PRN  
- Fluticasone propionate-salmeterol inhaler BID  
- Loratadine daily  
- Fluticasone nasal spray PRN  
- Aspirin 81 mg daily  
- Rosuvastatin 40 mg daily  
- Carvedilol 3.125 mg BID  
- Calcium carbonate/Vitamin D  
- Cimetidine BID  
- Cholecalciferol  
- Acetaminophen 500 mg QID PRN for pain  
- Oxycodone 5 mg PRN for breakthrough pain (early post-op period, now discontinued)

**Social and Family History**  
- Lives with husband, supportive; retired. Four adult sons.  
- Smokes: Currently 1 cigarette every few days; ongoing cessation efforts.  
- Exposure to secondhand smoke at home (husband smokes)  
- Alcohol: Rare use

**Functional Status**  
- Independent with ADLs  
- Ambulates independently  
- Engaged in physical activity as tolerated

- Mini-Cog: 4/5 (no impairment)

- Constitutional: No fever, chills, weight loss

[Deid: Name] is a 79-year-old female with a complex history including pulmonary hypertension, prior tobacco abuse, centrilobular emphysema, nocturnal hypoxemia, and a remote history of breast cancer (dx 2007, left-sided, ER+, PR-, pTis, pNx, pMx, s/p lumpectomy and 5 years of tamoxifen). She was evaluated after being found to have a spiculated nodule in the left upper lobe of the lung. Over the last 18 months, she has experienced gradually worsening exertional dyspnea, chronic productive cough, and increasing fatigue. She was hospitalized last year during which home oxygen therapy was initiated and has continued to use supplemental oxygen nightly and as needed when active. She denies current chest pain, syncope, palpitations, dizziness, or swelling.

She has had several episodes of cough productive of dark green sputum along with occasional wheezing and sinus drainage. She has not noted hemoptysis nor fevers. She has a long-standing diagnosis of centrilobular emphysema and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, for which she has been managed with inhaled and oral corticosteroids and bronchodilators. She has been on prednisone 5 mg daily and continues to use albuterol nebulizer as needed. She also reports a history of smoking from 2002 to 2017, approximately 0.25 packs per day (3.75 pack-years), and currently uses chewing tobacco and snuff but has not smoked cigarettes for over 6 years.

Recent diagnostic evaluation included a CT-guided core biopsy of the left upper lobe nodule, which showed a poorly differentiated non-small cell carcinoma with features consistent with squamous cell carcinoma (IHC: p40 positive, TTF-1 negative). Tumor PD-L1 testing is pending. PET/CT demonstrated a hypermetabolic left upper lobe nodule (max SUV 10.8), with an increase in size to 2.1 cm from prior scans, without convincing evidence of metastatic disease elsewhere. Mildly increased activity was seen in the hilar regions, but endobronchial ultrasound with transbronchial needle aspirations of bilateral hilar and subcarinal lymph nodes were negative for malignancy. Serial imaging showed no evidence of extrathoracic spread and no new pulmonary lesions. Recent CT showed central scarring and resolution of the previously biopsied mass, with persistent left perihilar changes and interval development of right lower lobe opacities concerning for possible pneumonia, which resolved after treatment. There have been multiple missed follow-up appointments, which delayed staging, and the patient endorsed anxiety about medical testing.

She was previously seen by thoracic surgery but declined surgical intervention after a multidisciplinary discussion, preferring non-surgical management. She subsequently met with radiation oncology and agreed to proceed with stereotactic body radiation therapy to the primary pulmonary lesion. **SUBJECTIVE**

**Reason for Consultation:**  
Patient referred for evaluation and management of incidentally discovered lung nodule.

**History of Present Illness:**  
The patient is a 72-year-old male with a significant past medical history of tobacco use (quit in the 1990s, prior pack-per-day for multiple decades), chronic cough, benign prostatic hyperplasia with urinary retention, prediabetes, hypercholesterolemia, and a history of bladder cancer s/p TURBT and intravesical BCG (currently in remission). He was initially evaluated after persistent cough led to imaging, which revealed a left upper lobe (LUL) spiculated pulmonary nodule. Review of prior imaging noted enlarging characteristics and PET scan (performed at Aga [Deid: Name] University Hospital) demonstrated avidity with an SUVmax of 5.6. A right upper lobe (RUL) nodular infiltrate was also metabolically active.

The patient’s chronic cough (present for over 20 years) had recently worsened, prompting urgent care visitation and initial workup. The cough has since returned to baseline and is not currently problematic. He denies hemoptysis, weight loss, night sweats, or systemic symptoms. He is currently in his usual health, ambulates independently, and denies new shortness of breath, chest pain, or exertional limitations.

He has not had prior lung cancer, and there is no family history of lung malignancy. He has no known environmental exposures other than previous tobacco use. He does not currently use tobacco, alcohol, or recreational drugs.

**ROS:**  
- Constitutional: No fevers, chills, night sweats, or weight loss.  
- Respiratory: Mild chronic cough, no hemoptysis, no dyspnea.  
- Cardiovascular: No chest pain or palpitations.  
- GI: No nausea, vomiting, or change in bowel habits.  
- GU: Baseline urinary symptoms, unchanged.  
- Neurologic: No new neurologic deficits.  
- Skin: No rashes or lesions.  
All other systems reviewed and negative.

**Allergies:**  
No known drug allergies.

- Amlodipine 10 mg daily  
- Valsartan 40 mg daily  
- Atorvastatin 40 mg daily  
- Aspirin 81 mg daily  
- Omeprazole 40 mg daily as needed  
- Finasteride 5 mg daily  
- Oxybutynin XL 10 mg daily  
- Sennosides-docusate 1-3 tablets twice daily as needed  
- Acetaminophen 1000 mg four times daily (as needed)  
- Hydromorphone 0.5–1 mg every 3 hours as needed (post-op)  
- Ibuprofen 600 mg four times daily as needed  
Other PRN and supportive agents as documented.

**Past Medical History:**  
- Bladder cancer s/p TURBT, BCG (remission)  
- BPH with urinary obstruction  
- Adenocarcinoma of lung, left (see below)  
- Persistent pancreatic cystic lesion (benign, non-malignant on prior workup)  
- Hypercholesterolemia  
- Prediabetes  
- Chronic cough (20+ years, ex-smoker)  
- History of vertigo  
- Diverticulosis  
- Erectile dysfunction  
- H. pylori infection (remote, treated)  
- Positive Mantoux (remote, no evidence of TB on workup)

**Past Surgical History:**  
- Left upper lobectomy and mediastinal lymph node dissection  
- Cystoscopy and transurethral resection of bladder tumor  
- Pancreatic cyst FNA (benign)  
- Right VATS wedge resection  
- Robotic assisted bronchoscopy (ION)  
- Cataract extraction, bilateral  
- Right inguinal hernia repair with mesh

**Social History:**  
- Former smoker, quit 1990s  
- No alcohol or illicit drug use  
- Lives independently, active with ADLs  
- Family: No known lung cancer. Mother died in childbirth (30s), father at 84 (possible liver disease).

---

**OBJECTIVE**

**Vital Signs:**  
BP: 122/74 mmHg (right arm, sitting)  
Pulse: 64 bpm  
Resp: 16 /min  
Height: 1.60 m (5'3")  
Weight: 75.3 kg (166 lbs)  
SpO₂: 98% (room air)  
BMI: 29.4 kg/m²

**General:**  
Well-developed, well-nourished male, not in acute distress.

**HEENT:**  
Normocephalic, atraumatic. Conjunctivae clear. No facial cyanosis.  
Mild chronic changes of periorbital tissue but no acute abnormality.

**Neck:**  
No JVD. Trachea midline. No lymphadenopathy.

**Cardiovascular:**  
Regular rate and rhythm, no murmurs, rubs or gallops.

**Respiratory:**  
Breath sounds clear bilaterally. No rales, wheezes, or rhonchi. Normal effort. No stridor.  
No chest wall tenderness or retractions.

**Lymphatic:**  
No cervical or supraclavicular adenopathy.

**GI:**  
Abdomen soft, non-tender, non-distended, normal bowel sounds.

**GU:**  
No CVA tenderness. Baseline lower urinary symptoms.

**Skin:**  
No rash or lesions.

**Neuro:**  
Alert, oriented, no focal deficits.

---

**LABORATORY AND IMAGING STUDIES**

**Imaging:**  
- Chest X-ray ([DATE: 26320] and [DATE: 26329]): LUL lesion becoming more prominent over time.  
- CT Chest ([DATE: 26439]): Spiculated LUL nodule 1.8 x 1.4 cm, ill-defined nodular RUL opacity 1.2 cm, persistent pancreatic lesion (biopsy negative for malignancy).  
- PET scan ([DATE: 26358]): 2 cm spiculated LUL nodule with SUVmax 5.6; metabolically active RUL infiltrate.  
- CT Chest ([DATE: 26451]): LUL mass, RUL nodular infiltrate; stable pancreatic cystic lesion.  
- CT and PET reviewed with lung nodule team; imaging reformatted for robotic navigation.

**Procedures:**  
- Robotic assisted bronchoscopy (ION protocol) targeting LUL nodule  
- CT-guided FNA / EBUS as indicated  
- Surgical resection (see below)

**Surgical Findings:**  
- Left upper lobectomy and mediastinal lymph node dissection performed.  
- Pathology: 1.1 cm adenocarcinoma, margins negative, no nodal involvement (N0); right upper lobe wedge resection with benign pathology.

**Labs:**  
- CBC: WNL  
- Basic metabolic panel: Within normal limits  
- LFTs: Notable only for mild elevation in glucose (112–132 mg/dL), due to prediabetes  
- Tumor markers as per prior workup

---

**HOSPITAL COURSE (Selected Events)**

- Underwent left upper lobectomy and mediastinal lymph node dissection for biopsy-proven LUL adenocarcinoma; intra-op and post-op course without major complication.
- Developed facial and periorbital subcutaneous emphysema post-right-sided wedge resection, attributed to difficult intubation and small air leak; managed conservatively with supplemental oxygen, antibiotics, close airway monitoring, and temporary NPO/clear liquids.
- Flexible laryngoscopy: Moderate to severe swelling of the soft palate bilaterally, moderate fullness in the lateral pharynx, but airway widely patent, no mucosal laceration visualized.
- Imaging (CT neck/chest): Extensive, improving subcutaneous emphysema, trace right-sided pneumothorax, apical chest tube in place.
- CXR: No evidence of persistent/recurrent pneumothorax, decreasing subcutaneous emphysema.
- Physical therapy: Tolerated ambulation, pain managed with acetaminophen, ibuprofen, and low-dose narcotics PRN.
- No evidence of post-op infection, no DVT/PE, no acute renal or cardiac events.

---

**OTHER/ADDITIONAL FINDINGS**

- Pancreatic cystic lesion stable by imaging; no symptoms of pancreatitis, GI bleeding, or malignancy.
- Bladder cancer: Currently in remission, no evidence of recurrence.
- BPH: Stable, managed with medications.

---

**COMMUNICATION / CARE COORDINATION**  
- Case discussed at multidisciplinary tumor board with consensus for initial surgical management and post-operative surveillance.
- Patient and his son designated as primary contacts; patient prefers all detailed information also be shared with his son.
- Patient and son have been updated at each stage and have had all questions addressed.

---

**ADDITIONAL COMMENTS**

- No acute complaints or complications at this time.
- Continues to recover well from thoracic surgery.
- Ambulating independently, tolerating diet as advanced.
- Scheduled for ongoing surveillance and follow-up per institutional protocol.

[Deid: Name] is a 73-year-old male with a significant medical history including type II diabetes mellitus, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, coronary artery disease (status post CABG), obesity (BMI >38), obstructive sleep apnea (CPAP declined), chronic gout, recurrent depression, carotid artery disease, and a remote 81 pack-year smoking history, quit in 1994.

He has been under surveillance for stable bilateral subcentimeter lung nodules. On interval chest CT performed [DATE: 26829] at [Deid: Name] Health, his previously noted left upper lobe groundglass opacity nodule increased in size from 1.3 cm to 1.8 cm with a new solid component (previously 6 mm), raising suspicion for malignancy. No mediastinal lymphadenopathy was identified. Additional stable, benign-appearing bilateral pulmonary nodules noted.

Symptoms at the time of evaluation were absent. He denied cough, hemoptysis, dyspnea, or constitutional symptoms. Functional status at baseline was independently ambulatory, active with hobbies (notably fishing), and no reported limitations in activities of daily living.

**WORKUP AND PREOPERATIVE COURSE:**  
Comprehensive preoperative workup included CT chest and PET imaging, which confirmed a solitary left upper lobe lesion, peripheral in location, with no radiographic evidence of regional or distant metastases. Pulmonary function tests demonstrated adequate reserve for surgical intervention.

Risks, benefits, and alternatives to tissue diagnosis and treatment were reviewed in detail with the patient and his spouse via in-person and virtual consultations. Options including navigational bronchoscopy, CT-guided biopsy, and excisional biopsy by thoracoscopic wedge resection were discussed, with consensus to proceed with the latter for both diagnostic and therapeutic purposes.

**OPERATIVE COURSE:**  
On [DATE: 26856], he underwent left video-assisted thoracoscopic (VAT) wedge resection of the left upper lobe with thoracic lymphadenectomy. The procedure was completed without intraoperative complication. Estimated blood loss was minimal. Intraoperative findings included a relatively superficial, spiculated left upper lobe nodule and otherwise unremarkable pleural surfaces.

**POSTOPERATIVE HOSPITAL COURSE:**  
Postoperative day 1:  
- Alert and oriented ×4, hemodynamically stable, saturating well on room air.  
- Mild-moderate chest wall pain at the thoracoscopy sites, effectively managed with scheduled oral acetaminophen and PRN oxycodone.  
- Chest tube on -20 cm H2O suction, intermittent air leak with cough overnight.
- Ambulated with assistance, transitioned to eating meals out of bed.
- No bowel movement on first postoperative day but passing flatus.

- Pain well controlled, no complaints of dyspnea, actively participating in ambulation.
- Clamp trial performed successfully, no air leak on repeated cough or Valsalva.
- CXR demonstrated small persistent left apical space, chest tube subsequently removed at bedside without complication.
- Patient and spouse reviewed discharge instructions, including wound care, incentive spirometry, activity progression, and signs of complications warranting urgent evaluation.
- Discharged home in stable condition on POD2 with scheduled follow-up.

- Left upper lobe, wedge resection: Adenocarcinoma in situ (AIS), 1.4 cm, with lepidic features. Surgical margins negative. No visceral pleural invasion. No evidence of spread through airspaces. - Lymph node station 5 (subaortic): One benign node, negative for metastatic carcinoma.
- Lymph node station 11L (interlobar): One node with a microscopic cluster (<1 mm) of neuroendocrine-type cells. No mitotic activity. The morphology and size raise the possibility of a well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumor (carcinoid), but the finding is likely incidental; rare benign presentations have been documented in the literature. Additional immunohistochemical analysis was noncontributory due to loss of area of interest in sectioning. No evidence of metastatic carcinoma.
- Pathologic staging: pTis (AIS), pN0, R0 resection.

**POST-HOSPITAL COURSE AND FOLLOW-UP:**  
- Nurse navigator and surgical team conducted phone check-in on [DATE: 26864], confirming continued wound healing, stable respiratory status, and adequate pain control on scheduled acetaminophen and ibuprofen.
- No fevers, chills, increased pain, or skin changes at incision sites. No new pulmonary complaints; incentive spirometer used regularly.
- Patient ambulating, tolerating diet, bowel movements and urination within normal limits. No symptoms concerning for recurrence or complications. Psychological state reported as positive, with strong family support.
- No barriers to ongoing care. Transportation and medication access stable. Patient prefers follow-up imaging and care locally when feasible.

**CONSENSUS FROM MULTIDISCIPLINARY LUNG TUMOR CONFERENCE:**  
- All attending subspecialists (Medical Oncology, Pathology, Pulmonology, Radiation Oncology, Radiology, Research, Clinical Data Abstractor, Surgery, RN Nurse Navigator) reviewed findings and pathology.
- Recommendation: No further therapy is indicated at this time.
- Surveillance to continue with CT chest at 6-month intervals. Radiologic monitoring will include evaluation for both recurrence of adenocarcinoma and stability of the incidental interlobar neuroendocrine cell cluster. No immediate additional workup or intervention for possible carcinoid is required.
- Patient and spouse were contacted after the tumor board to communicate the multidisciplinary consensus, address questions, and provide reassurance regarding the benign nature of the lymph node finding.

**SOCIAL HISTORY:**  
- Married, lives with spouse, independent with ADLs.  
- Former tobacco user (81 pack-year, quit 1994).  
- Drinks alcohol socially, denies illicit drug use.  
- Good social support, not isolated, no reported psychosocial crises.  
- Medication adherence and follow-up have been consistent.

**CURRENT MEDICATIONS:**  
- Cardiometabolic: metformin, ezetimibe-simvastatin, lisinopril, metoprolol
- Aspirin 325 mg daily, furosemide as needed, potassium chloride, magnesium oxide
- Others: albuterol HFA PRN, indomethacin PRN, cholecalciferol, tadalafil PRN, nitroglycerin SL PRN

**ALLERGIES:**  
- Contrast dye (rash, hives), statins (myalgia)

**REVIEW OF SYSTEMS:**  
- Negative except as detailed above

- Vitals: BP 126/60, Pulse 72, SpO2 94%, Temp 98.8°F, BMI 39.4

- Chest/Resp: Well-healed thoracoscopic incisions, clear to auscultation, no dyspnea  
- Cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm, no murmurs  
- Abdomen: Obese, soft, non-tender  
- Extremities: No edema  
- Skin: Incisions clean and dry, minimal drainage after suture removal  
- Neuro: Alert, oriented ×4

**LABS AND IMAGING:**

- Most recent post-discharge chest x-ray: Small, stable apical pneumothorax, no acute findings. Postoperative changes as expected.  
- Prior CT chest: No evidence of recurrence or new nodules

- All questions regarding future care to be directed to the multidisciplinary team or the presenting physician.

CHIEF COMPLAINT  
Follow-up and ongoing management of multiple primary lung cancers (NSCLC).

SUBJECTIVE  
The patient is a 71-year-old female with a significant oncologic history, including prior left breast cancer (ER/PR positive, status post lumpectomy and radiation therapy) and right breast cancer (ER/PR negative, HER2 unknown, status post lumpectomy and adjuvant chemotherapy), and subsequent recurrent left breast cancer (status post bilateral mastectomy, completed 3/4 planned cycles of adjuvant TC, declined endocrine therapy). Patient has a background history of hypothyroidism, idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura, and prior anemia associated with neoplastic disease.

The patient was lost to oncology follow-up but returned to care after developing persistent right shoulder and upper chest wall discomfort. She noted progressive right shoulder and rib pain, associated with intermittent numbness radiating down the right arm, without weakness. Patient has also reported moderate fatigue, reduced appetite initially, and weight loss over several weeks, but with some improvement in appetite since starting treatment. She denies fevers or night sweats. No new skin changes or palpable new lymphadenopathy reported.

She continues to live independently and is able to perform all ADLs and IADLs without assistance. She works full-time and intends to remain at work as tolerated. She is supported by her two daughters and a sister, all now aware of the diagnosis and prognosis.

She has a longstanding history of daily tobacco use (3–4 cigarettes/day), and drinks 2–3 glasses of wine per week socially. Denies illicit drug use.

OBJECTIVE  
**Vital Signs**  
BP: 130/72 mmHg | Pulse: 88 bpm | Temp: 97.7°F | Respirations: 16 | SpO₂: 98% | Weight: 61.7 kg | BMI: 23.3 kg/m²  
No weight change over the past week.

Pleasant, well-appearing female, in no acute distress.

Normocephalic, atraumatic. Sclera anicteric, conjunctivae without pallor. Oral mucosa moist, no lesions.

Supple. Mildly prominent right supraclavicular soft tissue mass, approximately 6 cm, intact overlying skin.

Unlabored respirations. Decreased air entry at right upper and posterior lung fields. Dullness to percussion at right base. No increased work of breathing.

Regular rate and rhythm. No murmurs, rubs or gallops.

Soft, non-tender, non-distended. Bowel sounds present. No hepatosplenomegaly, no rebound or guarding.

Right supraclavicular and anterior chest wall mass palpable. No significant cervical or axillary adenopathy.

**Extremities**  
No cyanosis, edema, or clubbing. Full muscle strength in all limbs.

Alert, oriented x3. Speech clear. No focal deficits. Reports intermittent numbness in right upper extremity, no motor weakness.

**Psychiatric**  
Normal affect. Appropriate mood and judgment.

**Skin**  
Right upper back palpable 3 cm subcutaneous mass over trapezius, unchanged.

**Performance Status**  
ECOG 0–1; fully ambulatory, able to work, minor symptoms.

**RECENT IMAGING**  
- CT chest/abdomen/pelvis: Large right apical lung mass (8.7 x 6.4 x 7.3 cm) extending into the right chest wall and involving right first and second ribs. Multiple right lung nodules, extensive right chest wall and intrathoracic lymphadenopathy, trace right pleural effusion, indeterminate right hepatic lesion, 4.6 cm infrarenal AAA.
- PET scan: FDG-avid right apical mass and involved lymph nodes, with additional possible hypermetabolic lesions in pancreas head and peritoneal nodules.
- CT-guided biopsy of right lung: Confirmed small cell carcinoma (high-grade neuroendocrine carcinoma).
- Brain CT: Two enhancing metastatic lesions—left temporal lobe (13 x 15 x 15 mm) and subependymal margin of left lateral ventricle (8 x 6 x 10 mm)—places patient at risk of CSF dissemination.

ALT: 10 IU/L | AST: 24 IU/L | AlkPhos: 78 IU/L  
Calcium: 10.4 mg/dL  
TSH: 4.23 mIU/L  
HBV labs: Non-reactive

- acetaminophen 500 mg q6h PRN  
- b complex vitamins 1 qd  
- cholecalciferol (Vitamin D3) 2000 units qd  
- levothyroxine 112 mcg qd  
- pravastatin 10 mg qd  
- riboflavin 200 mg qd  
- dexamethasone 8 mg qd on days 2–4 of cycles  
- lorazepam 0.5 mg q6h PRN  
- meclizine 12.5 mg tid PRN

- ondansetron 8 mg q8h PRN

- scopolamine patch

- Initial cycles administered via PIV access; transitioned to port once placed and healed.

- Lives alone; has strong support from two daughters and a sister, who are now fully informed and involved in care planning.

- Remains highly engaged in her care, has questions answered, and attended all required education.  
- Expressed some anxiety regarding imaging (claustrophobia/BMI brain), using lorazepam pre-scan as needed.  
- Reported ongoing efforts to coordinate radiation oncology care at a facility within insurance network; expressed concerns regarding logistics for transport and scheduling, particularly in context of her employment.

- Idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura  
- Anemia in neoplastic disease

- Breast cancer — paternal aunt  
- Kidney cancer — father and brother  
- Prostate cancer — brother  
- Thyroid cancer — sister  
- Hyperthyroidism — daughter

- Social alcohol use: 2–3 glasses wine/week  
- Denies illicit drugs

- ECOG 0–1  
- Independent in ADLs/IADLs  
- Working full-time  
- PROMI Total Score: 20

**EDUCATION & SUPPORT**  
- Comprehensive chemotherapy education review provided, including medication sheets for all planned agents, side-effect management, dietary recommendations, and MyChart access.  
- Appointment calendar, after-visit summaries, and contact information for triage nurse and navigator given.  
- Encouraged participation in cancer support group.

**INFUSION/THERAPY VISIT LOGS (SUMMARY)**  
- Treatment administered according to calculated doses, pre-treatment verification with positive blood return and appropriate drug checks.

**[CLINICAL NOTE — UNSTRUCTURED PHYSICIAN PROGRESS NOTE]**

Patient: [Deid: Name]  
MRN: [Deid: MRN]  
Date of service: [DATE: 31441]  
Location: Inpatient — Cardiothoracic Surgery Service

**SUBJECTIVE:**

[Deid: Name] is an 86-year-old woman with a history of hypertension, prediabetes, hyperlipidemia, osteopenia, age-related macular degeneration, urge incontinence, prior melanoma, and squamous cell carcinoma of the skin. She is a retired office worker and a former smoker (15 pack-years, quit over 35 years ago). She is widowed and lives alone; her daughter is present and actively involved in her care. Baseline functional status is independent with ADLs; she remains physically active (cuts her own grass, walks daily, does laundry for her children).

She was noted to have a cough and exertional shortness of breath with a non-contrast chest CT showing a 3.2 cm mixed solid and groundglass nodule in the right lower lobe, concerning for primary malignancy. Additional work-up with PET-CT demonstrated mild FDG avidity (SUVmax 2.3), without evidence of metastatic disease. Pulmonary function tests and pre-operative assessment were within acceptable limits for surgery.

She subsequently underwent right video-assisted thoracoscopic (VAT) right lower lobectomy with mediastinal lymph node dissection, with placement of a chest tube to water seal. No intraoperative complications were noted. Pathology revealed a stage IA (peripheral) lung adenocarcinoma, margins negative, no nodal involvement.

Her post-operative course has been notable for right-sided chest incisional pain, especially with movement and deep inspiration. She describes the pain as sharp and sometimes radiating to the right shoulder, improving at rest. Pain has been managed primarily with scheduled acetaminophen and as needed ibuprofen and dilaudid; an OnQ pain pump remains in place. The family has requested additional support with overnight pain. No complaints of shortness of breath at rest. Mild exertional dyspnea with ambulation around the nursing unit, without hypoxia.

She is otherwise tolerating a regular diet, with no nausea or vomiting. Bowel movements are regular; voiding independently in the bathroom. Denies fever, chills, cough, increased sputum, hematuria, or new neurologic complaints.

**OBJECTIVE:**

**Vital Signs:**  
BP: 126/64 RA, P: 72, T: 97.8°F (oral), RR: 20, SpO2: 96% on room air  
Weight: 64 kg

**General:**  
Alert and oriented x4. Ambulates with standby assist. Daughter at bedside.

**Chest:**  
Incision from thoracotomy and chest tube healing well; dressing clean, dry, and intact. No erythema, drainage, or crepitus. Occasional crackles at right base, clear with cough and deep inspiration. Good air entry bilaterally. Mild tenderness at surgical site. Incentive spirometry in use with encouragement.

**Cardiovascular:**  
Regular rate and rhythm. No murmurs.

**Abdomen:**  
Soft, non-tender, no distention, normal bowel sounds.

**Musculoskeletal:**  
Moves all extremities. Increased pain with right arm elevation; otherwise full strength. Up with assist x1; walked 150 feet with therapy today.

**Skin:**  
No breakdown. Incision sites intact. Bed alarm on for safety.

**Lines/drains:**  
Right chest tube to water seal, intermittent air leak noted. No evidence of obstruction or malfunction. Output in the last 8 hours: serosanguinous, 130 mL. Clamped at midnight per protocol for CXR, then reopened. OnQ pump in place.

**Intake/Output:**  
Oral intake adequate. Voiding independently; purewick used overnight.

**Labs/Imaging:**  
Pending morning CXR post-unclamp. No new lab abnormalities.

**Medications:**  
Reviewed and reconciled. Taking acetaminophen (scheduled), ibuprofen (PRN), hydromorphone (PRN), enalapril, simvastatin, multivitamin, calcium carbonate, Restasis, cyanocobalamin, CO Q-10, aspirin, vitamin D, and sennosides/docusate PRN.

**FUNCTIONAL STATUS:**  
Getting up with assist to chair and ambulating in the hallway with therapy. Occupational therapy and physical therapy involved; working on mobility, incentive spirometry, and basic ADLs.

**Safety:**  
Bed alarm engaged. Call light within reach. Family assisting with ambulation.

**NURSING FOCUS:**  
Pain controlled except with movement; able to rest. Diet tolerated. Goals for next shift: improved sleep, pain management, encouragement of activity, and continued use of incentive spirometry.

**DISCHARGE PLANNING:**  
No barriers anticipated if pain controlled and chest tube can be discontinued. Daughter remains primary support. Awaiting further evaluation for removal of chest tube.

---

**[END OF NOTE]**

Mother: hypertension (deceased age 36, pregnancy complication)

INTEGRATIVE HEALTH & HEALING CONSULT NOTE

Consult Date: [DATE]

Consultant: [Deid: Name], Integrative Medicine Provider  
Referring Service: Thoracic Surgery / Oncology

SUBJECTIVE:

The patient is a 59-year-old woman, recently admitted post-robotic-assisted right lower lobe superior segmentectomy and thoracic lymphadenectomy for invasive adenocarcinoma (acinar type) of the right lower lobe. She is recovering postoperatively, now post-op day 4. She remains concerned about pain management and the healing process, and has ongoing anxiety regarding her recent atrial fibrillation episode. She expresses significant emotional stress over learning her health insurance coverage will soon lapse. She lives alone in an apartment and her sister, previously a planned support person, cannot visit due to recent COVID exposure. Patient voiced worry about having visitors during the pandemic and expressed a desire for additional support and self-care education to facilitate her recovery and coping during this challenging time.

Patient goals for today’s session include learning practical skills for managing post-surgical symptoms (pain, gas, bowel function), reducing fear around movement, and exploring mind-body techniques for anxiety and coping. She is interested in learning more about acupuncture as a future supportive therapy.

OBJECTIVE:

Mental/Emotional:  
Patient appears alert, oriented, and engaged throughout the visit. Tearful at times when discussing insurance and cardiac issues, but asks clear, insightful questions and demonstrates motivation to participate in her own healing and recovery.

Physical:  
Sitting up in bed at the time of consultation. Pain reported over anterior VAT incision, described as controlled with current medications (notably Percocet and scheduled Toradol), but persists particularly with movement. Chest tube sites free of drainage, dressed appropriately, and healing as expected. Incentive spirometry use demonstrated. No shortness of breath at rest; mild exertional dyspnea with activity but able to perform incentive spirometry, ambulation, and basic self-care as tolerated. Bowels moving, voiding spontaneously. Appetite is intact; tolerating diet.

Integrative Interventions Performed:  
- Education provided on supportive self-care techniques, including instruction in abdominal self-massage (for 5 minutes per session, several times daily as needed; three different techniques reviewed to assist with bowel function and passing gas, with emphasis on using left lateral decubitus position and pillow support to optimize comfort and muscle relaxation).  
- Guidance provided on warm fluid intake to aid bowel function and overall healing.  
- Detailed coaching on breathing techniques to reduce anxiety and facilitate safe, confident movement (focus on “relaxation breaths”—inhalation through nose, exhalation through mouth, noticing temperature/moisture change; coached on synchronizing breath with movement for transitions, especially getting out of bed).  
- Counseling on positioning/posture to ease postoperative pain and gas (left side with joint alignment and pillow positioning demonstrated; knees drawn up toward abdomen to facilitate gas passage).  
- Mind-body strategies utilizing breathwork to address fear of pain during activity and encourage safe mobilization.  
- Reflective listening and supportive dialogue targeting patient’s coping, anxiety, and feelings of being overwhelmed.  
- Provided information regarding the process and expected timeframe for placement of an acupuncture order; encouraged patient to discuss interest in acupuncture therapy with her medical team for ongoing supportive care.

PRE-THERAPEUTIC SESSION SCORES:  
- Pain: 6 (0–10 scale)  
- Anxiety: Not rated  
- Nausea: Not rated  
- Ability to Cope: Not rated

POST-THERAPEUTIC SESSION SCORES:  
- Pain: 6 (0–10 scale)  
- Anxiety: Not rated  
- Nausea: Not rated  
- Ability to Cope: Not rated

MODALITIES UTILIZED:  
- Education: Integrative health overview, self-care strategies for bowel function and gas, safe activity and positioning, pain management tips.  
- Mind-Body: Breathwork for relaxation and movement, reflective listening, psychoeducation for coping and empowerment.

ADDITIONAL FINDINGS/FOLLOW-UP:

Discussed patient’s insurance concerns and provided resources for connection to the cancer social worker, legal assistance, and local support organizations. Patient encouraged to practice self-care tools, monitor for changes in pain or well-being, and advocate for further supportive therapies (i.e. acupuncture) as appropriate. She verbalized understanding of all instructions and demonstrated ability to repeat and clarify techniques taught during the session.

[DATE: 24270]

Present: [Deid: Name] here with her husband, [Deid: Name], for follow up following recent navigational bronchoscopy and biopsy. They met with [Deid: Name], thoracic surgery, to review recent biopsy findings and discuss the next steps in care.

Referred by: [Deid: Name], [Deid: Name]

**Patient Story:**  
66-year-old female with a remote history of stage IIIA NSCLC of the left upper lobe, previously treated with left upper lobectomy (done [DATE: 23088]) and adjuvant chemotherapy and immunotherapy (immunotherapy stopped early due to intolerance), now presenting for evaluation of an enlarging right lower lobe pulmonary nodule and multiple stable left lower lobe ground glass opacities.

She resides with her husband in St [Deid: Name], MN. She is a retired salesperson and has two adult children. She is a former smoker (quit 1996; 1.5 packs/day for 20 years).

**Recent Evaluations:**
- Imaging:  
  - PET/CT and chest CT ([DATE: 24248]): Showed a solid spiculated nodule in the medial right lower lobe (1.4 x 0.8 cm, Max SUV 1.9). Left lower lobe with multiple ground glass nodules (largest 1.1 x 0.7 cm, Max SUV 2.1). No evidence for distant metastases.
  - MRI brain: No evidence of metastatic disease.
  - Prior serial CTs: Right lower lobe nodule increased from 3 mm to 7 mm over sequential scans, now 1.4 cm.

- Bronchoscopy and EBUS ([DATE: 24264]):  
  - Right lower lobe nodule: Cytology positive for adenocarcinoma, pulmonary primary.  
  - Mediastinal/hilar lymph nodes (stations 4R, 7, 11R): All negative for malignancy.

- Pulmonary function ([DATE: 24241]): FEV1 1.63 L (80% predicted), DLCO 110% predicted.

**Diagnostic Summary:**
- New diagnosis: Biopsy-proven right lower lobe lung adenocarcinoma, clinical stage IA2 (cT1b cN0 cM0), no metastatic disease.
- Multiple subcentimeter ground glass opacities in left lower lobe, indolent on surveillance, without significant interval change; likely multifocal adenocarcinoma.

**Psycho-social/Support:**  
She reports good family support. She and her husband express understanding and are attentive, asking questions regarding the care trajectory. No dietary concerns; patient is well nourished.

- Attended thoracic surgical consult with patient and spouse; supported clarification of current clinical status and next steps.
- Provided education regarding the diagnosis, the rationale for further surgery, and the importance of mediastinal nodal sampling.
- Reviewed preoperative measures, including incentive spirometry, activity expectations, pain management, and wound care as well as the risks and steps of the planned lung surgery (right lower lobe resection).
- Supplied printed educational materials (Your Lung Care book, bronchoscopy education, Lung Program team contacts).
- Emotional support and transition planning reinforced. Patient instructed to call with any new or worsening symptoms.
- Encouraged review of provided materials and written preparation of questions ahead of the operative appointment.
- Confirmed understanding of teaching and plan.

**Materials Given:**  
- AV material  
- Bronchoscopy book  
- Contact information for Lung Program Team

**Education Provided:**  
- Explained the importance of understanding the diagnosis and available treatment options, including surgery vs. non-surgical options.  
- Outlined postoperative course, including monitoring for complications and expected recovery steps.
- Oriented patient and family to community resources and team approach.  
- Encouraged discussion of goals and personal preferences as decision-making continues.

**Follow-Up:**  
- Surgery scheduled for [DATE: 24282]: Flexible bronchoscopy, right VAT, right lower lobe resection, mediastinal lymphadenectomy, possible thoracotomy.  
- Will check in prior to and after surgery regarding progress, needs, and questions.
- Provided direct contact information for further support.

raw_note:
Clinical Note

SUBJECTIVE:
66-year-old male with chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) and a history of low back pain, Bell's palsy, and recurrent Clostridioides difficile colitis. He has a significant tobacco history but quit over 2 years ago. He is married and lives with his wife. He was referred for evaluation after an enlarging left upper lobe pulmonary nodule was identified on routine surveillance imaging. The patient denies baseline shortness of breath with mild exertion and has no prior history of primary lung cancer.

He underwent needle biopsy in February, which was non-diagnostic. Over subsequent months, the lesion increased in size. He has not reported recent hemoptysis or significant new cough, but has experienced intermittent chest pain over his left ribs and occasional heartburn. He denies dysphagia, dysphonia, or unexplained weight loss. His appetite has been somewhat decreased in the setting of recent infection and treatment side effects but has remained stable. He does endorse fatigue, which he attributes to his chronic illness and recent chemotherapy.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION:
General: Well-developed, well-nourished male, sitting comfortably in the exam chair.
Vital Signs: BP 120/73 mmHg, Pulse 99, Temp 97.8 °F, RR 16, O2 Sat 94% on room air, Height 1.75 m, Weight 79.3 kg, BMI 25.8.
HEENT: Normocephalic, mucous membranes moist, oropharynx clear, no exudates. No cervical adenopathy.
Lungs: Breath sounds diminished on the left, otherwise clear. No crackles or wheezes. Occasional productive cough with light-colored sputum.
Heart: Regular rate and rhythm, no murmurs. Extremities warm and dry. No edema.
Abdomen: Soft, non-tender, non-distended. Bowel sounds present. Negative for hepatosplenomegaly.
Skin: Incisions well approximated, no drainage. One incision with mild, stable erythema. No tenderness or warmth.
Neurologic: Alert and oriented x3. No focal deficits. Moves all extremities.
Musculoskeletal: Moves independently in the room. Up at bedside. Chronic low back pain reported but no acute findings.

HOSPITAL COURSE/PROCEDURES:
Patient was admitted for further evaluation, and a preoperative clinical assessment was completed. He was given educational materials about his upcoming surgery, including details about the anticipated length of stay, surgical approach (robotic), expected use of a chest tube, and post-op expectations.

He proceeded to robotic-assisted wedge resection and left upper lobectomy with mediastinal lymph node dissection. Intraoperative findings included no gross evidence of metastatic disease, and all sampled mediastinal nodes were removed where feasible. The procedure was well tolerated. Postoperatively, the patient was monitored in a step-down unit with a chest tube to suction.

On post-op day 1, the patient reported only mild chest pain at the surgical site, controlled with oxycodone-acetaminophen as needed. Pain rated 7–8/10 at worst, with adequate relief from scheduled and PRN doses. He was afebrile and breathing comfortably on room air, with oxygen saturation in the mid-90s. He experienced mild dyspnea on exertion but was able to sit up and ambulate short distances.

Incisional healing was appropriate, with no signs of infection. There was minimal serous output from the chest tube, no air leak, and daily imaging demonstrated expected postoperative changes with early volume loss of the left lung but no pneumothorax or significant effusion.

Lab monitoring revealed a stable hemoglobin in the low 12s, white count mildly decreased but stable, and normal renal function. Hyponatremia improved with hydration. No evidence of acute infection postoperatively.

The chest tube was converted to water seal and subsequently removed after interval imaging remained stable. The patient was encouraged to perform deep breathing exercises and was monitored for early complications (e.g., pneumonia, incisional infection).

PATHOLOGY:
Surgical pathology demonstrated non-mucinous adenocarcinoma of the left upper lobe with negative surgical margins. Hilar and sampled mediastinal lymph nodes were negative for metastatic carcinoma. Final pathologic stage: pT2aN0.

MOLECULAR/BIOMARKER TESTING:
Tissue sent for broad molecular profiling including EGFR, ALK, ROS1, BRAF, KRAS, MET, RET, and NTRK, as well as PD-L1 immunohistochemistry.

SURVEILLANCE AND OUTPATIENT FOLLOW-UP:
Following discharge, the patient was monitored closely in the outpatient setting. He reported ongoing but improving chest wall pain, managed with acetaminophen and low-dose oxycodone as needed. He has had no fevers, chills, or sweats. His surgical wounds continued to heal without complication, and he resumed light activities at home. He did not report new respiratory symptoms. No edema or signs of heart failure observed. He developed short-term heartburn and was treated with OTC antacid.

He was seen in telephone follow-up and in-person clinics for routine post-operative surveillance. He remained afebrile, maintained oxygen saturations >95% on room air, and noted continued improvement in functional status and energy. He was counseled regarding the importance of reporting new or worsening symptoms in the future.

ROUTINE IMAGING:
At scheduled intervals, CT imaging of the chest was obtained and showed expected post-lobectomy changes, with no new pulmonary nodules, masses, or evidence of recurrence. No locoregional or distant metastases were identified.

EDUCATION & SUPPORT:
Patient and his wife received education regarding recovery, symptom management, and the plan for ongoing surveillance. Dietary assessment revealed adequate oral intake with occasional use of nutritional supplements. Community and home resources were discussed and arranged as appropriate.

MEDICATIONS:
- Oxycodone-acetaminophen 5-325 mg, 1 tablet q6h as needed for pain
- Gabapentin 100 mg TID for neuropathic pain
- Acetaminophen 1,000 mg TID as needed
- Famotidine 20 mg BID for gastric protection
- Sennosides with docusate for constipation prn

ALLERGIES:
- NSAIDs: Itching and flushing
- Ibuprofen: Itching

SOCIAL HISTORY:
- Former smoker, quit >2 years ago, estimated 30 pack-years
- Occasional alcohol use, no illicit drugs
- Married, living at home with spouse
- Previously employed, now retired due to back issues

FUNCTIONAL STATUS:
Ambulates independently, performing light activities at home. No new falls. Continues to work with home nursing as needed for wound checks and symptom monitoring.

LABS (representative):
- CBC: WBC 5.1, Hgb 12.6, Plt 298
- Lytes: Na 135, K 4.1, Cl 101, CO2 22, Cr 0.8
- LFTs: Within normal limits
- Albumin: Stable
- Glucose: Mildly elevated at times

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS:
- General: Mild fatigue, no acute distress
- Skin: Incisions healing, no rash
- Pulmonary: Mild dyspnea with exertion, no cough or hemoptysis
- Cardiovascular: No chest pain, no edema
- GI: Tolerating oral intake, no nausea or vomiting, had heartburn
- GU: No dysuria
- Neurological: No focal deficits
- Musculoskeletal: Baseline chronic low back pain, no new issues
- Psychiatric: Mood and affect normal

Patient has demonstrated understanding of his postoperative course and surveillance plan, and his questions were addressed satisfactorily. He was encouraged to report any new or concerning symptoms and maintains regular follow-up with the lung program team and primary care.

[Deid:Location] Regional Medical Center

PULMONARY & CRITICAL CARE ASSOCIATES  
PROGRESS NOTE  
Date of encounter: [DATE: 29690]  

Chief Complaint  
Patient presents for re-evaluation of metastatic non-small cell lung cancer – adenocarcinoma, left upper lobe primary, with known metastases.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS  
[Deid: Name] is an 81-year-old male with a history of atrial fibrillation on anticoagulation, COPD with severe obstruction, hypertension, extensive 90 pack-year tobacco use, and hyperlipidemia. He was initially diagnosed with a left upper lobe well-differentiated adenocarcinoma after presenting with bilateral upper lobe nodules and cough. Initial PET imaging showed metabolically active, irregular, spiculated nodules in both upper lobes, and he subsequently underwent bronchoscopy with cryobiopsy. Pathology confirmed well-differentiated adenocarcinoma in the left upper lobe, while right upper lobe sampling was benign.

He was considered inoperable due to severe underlying COPD and underwent stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT) to the left upper lobe primary (50 Gy in 5 fractions, completed [DATE: 29496]). Follow-up chest CTs demonstrated a decrease in size of the treated LUL lesion and stability of the right upper lobe nodule, with no evidence of regional progression. Over the past several months, the patient has developed mild left pleural effusion and increased cough with congestion, but no hemoptysis, fever, or weight loss. He continues to smoke, albeit at a reduced rate, and remains noncompliant with recommended pharmacologic cessation aids due to cost.

Serial imaging revealed the presence of a 14 x 10 x 12 mm spiculated subpleural nodule at the left lung apex (previously up to 16 mm), and a stable right apical nodule measuring 2.4 cm, without new intrathoracic or extrathoracic lesions. Mediastinal and hilar lymphadenopathy has not emerged. Recent PET/CT did not show suspicious metastatic lesions elsewhere. The patient has experienced progressive fatigue and lower extremity edema, without any significant cardiopulmonary complaints. Mildly increased cough and respiratory congestion have been noted, with scattered wheezes and rhonchi on lung auscultation.

He continues long-acting inhaled therapy (tiotropium-olodaterol), roflumilast, and as-needed albuterol; he recently completed a 5-day course of azithromycin and prednisone for presumed COPD exacerbation. **Oncology Clinic Progress Note**

**Chief Complaint:**  
Follow-up evaluation for advanced lung cancer

**History of Present Illness:**  
Mr. [Deid: Name] is a 75-year-old Caucasian male with a recent diagnosis of stage IV lung adenocarcinoma, initially presenting several months ago with persistent cough and progressive dysphagia. Over a period of two months, he experienced approximately 30–40 lbs of unintentional weight loss, primarily attributed to inability to tolerate solid foods and, later, most liquids. He was admitted for further evaluation and underwent EGD revealing extrinsic compression of the distal esophagus along with subsequent imaging showing a right lower lobe cavitary lung mass and bulky mediastinal lymphadenopathy. There was additional evidence of osseous involvement at the T9 vertebral body without cord compromise on MRI, as well as two small asymptomatic brain lesions on initial brain MRI.

He underwent bronchoscopy with EBUS and biopsy, which confirmed large cell carcinoma with features of adenocarcinoma (positive cytology, FoundationOne CDx sent, and PD-L1 0%). No actionable driver mutation was detected. Due to ongoing dysphagia and progressive malnutrition, a PEG tube was placed for enteral feeding.

He received palliative radiotherapy to the T9 vertebra and began systemic therapy with carboplatin, pemetrexed, and pembrolizumab. The course was complicated by a severe grade 3 skin rash and worsening dyspnea. Imaging following treatment revealed increased patchy pulmonary consolidation suspicious for lymphangitic spread rather than infection or radiation pneumonitis. He developed persistent exertional dyspnea and hypoxia requiring home oxygen, and has become increasingly frail, with an ECOG performance status now estimated at 3. Chief Complaint:
Follow-up for metastatic non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), squamous cell subtype, stage IV (oligometastatic). Review of interval history and status post initiation of systemic therapy.

History of Present Illness:
[Deid: Name] is an 86-year-old man with a complex cardiac and medical history including severe symptomatic aortic stenosis (trileaflet, heavily calcified, severe), coronary artery disease with prior MI and PCI to OM1, hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, history of melanoma (excised 1980), chronic kidney disease stage 3, and COPD. He initially presented with progressive exertional dyspnea, fatigue, and intermittent left anterior chest pain.

Work-up for TAVR revealed a left upper lobe lung mass (initially 5.9 x 4.9 cm) and a separate right upper lobe spiculated nodule (1.2 x 0.9 cm). PET/CT demonstrated an intensely FDG-avid left upper lobe mass (SUVmax 15.5, centrally necrotic, 6.1 cm), highly suspicious right upper lobe nodule (SUVmax 14.0), and no pathologic lymphadenopathy or distant visceral metastases. Also noted was focal rectal wall hypermetabolism (history of prior adenomatous polyps, recent negative high-grade malignancy on colonoscopy). There was a hospitalization for RSV shortly after staging, resulting in acute weight loss and deconditioning; he has regained most of the lost weight since that time.

CT-guided biopsy of the left upper lobe lesion confirmed moderately differentiated squamous cell carcinoma (PD-L1 <1%, broad-NGS negative for actionable mutations). MRI of the brain was negative for metastasis. The right lung nodule has not been biopsied but remains unchanged in size and is considered suspicious for a second primary or limited metastatic disease. Multidisciplinary conference consensus was that the dominant left upper lobe lesion rendered him surgically inoperable, largely due to cardiac risk and poor pulmonary reserve.

He is accompanied to visits by his wife and daughter, who assist with appointments and care coordination. He remains at home, ambulates short distances with standby assist, and uses a wheelchair for longer distances. CLINICAL NOTE

SUBJECTIVE:  
The patient is a 67-year-old woman with a history of generalized anxiety disorder (GAD), emphysema/COPD, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and narcolepsy, presenting for hospital follow-up and ongoing care following right lower lobe lobectomy and mediastinal lymph node dissection for recently diagnosed right lower lobe adenocarcinoma. She was initially detected to have a pulmonary nodule on routine CT, with further work-up (including PET-CT and navigational bronchoscopy) confirming stage IA (pT1bN0) peripheral mucinous adenocarcinoma. She underwent a successful robotic-assisted thoracoscopic right lower lobectomy with mediastinal nodal sampling. Pathology demonstrated 1.3cm mucinous adenocarcinoma, margins negative, no nodal involvement. No adjuvant therapy was recommended postoperatively.

She is post-operative day 4 from surgery. Since discharge, the patient reports gradual improvement in breathing but continues to notice some shortness of breath with exertion, especially when ambulating or performing household tasks. She uses supplemental oxygen intermittently, mainly with activity, and is weaning down from continuous home use; resting SpO2 at home ranges from 93–96% on room air. She denies new or worsening cough, hemoptysis, fever, or chills. She has minimal to no pain at her incisional sites, controlled with scheduled acetaminophen and only rare use of dilaudid, and she rates her pain as 2–3/10 at rest. She ambulates independently, has resumed light activities at home, and reports normal appetite and bowel function.

She quit smoking at the time of diagnosis; she admits to rare cravings and has “taken a puff” on occasion but is motivated to remain abstinent. No recent hospitalizations or urgent care visits. She has not had any new chest pain, palpitations, orthopnea, PND, or lower extremity swelling. No symptoms suggestive of infection or respiratory exacerbation. No substantial challenges with mood or anxiety, though she has intermittent worries regarding prognosis and recurrence.

OBJECTIVE:  
Vital Signs:
- BP: 124/68
- Pulse: 93
- Temperature: 97.9°F

- Neurologic: Oriented x3, normal strength and sensation in all extremities.
- Psychiatric: Euthymic, appropriate affect, good eye contact, logical thought process.

Review of Recent Results:
- Surgical pathology: pT1bN0 (Stage IA) mucinous adenocarcinoma, margins negative, no lymphovascular invasion, no nodal metastasis.
- Labs: Stable CBC and chemistries.
- Recent chest x-ray: Interval improvement in post-surgical changes, no evidence of pneumothorax, stable elevation of right hemidiaphragm, clear left lung.
- Pulmonary function testing (PFT, post-op): Moderate obstructive ventilatory defect, FEV1 1.4L (78% predicted), DLCO 87% predicted, no significant bronchodilator response; no restrictive defect.

Medications:
- Acetaminophen 1,000mg PO q6h
- Gabapentin 100mg PO TID
- Hydromorphone 2mg PO q6h PRN
- Albuterol HFA inhaler PRN
- Losartan 25mg PO daily
- Atorvastatin 20mg PO at bedtime

- Calcium with vitamin D3 1 tab daily
- Oxygen: 1-2L NC as needed

- Reports independence with self-care and activities of daily living, with mild shortness of breath during exertion, but improvement over time.

Patient is a 75-year-old male presenting as a new patient, referred for evaluation and management of recently diagnosed locally advanced non-small cell lung cancer. Chief complaint at initial visit was intermittent chest pain, without associated shortness of breath, cough, hemoptysis, or constitutional symptoms. The majority of the history was obtained from the patient's wife, who reports the patient was diagnosed with lung cancer after an abnormal chest CT and PET scan performed at an outside facility. The exact stage and histologic subtype were initially unclear, but the referring records suggested involvement of mediastinal lymph nodes. There is no history of prior lung resections, and the patient has not received chemotherapy or radiation to the chest.

Past medical history is significant for longstanding COPD, type 2 diabetes mellitus, coronary artery disease with prior stent placement, depression, chronic GERD, and peripheral neuropathy. Surgical history includes remote cholecystectomy, appendectomy, spine and orthopedic procedures. The patient has a >30 pack-year tobacco history and continues to smoke, now about 8-10 cigarettes per day.

He reports mild dyspnea on exertion, attributed to baseline COPD, but denies orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, recent fevers, night sweats, weight loss, or hemoptysis. There are no current complaints of increased cough, chest pain, or new respiratory symptoms. Appetite is fair, but he notes some mild fatigue. Denies confusion, focal weakness, headache, or seizure-like activity. Bowel and bladder habits unchanged. No known drug allergies aside from adhesive tape.

**Laboratory and Imaging Data:**

- CBC: Hemoglobin 10.2 g/dL (low), Hematocrit 33.9% (low), WBC 9.28 x10^3/μL (normal), Platelets 274 x10^3/μL (normal), MCV 92.1 fL (normal), mild anisocytosis noted.
- Comprehensive metabolic panel notable for glucose 173 mg/dL (high), Creatinine 1.2 mg/dL (stable), BUN 16 mg/dL, eGFR 58 mL/min/1.73m^2.
- LFTs: AST 31 U/L, ALT 14 U/L, Alk Phos 85 U/L, bilirubin 0.9 mg/dL (all within normal limits).
- Electrolytes: Sodium 139 mmol/L, Potassium 3.8 mmol/L, CO2 24 mmol/L.
- Protein/albumin: 8.2/4.6 g/dL.
- Recent chest CTA (from outside facility): Bands of scarring and fibrosis in right middle lobe and left lower lobe, both stable in appearance. Enlarging nodule in left upper lobe suspicious for metastatic disease, no definite extrathoracic metastases.  
- Pathology (outside hospital): Biopsy of left upper lobe reveals large cell carcinoma with features of adenocarcinoma.
- ECOG performance status: 1.

**Medications:**
- Metabolic: Insulin glargine (Lantus), insulin lispro, empagliflozin, dulaglutide.
- Cardiac: Aspirin 81 mg, atorvastatin 40 mg, carvedilol 6.25 mg BID, isosorbide dinitrate, lisinopril, ticagrelor.
- Pulmonary: Albuterol, budesonide-formoterol (Symbicort), ipratropium-albuterol (Duoneb), umeclidinium (Incruse Ellipta).
- Pain: Oxycodone 20 mg TID.
- GI: Pantoprazole 40 mg daily, sucralfate.
- Depression: Sertraline 100 mg daily.
- Others: Magnesium oxide, midodrine, nicotine patch.

**Social History:**  
- Never used e-cigarettes, illicit drugs, or consumed alcohol.  
- Active tobacco use: currently 10-15 cigarettes per day (30+ pack-year history).

**Family History:**  
- Father with diabetes mellitus.  
- Sister and mother with cancer history (details unavailable).  
- Sister with history of breast cancer.

**Surgical History:**  
- Cholecystectomy, appendectomy, back and neck fusions, bilateral shoulder surgery (with hardware), remote left knee surgery.

**Allergies:**  
- Tape (rash reaction).

**Other Data:**  
- No evidence of disease outside the chest on current imaging.  
- No prior systemic therapy for lung cancer.

**Summary:**  
- 75-year-old male presenting for initial work-up and evaluation of pathologically confirmed non-small cell lung cancer with mediastinal lymph node involvement (N3 positive) and a left upper lobe nodule.  
- Stable comorbidities, ECOG 1, currently no acute distress.  
- Imaging and labs support recent diagnosis; all outside records pending.  
- Further staging and multidisciplinary evaluation in progress.
