She has restarted her antihypertensive medications and is tolerating them; she denies dizziness or lightheadedness. She is currently on 4L oxygen via nasal cannula. She denies chest pain, shortness of breath, or wheezing. No new complaints. Appetite is fair, tolerating oral intake in small amounts, and she is passing stool. Patient presents for evaluation and management of lung cancer.

[Deid: Name] is a 63-year-old female with a history of poorly differentiated squamous cell carcinoma of the left lower lobe of the lung (clinical stage IIB, T3 invasion) diagnosed last year. Pulmonary function tests demonstrated mild airway obstruction, with FEV1 at 97% predicted. Cardiac clearance was obtained due to her history of coronary disease and remote MIs. Multidisciplinary tumor board recommendation was for a multimodality approach due to apical (superior sulcus/Pancoast) location and apparent T3 invasion of adjacent structures, without frank resectability contraindications.

RELEVANT PAST MEDICAL HISTORY  
- Type 2 diabetes mellitus
- Hypertension
- Coronary artery disease, prior MIs in 2011 and 2017
- Hyperlipidemia
- Tobacco use (current, 3 cigarettes/day, ~35 pack-years)
- No known family history of cancer
- No prior radiation to the chest

SOCIAL HISTORY  
Lives with spouse. Continues to smoke cigarettes despite counseling. Drinks wine 1-2 times per month. Works part-time. No illicit drug use.

- Percutaneous biopsy of left lower lobe
- No prior thoracic surgeries

GENERAL: No fever, chills, or unintentional weight loss.  
HEENT: No headache, visual changes, or sore throat.

CARDIOVASCULAR: No chest pain, palpitations, or lower extremity swelling.  
GASTROINTESTINAL: No abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, or changes in bowel habits.  
GENITOURINARY: No urinary frequency or dysuria.

NEUROLOGIC: No focal deficits, numbness, or tingling.  
SKIN: No rashes or new lesions.  
PSYCHIATRIC: Mood appropriate, no cognitive changes.  
ENDOCRINE: No polydipsia or polyuria.

CURRENT MEDICATIONS  
- Basaglar KwikPen U-100 Insulin, 25 units SC every morning  
- Metformin 1,000 mg oral twice daily  
- Jardiance 10 mg oral daily  
- Lisinopril 20 mg oral daily  
- Atorvastatin 40 mg oral nightly  
- Aspirin 81 mg oral daily  
- Cholecalciferol 400 IU oral daily  
- Cyanocobalamin 1,000 mcg oral daily  
- Garlic 1,000 mg daily  
- Vitamin C 1,000 mg daily  
- Omega-3, 1,000 mg daily  
- Ibuprofen 800 mg as needed

Darvocet A500 (hallucinations)

PHYSICAL EXAM  
VITALS:  
BP 154/82, HR 65, Temp 36.3°C, SpO2 98% on room air, Height 159 cm, Weight 72.3 kg, BMI 29

GENERAL: Alert and oriented, in no acute distress.  
HEENT: Normocephalic, atraumatic. Oropharynx clear. No cervical or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy.  
PULMONARY: Chest wall intact, mild tenderness to palpation in left supraclavicular and axillary region. Breath sounds decreased at left apex but otherwise clear bilaterally. No rales or wheezing. No respiratory distress.

ABDOMEN: Obese, non-tender, no masses or hepatosplenomegaly.  
EXTREMITIES: No edema, pulses intact.  
NEUROLOGIC: Cranial nerves II–XII grossly intact. Motor and sensation normal throughout.  
SKIN: No rashes, surgical biopsy site well healed at left flank.

CBC, CMP, and cardiac biomarkers within baseline limits except for mild hyperglycemia (glucose 160–220 mg/dL). Hgb 14.1 g/dL, WBC 8.1 x10^3/mcL, platelets 311 x10^3/mcL, creatinine 0.7 mg/dL. LFTs normal. Cholesterol 196 mg/dL, triglycerides 147 mg/dL. Last A1c 7.8%.  
PD-L1 70%. EGFR, ALK, ROS1 negative.

PROCEDURES  
- CT-guided percutaneous biopsy, pathology confirming poorly differentiated squamous cell carcinoma.

SPECIALIST INPUT  
Multidisciplinary review with thoracic surgery, medical oncology, and radiation oncology concurred on diagnosis and agreed with need for multimodality management. Cardiology cleared for possible therapy after risk assessment.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS:  
[Deid: Name] is a 77-year-old widowed male with a significant past medical history notable for tobacco use (current smoker, ~0.4 packs/day for 57 years), coronary artery disease with remote stenting, chronic diastolic heart failure, hypertension, type 2 diabetes, DVT, GERD, hyperlipidemia, myelodysplastic syndrome with chronic anemia requiring intermittent transfusions, and chronic low back pain, presenting after evaluation for a left upper lobe pulmonary nodule found incidentally on imaging for back pain. Additional workup included chest CT and PET which demonstrated a left upper lobe spiculated nodule with mild FDG avidity, suspicious for primary lung cancer, with no evidence of metastatic disease on PET or brain imaging. There were smaller, non-FDG-avid right middle lobe nodules consistent with benignity by imaging criteria. Pulmonary function tests were within acceptable limits for surgery. He remained active in his daily life and was living independently.

After multidisciplinary tumor board review, thoracic surgery consultation was obtained. Surgical options versus radiation were discussed in detail; the patient and family elected to proceed with surgical management. He was asked to hold Eliquis prior to surgery.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY:
- Adenosquamous carcinoma, left upper lobe (biopsy proven)
- Chronic myelodysplasia with macrocytic anemia (requiring transfusions)
- CAD with prior MI (2006) and coronary stenting x3
- Chronic diastolic heart failure (HFpEF)
- DVT, recurrent, on anticoagulation
- Type 2 diabetes mellitus
- Hypertension
- GERD
- COPD / centrilobular emphysema (current smoker)
- Chronic low back pain
- Insomnia
- Hyperlipidemia
- Kidney stones
- Left anterior shoulder pain
- Right eye injury (remote)
- Seborrheic dermatitis of scalp

PAST SURGICAL HISTORY:
- Left thoracotomy, left upper lobectomy and mediastinal lymph node dissection (current admission)
- Coronary stent placement x3
- Cholecystectomy
- ERCP (stone removal)
- Multiple knee arthroscopies, left knee replacement
- Right and left shoulder procedures
- Carpal tunnel release, right
- Bilateral cataract surgery
- Vitrectomy, right eye
- Esophageal endoscopic dilations

FAMILY HISTORY:  
- Mother: cancer  
- Father: cancer, gout, alcoholism

SOCIAL HISTORY:  
- Lives independently with some family support; widowed  
- Smokes 8 cigarettes/day for over 57 years (current); attempted to quit several times, cut down recently  
- Drinks alcohol occasionally; denies illicit drug use  

ALLERGIES:  
- Indomethacin (nausea, dizziness, tachycardia)

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS:  
Constitutional: Negative for fever or weight loss. Reports chronic fatigue, attributed to anemia.  
Respiratory: Denies chronic cough or hemoptysis. No recent dyspnea on exertion above baseline.  
Cardiac: History of chest pain and palpitations, none currently.  
GI: Occasional reflux symptoms; denies dysphagia, melena, hematochezia.  
GU: No dysuria or hematuria.  
Neuro: No focal deficits.  
Psych: Reports insomnia, no acute mood symptoms.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION:  
Vitals: Afebrile, BP and HR stable, BMI 20.9.  
General: Pleasant, alert, in no acute distress.  
HEENT: Normocephalic, no scleral icterus, mucous membranes moist.  
Neck: Supple, no lymphadenopathy.  
Chest: Well-healed thoracotomy incision, dressing in place.  
Pulmonary: Breath sounds decreased at left upper field postoperatively, mild coarse breath sounds at left base, no active rales, no increased work of breathing. No crepitus.  
CV: Regularly irregular, normal S1/S2, no murmurs or rubs.  
Abdomen: Soft, non-tender, non-distended, bowel sounds present.  
Extremities: No edema, well-perfused, moves all extremities.  
Neuro: Alert, oriented, cooperative.  
Skin: Healed surgical sites, no evidence of breakdown.

HOSPITAL COURSE:  
The patient underwent left thoracotomy with left upper lobectomy and mediastinal lymph node dissection without intraoperative complications. Estimated blood loss was minimal. Postoperatively, he was managed with incentive spirometry, scheduled pain control (tylenol, PRN opioids), and early ambulation. A left chest tube was placed to water seal, with intermittent air leak initially, but with decreasing serosanguinous output and effective pain management. Incision and tube sites were monitored for infection or drainage. Pulmonary toilet with Aerobika was encouraged and well tolerated. Patient participated with physical therapy and was ambulating in the hallways within 24 hours. Cardiac rhythm monitoring continued, showing baseline atrial fibrillation without rapid ventricular response. There were no acute cardiac events.

Hemoglobin trended postoperatively with expected mild drop, but no evidence of new bleeding; the patient’s anemia remained stable for his known chronic baseline. Anticoagulation was held perioperatively as per protocol. He continued home medications as able, with temporary adjustments for perioperative needs (eg, holding metformin with altered renal function and warfarin perioperatively).

No perioperative infectious or thrombotic complications occurred. Chest imaging demonstrated expected post-lobectomy changes, with a small apical pneumothorax resolving and no evidence of significant effusion. The chest tube was clamped overnight and removed following stable imaging.

The patient steadily progressed to a regular diet, bowel and bladder function returned, and he was independent with ADLs at discharge. He was counseled on the importance of smoking cessation, activity restrictions, wound care, and signs/symptoms to report. Pathology returned as adenosquamous carcinoma, stage IB (pT2aN0M0), margins negative, with no nodal involvement.

DISCHARGE PHYSICAL EXAM:  
General: Sitting up in bed, pleasant, no acute distress.  
Cardiac: Irregularly irregular, no murmurs, normal perfusion.  
Pulmonary: Scattered crackles left base, otherwise clear, no respiratory distress.  
Surgical: Thoracotomy and chest tube sites healing, no erythema or fluctuance.  
Abdomen: Non-tender, soft, nondistended.  
Extremities: No edema.  
Neuro: Alert, conversant, grossly intact.

Gender: Male

CHIEF COMPLAINT  
Generalized weakness, failure to thrive, and progressive functional decline after recent initiation of pembrolizumab (Keytruda) for advanced non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC).

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS  
Patient is an 80-year-old Caucasian male with a known history of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and newly diagnosed multifocal non-small cell lung cancer (squamous cell carcinoma, PD-L1 90%, right lung primary with mediastinal lymph node involvement). He was previously in good health and functionally independent until his cancer diagnosis. He had been a long-term smoker (>60 pack-years), quit after recent hemoptysis and subsequent imaging revealed multiple hypermetabolic right lung masses and mediastinal adenopathy on PET/CT. Pathology from robotic bronchoscopy confirmed squamous cell carcinoma from right lower and middle lobes, and mediastinal station 7 (subcarinal) node.

His cancer has been staged at least T4 N3 M0 on available imaging and pathologic review, with no evidence of distant metastasis on PET/CT or brain MRI (which showed only age-related white matter changes, no masses). He is not a candidate for surgical resection or radiation due to extent of disease.

He was started on pembrolizumab monotherapy after tumor board review. Since receiving his first dose, he developed profound generalized weakness, decreased oral intake, fatigue, and multiple falls at home. He required assistance for most activities of daily living and was brought to the hospital after being found down at home. The patient and his family report no new cough, hemoptysis, nausea, vomiting, or fevers prior to hospitalization, but he has since developed intermittent low-grade temperatures and worsening malaise. There is also a recent history of constipation and poorly controlled pain, now being managed with hydrocodone-acetaminophen.

During this admission, he remains largely bedridden, requiring a rolling walker for limited transfers. Therapy assessments document severe deconditioning but with capacity for safe use of the walker. Family reports ongoing lethargy and intermittent confusion.

No history of exposure to tuberculosis. No recent travel.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY  
- Non-small cell lung cancer (squamous cell carcinoma, PD-L1 90%)  
- COPD (moderate, no prior hospitalizations for exacerbation)  
- Cataract surgery  
- No known cardiac, hepatic, or renal disease prior to cancer diagnosis

- Bilateral cataract extraction with intraocular lens implant

- Former heavy smoker (quit [Deid: Date], >60 pack-years)

- Retired service technician

- Maintained high functional and mobility status prior to cancer

Non-contributory

Bee venom protein (swelling)

Neurologic: Moves all extremities, non-focal, alert to name but sometimes repeats himself

Weight: 72.4 kg

- WBC: 7.2 ×10³/μL  
- Hgb: 9.1 g/dL (anemia, chronic)  
- Hct: 29.9%  
- Platelets: 311 ×10³/μL  
- Creatinine: 0.90 mg/dL  
- BUN: 21 mg/dL

- Albumin: 2.6-3.2 g/dL (low, with ongoing decline)  
- AST: mild transaminitis, resolving  
- TSH, B12: within normal limits

IMAGING  
- CT Chest/Abdomen/Pelvis: Multiple spiculated right lung masses with interval decrease in some since prior scan; right-sided pleural effusion with thickening; diffuse emphysematous changes; scattered mediastinal lymphadenopathy.  
- PET/CT: Multiple hypermetabolic right lung masses and nodules, mediastinal involvement, no extrathoracic metastasis  
- MRI Brain: No evidence of intracranial metastasis; moderate chronic small vessel ischemic changes  
- Chest x-rays: Unchanged right perihilar mass, new increase in right pleural effusion

MEDICATIONS  
- Pembrolizumab (Keytruda) – received 1 cycle, last given [Deid: Date]  
- Enoxaparin (Lovenox) 40 mg subcutaneous qDay (VTE prophylaxis)  
- Hydrocodone-acetaminophen for breakthrough pain  
- Sennosides-docusate sodium (bowel regimen)  
- Acetaminophen PRN  
- Prednisone 40 mg qDay (for symptomatic COPD and rash)  
- Ampicillin-sulbactam 3 g IV q6h (current, for recent pneumonia)  
- Ipratropium-albuterol nebulizer PRN  
- Umeclidinium-vilanterol inhaler daily  
- Dronabinol 5 mg PO BID before meals (for appetite)

FUNCTIONAL STATUS / PT/OT  
- Profound deconditioning and functional decline since last discharge.  
- Mobilizes with rolling walker and two-person assist for safety.  
- Unable to perform independent ADLs; requires help for transfers, dressing, toileting.  
- No evidence of cognitive or behavioral barriers to safe use of the walker.  
- PT/OT recommend ongoing rehab for strength and endurance.

HOSPITAL COURSE  
Admitted for failure to thrive after Keytruda, with severe weakness and inability to ambulate independently. Initial infectious workup was negative; ongoing constipation addressed with bowel regimen and enema as needed. Developed aspiration pneumonia with right parapneumonic effusion, completed antibiotics. Current disposition plan includes ongoing inpatient rehabilitation for mobility and strength. Family engaged in goals-of-care discussions. Social work and case management actively involved in discharge planning and assessment for safe transition home or hospice as appropriate.

[END OF NOTE]

No new neurological symptoms. Left upper extremity swelling (previous DVT) has resolved. No bleeding or bruising.

Direct extension into right 2nd rib with lytic lesion and pathologic fracture. Nodal metastases (mediastinal, bilateral hilar, bilateral supraclavicular, lower left cervical). Bilateral adrenal gland hypermetabolic activity and suspected soft tissue and bone metastases (gluteal muscle, C2 vertebral body).
- **MRI Brain:** Multiple (at least 3-4) enhancing metastatic lesions (left frontal, left periventricular, left cerebellar, right occipital), no significant edema. No acute infarct.
- **CT Head/Cervical:** Stable cerebral atrophy, changes compatible with known brain metastases. No acute bleed or infarct.
- **XR chest:** Stable right upper lobe mass, no pneumothorax or pleural effusion.
- **Pulmonary function tests:** Obstructive pattern, FEV1 ~39% predicted, FVC ~53% predicted.

---

**PATHOLOGY & MOLECULAR:**  
- **Bronchoscopy with biopsy (right upper lobe):** Non-small cell carcinoma (large cell carcinoma, NOS). Immunostain: CK7+, TTF-1-, NapsinA-, p40-.
- **Mediastinal node (station 7) FNA:** Positive for non-small cell carcinoma.
- **PD-L1:** 10% expression in tumor cells.
- **Broad molecular profiling:** ERBB2 (HER2) mutation detected. No other actionable driver (EGFR, ALK, ROS1, BRAF, RET, MET, NTRK) identified.

---

**CURRENT OUTPATIENT AND INPATIENT MEDICATIONS:**  
(Includes, but not limited to: amlodipine, losartan, rosuvastatin, pantoprazole, gabapentin, buspirone, baclofen, dexamethasone, ferrous sulfate, folic acid, gemfibrozil, lamoTRIgine, pancrelipase, sennosides, albuterol inhaler, benzonatate, diclofenac gel, ondansetron, promethazine, prochlorperazine, oxycodone ER, oxycodone/acetaminophen, fentanyl patch; HYDROmorphone PCA and IV; ipratropium-albuterol nebulizer as needed; enoxaparin for DVT prophylaxis; lorazepam, melatonin as needed.)

---

**ALLERGIES:**  
- Meloxicam: other reaction  
- Morphine: unknown/other

---

**HOSPITAL COURSE SUMMARY:**  
Patient with widely metastatic large cell non-small cell lung cancer (HER2 mutation, PD-L1 10%), with known brain, bone, adrenal, mediastinal, and soft-tissue metastases. Initial management included combination systemic chemotherapy and immunotherapy (pembrolizumab, pemetrexed, carboplatin), referral for stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS) to brain lesions, and aggressive symptom management. Pain management has required rapid escalation to high-potency opioids (hydromorphone PCA), with transitions considered towards oral methadone once pain is better controlled. The course has been complicated by increasing lethargy, confusion, and periods of agitation. Multiple palliative care and hospice discussions have taken place, with goals of care shifting increasingly toward comfort-focused measures.

**FUNCTIONAL STATUS:**  
Performance status declined during admission: currently predominantly bedbound, requires assistance with all ADL, fluctuates between somnolence and restlessness, progressive cachexia and weakness noted on exam.

---

**[END OF NOTE – NO ASSESSMENT OR PLAN INCLUDED]**

**Cardiothoracic Progress Note – [Deid: Name], 77 y.o. female, [Deid: MRN]**

**Admit Date:** [DATE: 28356]  
**Hospital Day:** 0  
**Surgery Date:** [DATE: 28356]  
**Procedure:** Robotic right upper lobectomy, mediastinal lymph node dissection

---

**Summary:**
[Deid: Name] is a 77-year-old woman with a history of cervical cancer (s/p hysterectomy at age 35), hyperlipidemia, sleep apnea (on CPAP), GERD, depression, hoh (hearing loss), and other comorbidities, who initially presented with respiratory symptoms and tested positive for RSV. Imaging revealed a 2.7 x 1.6 cm right upper lobe lung nodule without evidence of metastatic disease on PET. Bronchoscopy and biopsy confirmed a well-differentiated adenocarcinoma. Preoperative evaluation including pulmonary function testing and cardiac evaluation were performed, with FEV1 83% predicted and echo showing preserved biventricular function.

After multidisciplinary review, she was considered an appropriate surgical candidate and underwent robotic-assisted right upper lobectomy with mediastinal lymph node dissection. She tolerated the procedure well. Pathology revealed a 2.1 cm well-differentiated acinar adenocarcinoma involving the visceral pleura (T2a), with all surgical margins and sampled lymph nodes negative for malignancy (N0). There was no evidence of lymphovascular invasion or direct extension; pathologic staging pT2aN0 (Stage IB).

---

**Perioperative Course:**

- **Preoperative:** Patient was admitted from home following infectious symptoms and debility related to RSV. Prior to surgery, she underwent detailed workup including CT chest, PET-CT, and bronchoscopy with tissue diagnosis of adenocarcinoma. There was no radiologic evidence of mediastinal lymphadenopathy or distant metastases. Baseline labs were unremarkable apart from mild anemia and chronic stable renal insufficiency.
  
- **Intraoperative:** Right upper lobectomy and mediastinal lymph node dissection completed without intraoperative complications. Mediastinal and peribronchial nodes were sampled and sent for pathology. A chest tube was placed to water seal. The patient was transferred to CVICU for postoperative monitoring.

- **Immediate Postoperative:** Required supplemental oxygen for hypoxemia, with occasional BiPAP at night for sleep apnea. Initially experienced persistent cough, some right-sided chest pain at the robotic port sites, and moderate serosanguinous chest tube output (no airleak). Early labs showed mild postoperative leukocytosis, downtrending hemoglobin (remained stable, no transfusion needed), mild hyponatremia, and transient creatinine elevation, attributed to diuresis. No significant arrhythmia or hemodynamic instability.

- **Hospital Days 1-3:** Patient had persistent cough, intermittent low-grade fevers, and required chest physiotherapy and aggressive pulmonary toileting. Chest tube drainage continued to decrease, and there was no evidence of ongoing airleak. Imaging (serial chest radiographs and CT) showed expected postoperative changes, including small right apical pneumothorax and right middle lobe atelectasis, with gradual improvement. Sputum cultures were negative for significant bacterial pathogens. Empiric IV antibiotics (ceftriaxone) and steroids were administered for suspected postoperative pneumonia. Furosemide was used to manage fluid overload, with good response in oxygenation and mobilization of secretions. 

- **Hospital Days 4-5:** Oxygen requirements decreased and chest tube was successfully discontinued after confirming minimal drainage and absence of airleak on water seal. Ambulation and activity improved with physical therapy involvement. Serial labs demonstrated normalization of WBC, stable hemoglobin, and improved renal parameters. The patient remained afebrile, and all incisions remained clean and dry.

- **Hospital Day 6 (Discharge):**  
  The patient was weaned to room air, consistently maintaining SpO2 above 95%. She was able to ambulate independently, perform all activities of daily living without limitation, and had adequate oral intake. Surgical incisions were well-healed. No new neurological deficits or cardiac symptoms were observed. She was stable for discharge with arrangements made for close postoperative and oncology follow-up, pulmonary rehabilitation, and a surveillance imaging program.

---

**Vital Signs:**
- BP: Ranged from 93/55 to 148/85 mmHg
- Pulse: 71–101 bpm
- Resp: 15–22/min
- Temp: 35.9°–37.2°C (oral)
- Weight: 83–93.6 kg
- SpO2: 91%–98% (room air at discharge)

**I/O:**  
Intake and output were monitored closely, with adjustments to diuretics as needed for volume management.

---

**Allergies:**  
- Trolamine Salicylate (itching)  
- Azithromycin (unknown)  
- Meperidine (unknown)  
- Penicillins (unknown)  
- Tetracycline (unknown)

---

**Key Medications (Hospital Course):**
- Ipratropium-albuterol nebulizers
- Budesonide nebulization
- Ceftriaxone IV
- Methylprednisolone IV
- Furosemide PO and IV
- Escitalopram, bupropion, cetirizine, docusate, polyethylene glycol, pravastatin, pantoprazole, potassium chloride, ropinirole, enoxaparin

---

**Labs and Imaging:**

- **Labs:**  
  - Initial postop leukocytosis with gradual normalization  
  - Downtrending hemoglobin (lowest 10.6 g/dL, no transfusion required)  
  - Platelets mild transient decrease, stable  
  - Mild transient hyponatremia and creatinine bump, resolved with conservative management
  - Persistent mild hyperglycemia, managed per sliding scale
  - Coags remained normal (INR 0.99)

- **Imaging:**  
  - CXR and CT chest: Postoperative changes, right apical pneumothorax (small, stable), right middle lobe atelectasis, resolving subcutaneous air. No new pleural effusion or infiltrate on discharge imaging.

- **Pathology:**  
  - Lung, right upper lobe: 2.1 cm well-differentiated acinar adenocarcinoma; visceral pleural invasion present.
  - Resection margins negative (>2 cm from tumor)
  - 22 mediastinal and peribronchial lymph nodes: All negative for metastatic disease (pT2aN0, Stage IB)
  - Additional: Peribronchial non-necrotizing granulomatous inflammation; stains negative for organisms
  - Molecular: EGFR negative, PD-L1 0%

---

**Physical Exam (Discharge Day):**
- General: Alert, oriented, no acute distress, ambulating independently
- Skin: Surgical incisions well-healed, no erythema or drainage
- HEENT: Pupils normal, oropharynx clear, no lesions
- Heart: Regular rate and rhythm, no murmurs
- Lungs: Clear to auscultation, no rales or wheezing, no distress
- Abdomen: Soft, non-tender, normal bowel sounds
- Extremities: No edema, pulses present
- Neuro: A&O x3, full strength
- Wound: Incisions clean, dry, staples removed, well-approximated

---

**Social History:**
- Former smoker, quit 20+ years ago (2 ppd x 36 yrs)
- Lives with daughter, retired teacher, divorced, independent in ADLs
- Family history: Lung cancer (father), throat cancer (mother)

---

**Current Outpatient Medications (on discharge):**
- BuPROPion SR 100 mg BID
- Cetirizine 10 mg qday
- Escitalopram 20 mg qday
- Pravastatin 40 mg qHS
- Omeprazole 40 mg qHS prn
- Fluticasone furoate-vilanterol inhaler qAM
- Ropinirole 0.5 mg qHS
- Multivitamin qday

---

**Follow-up:**
- Postoperative visit with thoracic surgery and oncology arranged
- Surveillance CT chest scheduled per protocol (6, 12, 18... months)
- Wound review and laboratory check with PCP
- Pulmonary rehab referral in process

- **Preoperative:** Patient was admitted from home following infectious symptoms and debility related to RSV. Prior to surgery, she underwent detailed workup including CT chest, PET-CT, and bronchoscopy with tissue diagnosis of adenocarcinoma. There was no radiologic evidence of mediastinal lymphadenopathy or distant metastases. Baseline labs were unremarkable apart from mild anemia and chronic stable renal insufficiency.
 
- **Intraoperative:** Right upper lobectomy and mediastinal lymph node dissection completed without intraoperative complications. Mediastinal and peribronchial nodes were sampled and sent for pathology. A chest tube was placed to water seal. The patient was transferred to CVICU for postoperative monitoring.

- **Immediate Postoperative:** Required supplemental oxygen for hypoxemia, with occasional BiPAP at night for sleep apnea. Initially experienced persistent cough, some right-sided chest pain at the robotic port sites, and moderate serosanguinous chest tube output (no airleak). Early labs showed mild postoperative leukocytosis, downtrending hemoglobin (remained stable, no transfusion needed), mild hyponatremia, and transient creatinine elevation, attributed to diuresis. No significant arrhythmia or hemodynamic instability.

- **Hospital Days 1-3:** Patient had persistent cough, intermittent low-grade fevers, and required chest physiotherapy and aggressive pulmonary toileting. Chest tube drainage continued to decrease, and there was no evidence of ongoing airleak. Imaging (serial chest radiographs and CT) showed expected postoperative changes, including small right apical pneumothorax and right middle lobe atelectasis, with gradual improvement. Sputum cultures were negative for significant bacterial pathogens. Empiric IV antibiotics (ceftriaxone) and steroids were administered for suspected postoperative pneumonia. Furosemide was used to manage fluid overload, with good response in oxygenation and mobilization of secretions. 

- **Hospital Days 4-5:** Oxygen requirements decreased and chest tube was successfully discontinued after confirming minimal drainage and absence of airleak on water seal. Ambulation and activity improved with physical therapy involvement. Serial labs demonstrated normalization of WBC, stable hemoglobin, and improved renal parameters. The patient remained afebrile, and all incisions remained clean and dry.

 The patient was weaned to room air, consistently maintaining SpO2 above 95%. She was able to ambulate independently, perform all activities of daily living without limitation, and had adequate oral intake. Surgical incisions were well-healed. No new neurological deficits or cardiac symptoms were observed. She was stable for discharge with arrangements made for close postoperative and oncology follow-up, pulmonary rehabilitation, and a surveillance imaging program.

Patient: [Deid: Name]

**Reason for Visit:**  
Follow-up evaluation for non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), surgical resection/post-op, ongoing surveillance and management.

---

**History of Present Illness:**  
[Deid: Name] is a 77-year-old male with a known history of non-small cell lung cancer (squamous cell carcinoma), status post right lower lobectomy with mediastinal lymph node dissection. The initial diagnosis was established following interval enlargement of a right lower lobe (RLL) nodule—PET/CT imaging demonstrated slow growth and no evidence of distant metastatic disease. Preoperative pulmonary function tests demonstrated mild airflow obstruction, but patient was deemed an appropriate surgical candidate following multidisciplinary review. The tumor was located in a superior sulcus (apical) position, with clinical staging consistent with T3 invasion, without evidence of N2/N3 nodal disease or distant metastases. Other relevant history includes atrial fibrillation (status post ablation and later pacemaker implantation), hypertension, type 2 diabetes, hyperlipidemia, OSA (untreated), iron deficiency, history of tobacco use (quit 2 years ago), and remote pneumonia.

He underwent right video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS) with conversion to limited thoracotomy, right lower lobectomy, and mediastinal lymph node dissection on [DATE: 27105]. The postoperative course was notable for appropriate pain control, temporary chest tube placement for a small apical pneumothorax, and unremarkable wound healing. Discharge occurred on [DATE: 27108] with no significant complications. Pathology confirmed moderately differentiated squamous cell carcinoma, with invasion into the chest wall (superior sulcus), pathologic stage pT3N0, and negative (R0) surgical margins. Several sampled mediastinal lymph nodes were negative for metastatic involvement.

Since surgery, the patient has participated in scheduled surveillance visits and imaging. He remains under close oncologic and pulmonary follow-up. Interval history is negative for new cough, hemoptysis, hoarseness, bone pain or neurologic changes. He continues to report mild exertional dyspnea, which is unchanged since the postoperative period, attributed to both lung resection and underlying mild COPD. His activity level is stable; no recent hospitalizations for pulmonary or cardiac issues. For cough and sputum, he uses albuterol inhaler intermittently, and maintenance pulmonary regimen is unchanged. No constitutional symptoms reported.

**Review of Systems:**

[Deid: Name], a 77-year-old female, presents for evaluation of a persistent cough productive of yellow phlegm for 15 days, which is notably worse at night and associated with sore throat, nasal congestion, sinus pressure, intermittent hoarse voice, headache, and increased fatigue. She has also experienced left eye erythema and watery discharge for the past 5 days. In addition, she describes urinary symptoms, including persistent pressure, increased frequency, and urgency over the past 1–2 weeks, as well as suprapubic discomfort after voiding. She denies fevers, chills, photophobia, eye pain or pruritus, constipation, diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, ear pain, or rhinorrhea.

The patient is the sole historian and required no interpreter. She has a history of non-small cell lung cancer for which she underwent left upper lobectomy with mediastinal lymph node dissection (by thoracotomy) approximately seven years ago. Additional history includes stage 3 chronic kidney disease, hypertension, panlobular emphysema, osteoarthritis in both knees, hyperlipidemia, chronic cough, eczema, post-nasal drip, stress incontinence, primary osteoarthritis, and a personal history of colonic polyps. She is a former smoker (27 years, 0.5 pack/day; quit ~20 years ago) and is currently retired, living independently with her spouse, and reports good social support. Her family history is notable for lung cancer in her father and osteoporosis in her mother.

Her current medications include acetaminophen as needed, alendronate, low-dose ASA, atorvastatin, azelastine, vitamin D3, fluocinolone otic drops, metoprolol succinate, omeprazole, raloxifene, tiotropium, triamcinolone cream and nasal spray. Allergies are noted to aspirin (nausea with large quantities), and to levofloxacin (tendonitis).

Review of systems is positive for changes in appetite and fatigue; nasal congestion with intermittent postnasal drip, sinus pressure, and sore throat; headaches; cough with yellow sputum; suprapubic pressure after voiding, urinary urgency and frequency; left eye discharge and erythema. The patient denies fever, ear pain, rhinorrhea, photophobia, eye pain or pruritus, constipation, diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, chest pain, shortness of breath, and wheezing.

On physical examination, she appears well and not in acute distress. Vital signs are within normal limits: BP 122/76, pulse 84, oral temperature 98.3°F, SpO2 96%, BMI 25.0. HEENT: Normocephalic. Ear exam is unremarkable bilaterally. Swollen erythematous turbinates and mild purulent rhinorrhea are present. Oropharynx is moist with mild posterior erythema. No cervical lymphadenopathy. On ocular examination, conjunctivae are normal; no discharge is currently noted in either eye. Cardiovascular exam reveals a normal rate and rhythm, without murmurs. Lungs reveal sparse, bilateral wheezes but otherwise normal effort, no distress, no rales or rhonchi. Abdomen is soft, non-tender, with normal bowel sounds and no costovertebral angle tenderness. Musculoskeletal and skin exams are unremarkable. Neurologically, she is alert and oriented.

Urinalysis reveals yellow, clear urine with 1+ leukocyte esterase, 6–10 WBC/hpf, moderate bacteria, and moderate mucus threads. Urine culture is pending.

Recent physical therapy records indicate ongoing improvement in stress incontinence symptoms, with a reduction in pad use and increased confidence in pelvic floor exercises. She is compliant with her home exercise program and progressing toward goals, but reports that symptoms are most noticeable if she delays voiding and then coughs. No adverse effects or falls have occurred.

There has been no return or progression of her lung cancer symptoms. She continues regular follow-up with oncology, and her most recent imaging (as per prior notes) shows no evidence of recurrence.

No further assessment or plan included.

Follow-up for advanced lung cancer (adenocarcinoma, HER2-amplified), chronic fatigue, progressive memory loss, routine device (pacemaker) evaluation, and ongoing symptom management.

She is a former smoker (quit >20 years ago), divorced, and currently resides in an assisted living facility with support from her son (POA) and daughter.

She was diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma after care for an incidental finding on imaging. Subsequent PET/CT and biopsy confirmed malignancy with HER2 amplification and no actionable driver mutations otherwise; mediastinal lymph nodes were negative. MRI brain for staging was planned but ultimately declined by the patient/family. She is functionally limited (ECOG 1-2), primarily due to fatigue, chronic pain, and advanced age.

The patient has declined definitive cancer treatment, including surgery, chemotherapy, and radiation, after multidisciplinary discussions and given her comorbidities and personal wishes. She transitioned to a palliative, symptom-directed approach. Since diagnosis, she has experienced progressive fatigue, chronic pain (multifactorial—cancer, arthritis), worsening short-term memory, easy satiety, intermittent constipation, and insomnia. She has not noted significant cough, hemoptysis, chest pain, or acute respiratory symptoms. She denied new focal neurologic deficits.

She continues to have daily somnolence, often napping after meals and during passive activities. She remains independent with self-care tasks, though she requires supervision and cueing by ALF staff for medications and meals. She ambulates with a cane or rollator; no recent falls. She enjoys reading and puzzles but requires frequent breaks due to fatigue and drowsiness. Her son expresses increasing concern about memory lapses and occasional confusion, but the patient remains oriented to person and place.

She recently suffered from a norovirus infection, now resolved, after which her fatigue and anorexia worsened temporarily. She notes ongoing foot pain due to left first toenail onychodystrophy, previously treated with partial nail removal. She uses wide, soft footwear as advised.

Her pacemaker continues to be monitored remotely. Recent device checks confirm atrial pacing >90% with <0.1% ventricular pacing, no high-rate episodes, and stable device parameters. She remains non-pacemaker dependent.

She and her son question ongoing necessity for amiodarone and Plavix in the setting of no new arrhythmias and in light of potential medication-related side effects. She is maintained on aspirin and statin for secondary prevention. Amiodarone was originally prescribed for frequent PVCs; there has been discussion about possible discontinuation if monitoring remains stable.

Inpatient Palliative Care and Hospice Physician Progress Note

SUBJECTIVE

History of Present Illness / Chief Complaint:
79-year-old male with a medical history of stage IVB metastatic non-small cell lung cancer (adenocarcinoma, ALK fusion-positive), as well as multiple comorbidities including paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, ischemic cardiomyopathy with reduced ejection fraction (EF 45–50%) s/p cardiac defibrillator and 4-vessel CABG, DM2, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia.

The patient was initially diagnosed with metastatic lung cancer after presenting with significant left supraclavicular and sternal masses, later confirmed to harbor ALK rearrangement. He was started on first-line ALK TKI therapy with alectinib. He initially experienced partial response with significant reduction in chest wall and nodal lesions, with improved functional status; he became more active and regained weight with therapy, with his wife reporting improved ability to ambulate and participate in activities of daily living. The chest wall and left neck masses nearly resolved.

After approximately 14 months of therapy, the patient began to experience increased fatigue, intermittent right shoulder pain, and the return of new nodules in the left neck region. Serial imaging and labs revealed rising tumor markers, and more recently, he developed progressive right shoulder pain and weakness, affecting his ability to use his right hand and perform fine motor tasks. He has reported progressive decline in performance status, with increased time spent seated, difficulty ambulating without assistance, and increased emotional lability. Pain control became more challenging, with increased opioid requirements and persistent discomfort despite oxycodone and morphine.

His wife has been his primary caregiver, but she notes he is now unable to reliably manage daily tasks and has become more withdrawn, requiring additional care and frequent prompting for activities. The patient reports feeling “more weak,” with occasional difficulty swallowing oral medications and a few recent episodes of coughing/choking with liquids. CHIEF COMPLAINT:
Patient brought to ED via EMS for progressive lower extremity weakness, urinary retention, and failure to thrive. Sent in by oncologist for evaluation of worsening functional status. Known history of stage IV non-small cell lung cancer (adenocarcinoma, mucinous features) with extensive spinal metastasis.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS:
This is a 74-year-old male with a significant medical history including hypertension, type 2 diabetes with neuropathy, COPD, GERD, and advanced lung adenocarcinoma with bony metastatic involvement. He was diagnosed several months ago after presenting with rapid unintentional weight loss (~20 lbs over a few weeks), left shoulder pain, and a palpable lump. Imaging at that time (MRI shoulder and thoracic spine) showed a right lung mass with mediastinal adenopathy and extensive thoracic spine involvement (notably T3–T5) with epidural extension and impending cord compression. CT-guided biopsy confirmed lung adenocarcinoma (negative for actionable mutations; PD-L1 <1%).

He was initially started on high-dose corticosteroids and underwent urgent radiotherapy to the upper thoracic spine (30 Gy over 10 fractions, T1–T6) to preempt neurologic decline; however, his course has since been complicated by progressive disease. PET/CT demonstrated right upper lobe hypermetabolic mass, multifocal nodal and osseous metastases—including multiple thoracic, lumbar, and pelvic lesions, as well as soft tissue deposits. Recent MRI confirmed massive epidural tumor extending from T2–T6 with spinal cord compression and abnormal cord signal, as well as compression fractures of T3–T5. Neurosurgery was consulted but intervention deferred due to the extent of disease and limited benefit.

The patient’s functional status has continued to deteriorate. He was recently admitted for worsening lower extremity weakness, inability to ambulate, and urinary retention. Foley was placed; initial workup ruled out cauda equina, but confirmed ongoing spinal cord compromise. He was started on intravenous steroids (dexamethasone) and tamsulosin. Pain regimen includes escalating opioids. Outpatient therapy with carboplatin, pemetrexed, pembrolizumab, and zoledronic acid was planned but delayed due to acute decompensation. He is now essentially bedbound, anorexic, with further decline over the last two weeks. The home health nurse noted complete inability to mobilize even to wheelchair, poor oral intake, confusion, and the development of a small sacral pressure ulcer. Wife and daughter at bedside report ongoing weight loss (now ~60 lbs over five months), profound fatigue, and episodes of incontinence.

In the emergency room, labs were remarkable for anemia (recent Hgb 8.9 g/dL), mild hyponatremia, elevated BUN, hypoalbuminemia (2.8 g/dL), protein-calorie malnutrition, and multiple electrolyte abnormalities (notably hypomagnesemia). Urinalysis from the Foley catheter revealed evidence of infection (many WBCs, bacteria, positive leukocyte esterase), with subsequent urine culture pending.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS:
- Constitutional: Noted weight loss, progressive debility, and poor oral intake.
- Eyes: Denies vision changes.
- ENT: No sore throat, dental pain, or epistaxis.
- Cardiovascular: Denies chest pain or palpitations.
- Respiratory: Denies cough, hemoptysis, or dyspnea at rest.
- GI: Denies abdominal pain or vomiting; reports constipation.
- GU: Urinary retention requiring Foley; recent hematuria has improved; denies dysuria.
- Musculoskeletal: Profound bilateral lower extremity weakness; right greater than left; unable to ambulate.
- Neurologic: No new headache or seizures; persistent paraplegia; denies acute mental status changes.
- Skin: Developing sacral decubitus.
- Psychiatric: Depressed affect; reports anhedonia.
- Endocrine: No polydipsia or polyuria.
- Allergic/Immunologic: No new rash or allergic symptoms.

PHYSICAL EXAM:
Vital Signs: Temp 36.3°C, HR 81, BP 92/59, RR 18, SpO2 98% on room air, Weight 65.3 kg.
General: Alert, cachectic, moderate temporal wasting, appears older than stated age, malnourished, no acute distress.
HEENT: Normocephalic, atraumatic, oropharynx clear, moist mucous membranes.
Neck: Supple, no JVD or bruits.
Eyes: PERRL, EOMI, no scleral icterus.
Cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm, S1/S2 normal, no murmurs, gallops, or edema.
Respiratory: Lungs clear to auscultation bilaterally, no rales or rhonchi.
Abdomen: Soft, nontender, nondistended, no hepatosplenomegaly, bowel sounds present.
Genitourinary: Foley catheter in place, normal external genitalia, no lesions.
Musculoskeletal: No gross deformity, normal distal pulses, no edema.
Skin: Warm, dry, with a stage I sacral decubitus ulcer midline.
Lymphatic: No palpable lymphadenopathy.
Neurologic: Paraplegic—no voluntary movement of right lower extremity, minimal in left; upper extremities intact; sensation diminished but present in lower extremities; normal cranial nerves.
Psychiatric: Blunted, depressed affect, cooperative.

SOCIAL HISTORY:
- Retired painter, lives with wife, daughter present for support.
- Former cigarette smoker; quit >30 days ago.
- Denies current alcohol or illicit drug use.

FAMILY HISTORY:
- Brother: Heart disease and alcohol abuse.

ALLERGIES:
- Penicillin (rash)
- Bee stings (swelling)

PAST MEDICAL & SURGICAL HISTORY:
- COPD, GERD, hypertension, type 2 diabetes with neuropathy.
- Left knee surgery (MRSA), bilateral rotator cuff repair, coronary stent placement, lumbar spine surgery.

RECENT LABS:
- Hgb: 8.9 g/dL (low), Hct: 27% (low)
- Na: 132 mmol/L (low), BUN: 27 mg/dL (high), Creatinine: 0.48 mg/dL (low)
- Albumin: 2.8 g/dL (low), Total protein: 5.2 g/dL (low)
- WBC: 7.79 x10^3/μL; Platelets: 265 x10^3/μL
- Glucose: 124 mg/dL; A1c 6.3% (previously)
- Mg: 1.2 mEq/L (low), improved after repletion
- UA: Pyuria, bacteriuria, positive for UTI; culture pending
- CXR: Stable right midlung mass, increasing lucency left lateral 5th rib, suggesting bone mets progression
- XR/CT/MRI: Massive thoracic epidural tumor T2–T6, severe cord compression with abnormal cord signal, bony mets throughout thoracic/lumbar vertebrae and paraspinal tissue.

HOSPITAL COURSE (to date):
- On admission: IV fluids, cefepime for UTI, magnesium repletion, resumption of dexamethasone 8 mg BID.
- Pain managed with high-dose oxycodone; previously prescribed but rarely took extended-release morphine.
- Foley changed; sacral ulcer managed with wound care and repositioning.
- Consults: Oncology, palliative care team at bedside; hospice arranged on patient/family request after extensive goals-of-care conversations.
- Family has decided on DNR/DNI code status; patient is aware and expresses desire for comfort-focused care.

Additional palliative measures and transition planning ongoing; patient remains alert and able to participate in discussions, but is bedbound, progressively weak, and requiring full assistance with all ADLs.

**INTERVAL HISTORY:**  
[Deid: Name] is a 56-year-old female with histopathologically confirmed stage IIIA (pT1b, pN2, cM0; AJCC 8th) adenocarcinoma of the left upper lobe, s/p left upper lobectomy with R0 resection. Initial diagnosis was made following incidental detection of a left upper lobe nodule during trauma workup in summer last year, subsequently confirmed as adenocarcinoma with MET exon 14 skipping mutation and high PD-L1 expression (TP 75%). The patient completed 4 cycles of adjuvant carboplatin and pemetrexed, followed by adjuvant atezolizumab, per contemporary management standards for surgically treated high-risk disease with actionable drivers.

She presents today for ongoing evaluation and management. Since her last visit, she reports persistent but gradually improving fatigue. She continues to endorse mild neuropathic symptoms involving her right hand and foot, mainly morning burning and tingling, which resolve after activity. There have been intermittent episodes of arthralgia and morning stiffness involving the wrists and ankles, which have lessened with the use of Tylenol as needed. She denies new fevers, chills, or sweats. She had a brief upper respiratory illness earlier this month with a cough and sputum production, now resolved. Appetite remains stable with steady weight since starting MET-targeted therapy.

No hemoptysis, pleuritic chest pain, or increasing dyspnea reported. She continues to follow up with OB/GYN for prior incidental finding of endometrial thickening; no abnormal uterine bleeding, pain, or gynecologic complaints. Her sleep and mood remain stable with ongoing mental health support and continuation of olanzapine at bedtime. She denies suicidal or homicidal ideations. [Deidentified Name] is a 74-year-old woman with a medical history significant for non-small cell lung cancer (right lower lobe, s/p lobectomy), hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus (on insulin and metformin), coronary artery disease (with RCA stent), chronic kidney disease stage 3, Alzheimer’s dementia, chronic anemia, fibromyalgia, GERD, obesity, and mild intermittent asthma. She follows up today accompanied by family following her recent hospitalization.

The patient was originally diagnosed with stage IV (M1b, limited) squamous cell carcinoma of the right lower lobe in May, confirmed by pathology following surgery (right lower lobectomy with mediastinal nodal dissection). Metastatic evaluation demonstrated a solitary, limited site recurrence (oligoprogressive disease), with repeat imaging confirming less than five lesions and no evidence of disseminated disease.

She completed initial local ablative treatment for thoracic recurrence per oncology recommendations. There have been no new focal neurologic deficits, bone pain, or symptoms suggestive of brain metastases. She does not describe new skin nodules or abdominal discomfort. CLINICAL NOTE

Subjective:

The patient is a 78-year-old African-American male with a history of hypertension, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), hyperlipidemia, prostate cancer (status post radiation), depression, and prior recent pneumonia, who presented following a minor motor vehicle accident as a restrained passenger (no loss of consciousness, air bag deployment). He was previously independent but has experienced progressive cognitive decline, impaired memory, disorientation, and increasing functional dependency over the last several weeks. Family reports significant weight loss (~30 lbs over 3 months), decreased appetite, reduced mobility, and episodes of confusion. He is noted to be hard of hearing and frequently requires assistance from family for communication and medication management.

The patient most recently was hospitalized for confusion, right-sided weakness, and difficulty ambulating. He had been receiving prophylactic anticoagulation (Lovenox) due to recent embolic events. During his admission, a CT of the chest/abdomen/pelvis revealed an incidentally found 7.2 cm right paratracheal lung mass with multiple hypodense liver lesions. Brain MRI identified multiple small foci of acute ischemia bilaterally in cerebral and cerebellar hemispheres, as well as a 1.5 cm cystic mass lesion in the right cerebellar hemisphere, consistent with metastasis and vasogenic edema.

A CT-guided biopsy of the lung mass was performed, revealing adenocarcinoma. Additional workup included a bone scan, which showed areas of uptake in multiple axial skeletal sites (ribs, lumbar and cervical vertebrae, left hip, right scapula) consistent with osseous metastases. No evidence of separate primary lung cancers or multiple synchronous pulmonary nodules was found. The patient’s daughter is actively involved in his care and participates in discussions regarding diagnosis and next steps. The patient’s prior home regimen includes levofloxacin, lisinopril, metoprolol, sertraline, simvastatin, terazosin, and trazodone, which he has been taking with the help of his family.

CHIEF COMPLAINT  
Patient brought to the Emergency Department from home by EMS for worsening weakness and confusion. Per family, the patient has a known history of lung cancer and has not been eating well for several days. On EMS arrival, patient was found to have blood glucose of 43 mg/dL, which improved after oral glucagon and juice en route to ED (repeat BGL: 197 mg/dL).

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS  
This is a 74-year-old African-American female with a history of stage IIIA (T4, N0) lung adenocarcinoma initially diagnosed [DATE: 27149]. Diagnosis was established via CT-guided biopsy of a left lower lobe mass, with histopathology confirming adenocarcinoma. PET/CT at diagnosis showed a hypermetabolic left lower lobe lesion, small irregular nodular densities in the left upper lobe, and hypermetabolic left hilar lymph nodes (SUV max 10.9), but no evidence of abdominal or pelvic metastases. She is a former smoker (quit >30 days ago), previously independent in ADLs with some early cognitive decline.

The patient has notable comorbidities including chronic kidney disease, COPD, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, GERD, and early to moderate dementia. She is accompanied by her daughter, who provides most of the history given the patient's baseline cognitive deficits.

Since her diagnosis, initial work-up included bronchoscopy with EBUS and staging procedures, which revealed no evidence of mediastinal nodal involvement. Staging was completed with brain MRI and other imaging, which were negative for extra-thoracic disease.

She was treated with stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT) to three separate left lung lesions and received one cycle of pembrolizumab. Pembrolizumab was held due to worsening renal function, and she has not received further systemic therapy. Recent oncology notes document declining performance status, poor appetite, and multiple missed oncology follow-up visits over the last several months.

The patient's daughter reports progressive functional decline over the past two weeks with decreased oral intake, weight loss, increased sleepiness, and new-onset urinary incontinence. Over the last 24 hours, the patient became increasingly lethargic and is unable to provide reliable history or participate in self-care. She also reports dark, possibly bloody stools overnight.

No fever, chills, or recent sick contacts. No chest pain, cough, or hemoptysis reported. She has not had falls, although she appears frail and requires assistance with transfers.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS  
Constitutional: Reports weight loss, loss of appetite, and profound fatigue per daughter. No recent fever or chills.  
Eyes: Denies vision changes.  
ENT: Denies sore throat, rhinorrhea, or dysphagia.  
Cardiovascular: Denies chest pain or palpitations.  
Respiratory: Denies cough, hemoptysis, or new shortness of breath.  
GI: Family notes possible melena/BRBPR; no abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting.  
GU: Increased urinary incontinence, no dysuria or flank pain.  
Musculoskeletal: Denies focal joint pain or swelling, but generalized weakness is present.  
Neurologic: Increasing confusion, poor attention, no new focal deficits.  
Psychiatric: Baseline memory loss; no known history of depression or anxiety.  
All other systems reviewed and otherwise negative as per above.

SOCIAL HISTORY  
Lives with significant other in a one-level home. Daughter is frequently present and now providing most self-care. Former tobacco user (last cigarette >30 days ago). No illicit drug use. Past alcohol use, now abstinent.  
No current home health services at the time of admission. Previously independent with intermittent cane use.

FAMILY HISTORY  
Sister with diabetes and hypertension. No known hereditary cancer syndromes.

PHYSICAL EXAM  
General: Elderly, cachectic female, frail-appearing, lying in bed, initially arousable but rapidly tires with questioning.  
Vital Signs:  
- Temp: 36.9°C (oral)  
- HR: 102 bpm, irregularly irregular  
- RR: 20  
- BP: 106/64 mmHg  
- SpO2: 89% on high-flow nasal cannula (25 L/min, 55% FiO2)  
- Weight: 39.7 kg

HEENT: Normocephalic, atraumatic, oropharynx moist, no lesions.  
Neck: Supple, no lymphadenopathy.  
Cardiac: Tachycardic, S1/S2, no murmurs, no JVD, no edema.  
Respiratory: Increased work of breathing, bibasilar crackles, using accessory muscles; oxygen via high-flow nasal cannula.  
Abdomen: Soft, nontender, nondistended, normal bowel sounds, no organomegaly.  
Extremities: No edema, no cyanosis, poor muscle mass bilaterally.  
Neurologic: Lethargic, arousable, oriented to self only; follows only simple commands. CN II-XII grossly intact on limited exam.  
Skin: Warm, dry, no rash, notable for pressure areas on sacrum.  
Psychiatric: Flat affect, minimal spontaneous speech, cooperative.

LABORATORY DATA  
- WBC: 10.4 x 10^3/μL  
- Hgb: 8.3 g/dL  
- Plt: 57 x 10^3/μL  
- Na: 133 mmol/L  
- K: 3.6 mmol/L  
- Creatinine: 0.47 mg/dL (baseline CKD)  
- Albumin: 1.8 g/dL (markedly low)  
- AST: 38 U/L, ALT: 47 U/L  
- Calcium: 7.4 mg/dL (low)  
- Procalcitonin: 0.219 ng/mL  
- Troponin: 0.13 ng/mL (elevated)  
- BNP: 2170 pg/mL

IMAGING  
- Recent chest CT: Chronic left lower lobe spiculated mass with interval decrease in size post-SBRT; new AP window lymphadenopathy; worsening bilateral interstitial changes consistent with fibrosis; no evidence of distant metastases.  
- CXR: Coarse interstitial markings, new diffuse hazy opacities, left-sided pleural thickening.  
- Brain MRI: No acute infarct or metastasis.

HOSPITAL COURSE TO DATE  
Since admission, patient has had progressive decline in functional and nutritional status, persistent hypoxemia requiring escalation from nasal cannula to high-flow oxygen support, and increasing somnolence. She has received empiric IV antibiotics and corticosteroids for concern of pneumonia and possible immune-related pneumonitis. Infectious work-up, including blood and urine cultures, is ongoing; initial set grew Streptococcus species. Concomitant hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia have been corrected. She required transfusion for acute anemia associated with GI blood loss. Lovenox was held due to ongoing GI bleeding. Oncology, pulmonology, cardiology, and palliative care have all been consulted.

PROCEDURES  
- Bronchoscopy with BAL (recent, cytology: atypical but non-diagnostic)  
- Prior CT-guided lung biopsy confirming adenocarcinoma  
- EBUS with negative mediastinal nodes  
- No evidence of actionable EGFR, ROS1, BRAF, ALK-negative; broad molecular profiling was performed and returned positive for ALK gene rearrangement.

MEDICATIONS (current inpatient)  
- Cefepime, vancomycin (IV, for pneumonia/sepsis)  
- Prednisone (IV and PO, corticosteroid for pneumonitis/COPD)  
- Bronchodilators: Albuterol/ipratropium nebulizer, Anoro Ellipta  
- Supplemental oxygen escalated to high-flow nasal cannula  
- Morphine PCA and Ativan as needed for symptoms  
- Other supportive: DVT prophylaxis, PRN Tylenol, magnesium/potassium repletion, PPIs, senna

SUMMARY  
ECOG performance status is poor (3-4), with functional decline, poor oral intake, persistent hypoxemia, and progressive end-organ dysfunction, all in the setting of advanced ALK-positive lung adenocarcinoma previously treated with SBRT and one cycle immunotherapy. Palliative care and comfort measures have been emphasized in discussions with family.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Follow-up for lung cancer.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
The patient is a 58-year-old woman with a history of hypertension and recent cervical spine fusion, now with newly diagnosed stage IIIB (T1-2 N3) non-small cell lung cancer (large cell neuroendocrine carcinoma, per liver biopsy), presenting for ongoing care. She was admitted several weeks ago for progressive upper and lower extremity weakness and numbness, found to have left lower lobe lung mass, extensive liver and bone metastases, and multiple brain metastases on imaging. Further work-up included MRI of the brain, cervical, thoracic, and lumbar spine, confirming multifocal metastatic disease with spinal cord compression at multiple levels and brain involvement (right frontal lobe, left cerebellum) with cerebral edema. Her initial admission was complicated by myelopathic symptoms and functional decline.

After multidisciplinary tumor board review, she was deemed inoperable due to extent of metastatic disease and N3 nodal involvement. She was started on concurrent chemoradiation, with initiation of platinum-based doublet chemotherapy (carboplatin and etoposide) combined with atezolizumab (as part of concurrent CRT) and radiation therapy to the involved spine, pelvis, and brain lesions. She completed radiotherapy to her cervical, thoracic, and sacral spine and received stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS) to brain metastases. She tolerated initial cycles of chemotherapy and RT well, with improvement in lower extremity strength and gait stability, though persistent upper extremity weakness remains (right worse than left). No acute complications reported from therapy; nausea well-managed with antiemetics, no significant neutropenia, and no infectious symptoms.

She completed 3 cycles of concurrent chemotherapy and immunotherapy, alongside chest and mediastinal irradiation. She reports better mobility and is now able to ambulate without her [Deid:Name] in the house, though still uses it at times when outside. Her pain is managed on hydrocodone-acetaminophen as needed, primarily for chest wall and right upper quadrant discomfort (area of known bone and liver disease).

Following completion of concurrent CRT, she was reviewed for consolidation immunotherapy. She maintained good performance status (ECOG 1), no new symptoms, and labs showed adequate marrow recovery. Durvalumab is being considered for consolidation, and the risks/benefits were discussed at length with the patient and her family. She continues on Zometa for bone metastases. A follow-up PET/CT is planned after full response assessment.

raw_note:
CLINICAL NOTE

Oncologic History:
49-year-old male with a known history of tobacco use, COPD, asthma, and diabetes mellitus. No prior neoplastic diagnoses until recent evaluation for new neurologic and systemic symptoms. Social history is significant for smoking (2 packs per day for nearly 40 years). No significant occupational exposures. Family history notable for mother deceased from metastatic breast cancer.

History of Present Illness:
The patient initially presented with a 3-4 week history of progressive lower extremity weakness, worsening right anterior thigh pain, urinary retention, and new-onset diplopia. He also reported persistent headaches, episodes of blurred vision, and recurrent falls due to poor balance. His appetite diminished over the preceding week, with unintentional weight loss, though the exact amount is unknown. He denied overt respiratory complaints such as cough or chest pain but described fatigue and intermittent shortness of breath. No hemoptysis, fever, or night sweats. Urinary retention prompted Foley catheter placement in the emergency department. No gross hematuria but poor sensation in the perineal area. Gastrointestinal review revealed new constipation and absent perianal sensation for several days, with uncertainty about bowel movement frequency due to lack of rectal sensation.

Initial imaging at presentation included MRI of the lumbar spine, which demonstrated numerous nodular lesions throughout the cauda equina and a suggestion of leptomeningeal enhancement. Brain CT revealed multiple bilateral hyperdense lesions, and follow-up MRI brain showed innumerable enhancing lesions across both cerebral and cerebellar hemispheres, consistent with widespread brain metastases. Subsequent MRI of the neuroaxis revealed extensive leptomeningeal metastatic disease throughout the thoracic and cervical spine. CT chest identified a spiculated mass in the right upper lobe measuring approximately 3.4 cm, associated with mediastinal adenopathy. No initial pleural effusion. CT-guided lung biopsy was performed, and final pathology confirmed primary adenocarcinoma; broad molecular and PD-L1 profiling were ordered and results are pending.

Hospital course has been notable for persistent leg weakness (right greater than left), with mild to moderate paraparesis and decreased sensation in the right leg. Foley catheter remains in place due to neurogenic bladder; repeated voiding trials have failed. The patient has required increasing support for ADLs, with deconditioning ongoing despite physical therapy involvement. Bowel management has required laxatives and intermittent enemas for impaction. Pain has generally been controlled with scheduled and breakthrough analgesics. Throughout admission, the patient has been receiving palliative radiation therapy to both the brain and lower spine, with a total of 8 out of 10 fractions completed as of this note. He continues on a high-dose dexamethasone regimen for cerebral edema and neurologic symptoms, with plans for later taper after radiation completion. Seizure prophylaxis is maintained with levetiracetam. Glycemic control has been challenging due to steroid-induced hyperglycemia, requiring insulin titration and correctional dosing. He has demonstrated persistent mild hyponatremia (Na 129-134 mmol/L) and leukocytosis without evidence of infection.

The patient expresses a strong desire to return home. Discharge planning is ongoing and will depend on completion of the planned course of palliative radiotherapy, stabilization of neurologic and urinary function, and adequate support and equipment in the home environment. Palliative care and social work have been closely involved.

Subjective

Patient is a 59-year-old Caucasian male with a history of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and right middle lobe lung cancer (adenocarcinoma, moderately differentiated, status post robotic right middle lobectomy with mediastinal lymph node dissection). He presents post-operatively for ongoing evaluation. He reports that after an initially uneventful post-op recovery, he began to develop sudden shortness of breath with minimal exertion, associated with diaphoresis but without cough, fever, chills, or chest pain. He sought evaluation at an outside emergency department, where imaging revealed a residual right-sided pneumothorax and subcutaneous emphysema. He was subsequently transferred to this facility.

In the hospital, he underwent placement of a right-sided pigtail catheter with immediate improvement in symptoms. He continues to report gradual improvement in dyspnea, and states that he currently has no significant pain, cough, or wheezing. He denies hemoptysis, fevers, chills, night sweats, or recent weight loss. He has noticed facial swelling that is gradually improving. He has no voice changes, and maintains an adequate appetite. No nausea, vomiting, or abdominal pain. He remains afebrile and hemodynamically stable.

Patient is a 77-year-old man with a history of stage IIA poorly differentiated squamous cell carcinoma of the right upper lobe (ROS1 fusion positive), severe COPD, and prior tobacco abuse. Reports mild right-sided chest wall ache, especially with movement. He is able to speak in full sentences at rest, but more winded after modest exertion than baseline. Occasional non-productive cough. No headache, focal neurologic symptoms, or visual changes. No dizziness or confusion. He is aware of increased oxygen requirement and is anxious about disease recurrence, but remains optimistic.

**REVIEW OF SYSTEMS**  
- General: Fatigue with activity, weight loss over several months, no fever or chills.  
- Respiratory: Progressive dyspnea on exertion, no hemoptysis or pleuritic pain.  
- Cardiac: No palpitations, syncope, or orthopnea.  
- GI: Decreased appetite, mild bloating, no N/V.  
- Neuro: No headache, focal deficits, or vision changes.  
- GU: No dysuria, hematuria.  
- MSK: Mild right thoracotomy site discomfort, otherwise no myalgias or arthralgias.

**OBJECTIVE**  
**Vital Signs:**  
BP: 123/75 mmHg | HR: 86 | RR: 22 | O2 Sat: 90–92% on 4 L/min nasal cannula at rest, requirements increased with activity | Temp: 98.0°F (36.7°C)  
HT: 1.78 m | WT: 49.5 kg | BMI: 15.6 kg/m²

**General:**  
Thin, chronically ill-appearing male, alert and cooperative, no acute distress. Breathless with minimal exertion, able to speak full sentences at rest.

**HEENT:**  
No oropharyngeal lesions. Mild temporal muscle wasting.

**Neck:**  
Supple, no JVD, no cervical adenopathy.

**Lungs:**  
Inspection: Mildly increased work of breathing; no tracheal deviation.  
Palpation: Mild right chest wall crepitus near prior incision, no tenderness.

Accessory muscle use absent at rest; mild intercostal retractions with activity.

**Cardiovascular:**  
Regular rhythm, no murmurs/rubs/gallops. Distant heart sounds, no peripheral edema.

**Abdomen:**  
Soft, non-tender, non-distended. Bowel sounds present.

**Extremities:**  
No clubbing or cyanosis. No lower extremity edema.

**Skin:**  
Surgical incision right lateral chest well-healed, no erythema or drainage. Thin skin with evidence of muscle wasting.

**Neurologic:**  
Alert and oriented x3. No focal deficits.

**Mood/Affect:**  
Engaged, expresses anxiety about prognosis but overall appropriate.

**Pulmonary Hygiene/Interventions:**  
- Patient consistently uses incentive spirometry and is compliant with prescribed home and inpatient pulmonary rehab exercises.  
- Cough is minimally productive. Sputum clear.  
- No need for airway suctioning.  
- Patient educated on airway clearance techniques and continues to use oscillatory PEP device as instructed.  
- Chest tube removed prior, incision clean and dry, no evidence of subcutaneous emphysema change.

**Respiratory Therapy**  
- Actively followed by RT for titration of supplemental oxygen and assessment of exertional desaturation.  
- Nebulized bronchodilators with good technique.  
- Maintains scheduled inhaled tiotropium and albuterol as needed.

**Recent Labs:**  
CBC: Mild leukocytosis (WBC 11.7–13.5), chronic anemia (Hgb 11.8–12.6), thrombocytosis.  
BMP: Mild hyponatremia, stable K+, BUN/Cr WNL.  
No acute metabolic derangements.  
Coags: INR therapeutic.

**Imaging:**  
- CXR: Postoperative changes of right thoracotomy and lobectomy. No new large pneumothorax. Persistent right pleural space with incomplete re-expansion of right lower lobe, no new consolidations. Left lung clear.  
- CT chest (recent): Stable surgical changes. No clear evidence of new masses or significant progression in lungs or mediastinum. Previous findings of post-surgical right pneumothorax and pleural space mostly resolved.  
- Brain MRI (surveillance): No evidence of intracranial metastases.

**Medications:**  
- Entrectinib continued; no dose reductions.  
- Inhaled tiotropium daily.  
- Albuterol inhaler as needed, up to four times daily.  
- Low-dose prednisone for baseline COPD, no recent changes.  
- Senna, simethicone for constipation/bloating.  
- Oxycodone as needed for incisional pain, minimal use.

**Rehabilitation/Nutrition:**  
- Continues pulmonary rehab with documented improvement in 6MWT distance but limited by dyspnea and muscle wasting.  
- Dietary intake suboptimal, ensure supplementation ongoing, being monitored by nutritionist.  
- Goal BMI not met; weight loss persists.

**Additional Relevant Observations:**  
- No new findings on skin or extremities.  
- Family present and supportive, patient expresses understanding of clinical status and therapies.  
- No evidence of acute infection or new paraneoplastic syndrome.

---

**[End of Note – No assessment/plan per instructions]**

Nursing Shift Care Plan Summary Note

Pain/Comfort: Patient denies pain this shift. Reports mild intermittent discomfort with breathing, relieved by adjusting position or with low-dose oxycodone as needed. Continues to prefer sitting upright in bed to ease dyspnea. No reports of chest pain or significant distress. Roxanol ordered and administered for breakthrough dyspnea, with reported relief.

Precautions: Fall; Chemotherapy

ASSESSMENT FINDING / INTERVENTION / EVALUATION FOR ACTIVE PROBLEMS DURING THIS HOSPITALIZATION:
Active Problems: Right malignant pleural effusion; metastatic lung adenocarcinoma with ERBB2 (HER2) mutation

Assessment/Interventions:
Patient is alert and oriented x4, but appears fatigued and mildly cachectic. Reports ongoing shortness of breath at rest and with minimal activity, requiring 3 L O2 via nasal cannula to maintain SpO2 >92%. Respiratory rate remains elevated in the 24-32 range, with shallow breathing and increased work of breathing noted on exam. Breath sounds are markedly diminished on the right, with clear left lung. PleurX catheter remains in place, most recently drained 400 mL serosanguinous fluid during the shift, with site dressing clean, dry, and intact. Albumin infused per protocol prior to drainage. Productive cough continues, with intermittent desaturation improved after drainage.

Vital signs show persistent tachycardia (HR 102-120), soft blood pressures (MAP typically 60-68). No current fever. Continuous pulse oximetry in place.

Daily lab results note persistent anemia (Hgb 8.8), mild leukocytosis, low serum albumin, and mild hyponatremia (Na 129); potassium stable with recent mild elevation, resolved after insulin and dextrose per protocol for hyperkalemia.

Patient remains at high risk for falls due to fatigue, intermittent dizziness, and orthostasis, especially when transferring in and out of bed. Foley catheter is draining clear yellow urine throughout the shift, with no signs of retention; patient remains incontinent of stool. Perineal care performed frequently. Skin monitored for breakdown—denuded perianal area treated with Mepilex as ordered.

Gastrointestinal tolerance: Appetite poor, consuming approximately 25–50% of meals. Nutritional supplements declined; patient prefers regular, small meals. Weight stable over past 48 hours per bedscale.

Progress:
Patient reports breathing improved after pleural drainage but continues to tire easily. Remains on scheduled and PRN midodrine for hypotension. Continues to require O2 support for hypoxic events and reports improvement with use of morphine for dyspnea. Fatigue is profound; patient spends most of the time in bed. No new bleeding, nausea, or vomiting. Family present at bedside, actively engaged in care discussions.

ADDITIONAL NURSING FOCUS AREAS (include assessment, interventions, and evaluation details as appropriate):

Activity: Bedrest with assist x2 for repositioning. Too weak to ambulate or transfer to chair today due to increased work of breathing and fatigue. Patient prefers left side lying for comfort and avoids turning to right due to PleurX site.

Nutrition: Regular diet as tolerated, fluid restriction 2000 mL/24hr. Encouraged small, frequent meals. Monitored for intake; prompt assessment of nutritional status ongoing.

Skin: Perianal area and sacrum protected with appropriate barrier products. No evidence of pressure injury at this time.

Goals/Barriers:
Patient Goals for Next Shift: Comfort, continued symptom control for dyspnea, and rest. Wishes to spend time with family and prepare for transition to home hospice tomorrow. Continued monitoring of respiratory status, BP, and effectiveness of symptom interventions.

Discharge Plan/Barriers to Discharge: DC home with hospice support in the morning, pending final symptom management teaching for family, medication review, and home equipment delivery. Barriers include ongoing need for symptom control and physical weakness; family prepared to provide 24/7 support. Hospice to assume primary management following discharge.

Chief Complaint:
Follow-up after surgery for right upper lobe lung mass (NSCLC path: surgical pathway post-resection, adjuvant context). Patient here for post-operative visit. No current complaints but reports expected post-surgical fatigue.

History of Present Illness:
The patient is a 67-year-old male with a history of clear cell carcinoma of the right kidney (s/p right radical nephrectomy in 2016), metastatic at diagnosis to the lung and liver. He also has a history of prostate adenocarcinoma (Gleason 7, T2bN0, post-radiation, with last PSA 6.7), stage 3b chronic kidney disease, coronary artery disease with prior NSTEMI, and chronic heart failure with mildly reduced ejection fraction (~40-45%). He was initially started on sunitinib for RCC, and transitioned to cabozantinib due to progression. He has also experienced prior admissions for GI bleeding related to jejunal angioectasias, treated with argon plasma coagulation.

He was referred for evaluation and management of a right upper lobe lung mass, which was detected on surveillance imaging. PET/CT demonstrated hypermetabolic activity in the right perihilar mass and subcarinal lymph node. Mediastinal staging with EBUS and biopsy confirmed metastatic clear cell renal cell carcinoma. CT chest/abdomen/pelvis showed no evidence of other metastatic disease or local recurrence in the renal bed.

The patient was assessed in the multidisciplinary tumor board. He was determined to be a good surgical candidate based on functional status and adequate perioperative risk profile. He underwent right upper lobectomy with mediastinal lymph node dissection. The pathology revealed clear margins (R0) and no nodal involvement (pN0). The post-operative course was uncomplicated.

He reports moderate post-surgical fatigue but otherwise feels well. No fevers, chills, dyspnea, or wound issues. Denies chest pain, palpitations, hemoptysis, or hematuria. No new neurological symptoms. Diet intake is improving.

CLINICAL NOTE

Chief Complaint:
Has nodule in lung

History of Present Illness:
This is a 65-year-old Caucasian male with significant past medical history including coronary artery disease status post CABG x2, peripheral vascular disease, COPD, prior MI, diastolic congestive heart failure, chronic kidney disease stage III, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, anemia, and arthritis. The patient was admitted for evaluation and management of a recently discovered right upper lobe pulmonary nodule, with associated mild dyspnea on exertion and cough progressing over the prior weeks. Initial outpatient work-up with CT and PET imaging was concerning for a hypermetabolic right upper lobe lesion; tissue diagnosis confirmed adenocarcinoma.

The patient underwent right video-assisted thoracoscopic (VAT) upper lobectomy with mediastinal lymph node sampling. Postoperative recovery was initially unremarkable.

On postoperative day 1, the patient acutely developed left hemiplegia, right gaze deviation, and aphasia. Imaging revealed acute right middle cerebral artery (MCA) infarct, with CT angiogram showing chronic right common carotid artery occlusion and superimposed acute right M1 segment MCA occlusion. The patient was deemed not a candidate for systemic thrombolysis or mechanical thrombectomy due to the chronic carotid occlusion and recent major surgery. He subsequently experienced progressive lethargy and difficulty managing secretions, necessitating intubation for hypoxic respiratory failure.

Hospital Course:
- Pathology from surgical resection showed adenocarcinoma, with tumor distribution and lymph node involvement consistent with advanced stage. 
- The patient was placed on broad molecular testing as per guidelines for all new diagnoses of metastatic adenocarcinoma.
- During the admission, clinical status continued to deteriorate with neurological impairment and persistent ventilator dependence.
- Molecular testing returned positive for ALK rearrangement.

Unable to obtain directly due to intubation and sedation. Review by nursing, medical records, and daughter reveals:

- Lipids: TC 157, TG 184, HDL 44, LDL 76

- CT chest: Review of recent imaging reveals enlarging left lower lobe nodule, peripherally located, without evidence of mediastinal lymphadenopathy or distant metastases.
