She is to follow up in thoracic surgery and oncology clinics for results of final pathology, pathologic staging, and recommendations for further treatment and surveillance. Received written and verbal instructions regarding post-surgical care, signs of infection or pneumothorax, wound management, and return precautions. Also provided education on smoking cessation resources, reviewed lung cancer diagnosis and the importance of routine follow-up for surveillance.

Patient seen in follow-up today following his prior right frontal craniotomy for metastatic adenocarcinoma of the lung. He is here with his wife, who provides most of the collateral history. CLINICAL NOTE

DATE OF SERVICE: [DATE: 29737]

SUBJECTIVE:
Patient is an 81-year-old male with a history of coronary artery disease (remote MI and PTCA in the 1980s), essential hypertension, and mixed hyperlipidemia. He is hard of hearing and uses hearing aids at baseline. He previously lived independently. 
He initially presented with several months of a non-productive cough, which did not respond to antibiotics. Imaging revealed a 3.5 cm left lower lobe lung mass; CT and subsequent surgical resection pathology confirmed moderately to poorly differentiated squamous cell carcinoma (pT2aN1M0, Stage IIA), with metastatic involvement in 2 of 4 resected lymph nodes. Preoperative evaluation was unremarkable apart from mild anemia and elevated WBC. He is a lifelong non-smoker. 

He underwent left lower lobectomy with mediastinal lymph node dissection. Postoperatively, he developed progressive hypoxemia beginning on POD1, escalating to acute respiratory failure on POD3, and was transferred to the ICU and intubated. Since that time, his hospital course has been prolonged and complicated by multiple issues as summarized below.

Since intubation, he has undergone two extubations (post-POD7 and again on POD13), but each time suffered recurrent hypoxic respiratory failure necessitating reintubation and ultimately tracheostomy (placed on hospital day 20). He required intermittent pressor support for hypotension.  
He has experienced persistent right-sided airspace opacities and eventually right pneumothorax, requiring two right-sided chest tubes for ongoing large air leak. He has required high levels of ventilatory support with high PEEP, high FiO2, and is currently on full ventilatory support via tracheostomy. Multiple attempts at weaning have not been tolerated due to hypoxemia and tachypnea. He remains sedated, with periods of deep and moderate sedation, minimal spontaneous movement, and fluctuating (now minimal) responsiveness.

His course was further complicated by paroxysmal atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response and episodes of hypotension, at times requiring vasopressors, and treated with amiodarone, esmolol, and diltiazem at different times. He is now also on therapeutic enoxaparin for atrial fibrillation, and recent episodes of RVR have required IV beta-blockers and rate control.

Family meetings have occurred repeatedly to discuss prognosis and goals of care. The patient previously indicated he wished for life-sustaining treatment but did not want prolonged support if clearly not recovering. His wife and two sons have been present at bedside. Most recently, after discussion of poor prognosis and the likelihood that further recovery is not possible, the family requested transition to comfort-focused care.

OBJECTIVE:
General: Patient is intubated via newly placed tracheostomy, sedated, and appears frail and cachectic. No spontaneous movement. Periods of mild eye opening with stimulation, but no tracking and remains non-verbal. Pupils equal and reactive. No gag reflex. No withdrawal to pain.
Vital Signs: BP ranging from 70s/50s to 110s/60s, HR 80s–130s, T 98–100.6°F, SpO2 90–97% on FiO2 40–70% with PEEP 8–10. Respiratory rate on vent 26–42; spontaneous effort minimal, over-breaths vent intermittently. Weight has decreased from 80 kg (admission) to low 70s (current 74.4 kg).
HEENT: Tracheostomy in place, oral cavity pale and dry.
Cardiac: Irregularly irregular rhythm throughout stay, with periods of sinus rhythm. Soft heart sounds, no murmurs. MAP sometimes <65 mmHg, requiring vasopressors at times.  
Pulmonary: Mechanically ventilated, coarse rhonchi and diminished breath sounds bilaterally, decreased at left base. Two right chest tubes in place, both with continuous air leak and intermittent scant serosanguinous drainage. CXR with persistent bilateral patchy opacities, volume loss at left base, persistent small right apical pneumothorax; no significant interval improvement.  
Abdomen: Soft, nontender, hypoactive to absent bowel sounds. Slight abdominal distension. Last bowel movement several days ago.
Extremities: Warm, no edema. Capillary refill <2s. Pulses present. No clubbing or cyanosis.
Skin: No active rashes. Skin fragile, pale. Scattered ecchymoses, pressure injury at left heel (now resolving).
Neuro: Sedated, unresponsive, PERRL, no withdrawal, no following commands.
Lines/Devices: Right arm PICC, indwelling Foley, tracheostomy, two right chest tubes, GJ tube (pending).

NUTRITION:
Initially on NPO post-op, then surgical soft diet post-extubation with variable oral intake (as low as 25–50%, up to 100%). Noted significant, acute weight loss (~9–11% in first 2 weeks). Barriers to oral intake included severe deconditioning, fatigue, desaturation off BiPAP, and cognitive fluctuations. Oral nutrition supplements (Ensure Complete and Ensure Plus) were trialed, but with fluctuating adherence and overall inadequate intake. After re-intubation, enteral nutrition was provided via NG then GJ tube, with continuous tube feeds titrated based on propofol (Diprivan) administration, meeting estimated energy and protein requirements. Tube feeds were briefly interrupted for planned procedures. Current regimen is Vital AF at 35–45 ml/hr with Pro-Stat supplement, providing 100–100% of needs (caloric and protein). Nutrition status is severely compromised, with acute severe malnutrition by AND criteria. RD continues twice-weekly reassessment; team has considered need for further escalation but now goal of care changed to comfort.

LABS/STUDIES (representative after most recent decompensation):
CBC: WBC 14–20.5 (peak), now ~15.5; Hgb 9.2; Plt 307
Chem: Na 137–141, K 4.0–4.7, CO2 24–32, BUN 39–46, Cr 0.62–0.78  
Glucose: Multiple readings 160–300s, on IV insulin per protocol
ABG (on vent): pH 7.51, PaCO2 39, PaO2 84, HCO3 31, O2sat 98%
PT/INR: 1.2
CXR: No significant change; bilateral patchy airspace disease, persistent right apical pneumothorax, bronchopleural fistula, left lower lobe post-lobectomy changes
Pathology: Final surgical pathology pT2aN1M0 squamous cell carcinoma, 2/4 nodes positive, margins negative (R0), background organizing pneumonia, necrotizing granulomas with yeast forms (compatible with Histoplasma), AFB negative.
BAL: Negative for bacteria and typical fungi; rare yeast on cytology, not cryptococcus/albicans.

MEDICATIONS (current or most recent): 
- Amiodarone, diltiazem, metoprolol as needed for AF with RVR
- Vasopressors (norepinephrine, vasopressin) as needed for hypotension
- Enoxaparin for anticoagulation
- Enteral feeds as above, IV/enteral electrolytes, stress ulcer prophylaxis, insulin infusion
- Fentanyl infusion for comfort
- Antibiotics (Zosyn, vancomycin, levofloxacin, ancef)
- Steroids (methylprednisolone, now discontinued per ID)
- Other chronic home medications as previously listed, held unless able to restart

SOCIAL:
Patient’s wife and sons are present and actively involved in care and decision making. Advanced directive is on file indicating full code status but with a clear preference against prolonged, non-recoverable life support. Family has decided to proceed with comfort-focused measures.

HOSPITAL COURSE SUMMARY:
- Left lower lobectomy for NSCLC (Stage IIA, pT2aN1M0, SCC)
- Multiple ICU transfers, prolonged mechanical ventilation
- Recurrent acute hypoxemic respiratory failure, ARDS
- Refractory atrial fibrillation with RVR and hypotension, requiring high-intensity pharmacologic management and periods of pressor support
- Persistent right pneumothorax, 2 chest tubes for ongoing large air leak, unlikely to close
- Severe acute malnutrition, profound deconditioning and frailty; cachexia
- Recurrent delirium, now unresponsive, deeply sedated
- Hospital-acquired infections ruled out; BAL with yeast suspicious for underlying fungal infection (histoplasma) complicating course
- Goals of care transitioned to comfort as of today after family discussion and with full agreement of care team

[CLINICAL NOTE]


Subjective / History of Present Illness

The patient is an 80-year-old male with a history of hypertension, hyperlipidemia, atrial fibrillation post-ablation, and GERD who was initially hospitalized for severe, persistent back and chest wall pain. Over the last seven months, he has experienced progressive thoracic back pain radiating to the right chest and abdomen, as well as unintentional weight loss of approximately 20 pounds over three months. Appetite has been poor, with anorexia attributed in large part to pain. He also notes dyspnea with exertion but is able to ambulate short distances. There is no hemoptysis or hematuria, but he reports chronic constipation, with bowel movements every three to four days, and a remote episode of hematuria followed by negative urologic workup. No fevers, chills, or night sweats. No headaches or focal neurologic complaints.

Extensive imaging and work-up revealed a spiculated mass in the right upper lobe of the lung, multiple lytic lesions of the thoracic spine and right ribs with associated soft tissue masses, as well as a renal cyst. Biopsy of the right 8th rib confirmed squamous cell carcinoma. MRI of the brain showed no evidence of metastatic disease. PET scan demonstrated metabolically active lesions in the right lung mass, right-sided chest wall/ribs, and evidence of diffuse bone metastasis. There are no symptoms suggesting paraneoplastic syndrome, and no findings suggestive of a second primary or synchronous malignancy.

The patient completed a course of palliative radiation to the T8 vertebral body and right eighth rib with improvement in pain. He was subsequently started on systemic therapy with carboplatin, paclitaxel, and pembrolizumab. Following his initial chemotherapy cycles, he developed significant diarrhea, managed with high-dose steroids, and transient hypoxia requiring low-flow supplemental oxygen. The diarrhea resolved with corticosteroids, and oxygen requirements diminished over time.

He has had intermittent admissions for pain control and associated symptoms (e.g., constipation, fatigue, weakness). Palliative care was extensively involved to optimize analgesic regimens and establish goals of care. He reports significant improvement in pain control with long-acting morphine and occasional hydromorphone for breakthrough pain, along with gabapentin for neuropathic symptoms. Bowel regimen (senna, polyethylene glycol) has kept constipation manageable.

He now resides in an assisted living facility, is supported by his family, and has completed two cycles of systemic therapy. Pain remains well controlled, and he is able to eat and perform basic activities of daily living. He reports no new complaints. He is aware of his metastatic diagnosis and is focused on maintaining quality of life and independence. He has discussed advance care planning and is designated as DNR. 

No recent falls or acute events. He denies fever, chills, cough, or new neurologic symptoms. No shortness of breath at rest, mild with exertion only.

[Deid: Name] Cancer Institute, LUNG PROGRAM  
[Deid: Name] Northwestern Hospital

CLINICAL NOTE

CHIEF COMPLAINT  
Patient is a 73-year-old man with a remote history of left upper lobe lung adenocarcinoma with prior thoracoscopic wedge resection, ongoing metastatic disease, and complex cardiac history, presenting for ongoing follow-up and evaluation.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS  
The patient was originally diagnosed with stage IVB (M1c) non-small cell lung cancer (adenocarcinoma) following a workup for an incidentally found left upper lobe mass after a mechanical fall precipitated by ICD shock (for underlying non-ischemic cardiomyopathy with LV non-compaction and ventricular arrhythmia). Initial staging with PET/CT and subsequent tissue biopsy confirmed a moderately differentiated adenocarcinoma with lepidic features, and genetic profiling revealed a MET exon 14 skipping mutation.

Since diagnosis, the patient has had periodic imaging surveillance and molecular profiling, which has demonstrated disseminated metastatic disease. There is no history of brain metastases or leptomeningeal involvement. Over the past several months, he has reported mild cough but no hemoptysis, weight loss, or worsening respiratory symptoms. He denies new chest pain, dyspnea, or fevers. There have been transient episodes of loose stools, which have resolved. He has tolerated palliative systemic therapy, including targeted therapy with capmatinib, with manageable fatigue and mild peripheral edema but no severe adverse events.

Cardiac status has remained stable. He follows with the advanced heart failure and electrophysiology teams for his non-ischemic cardiomyopathy (EF 30–35%), LV non-compaction, and history of ventricular tachyarrhythmia. His ICD was recently replaced due to battery depletion, with remote monitoring showing appropriate function and no recent arrhythmic events. He is anticoagulated with warfarin for atrial fibrillation and LV thromboembolism risk. He also has a history of hypertension, CKD stage 3, hyperlipidemia, and BPH. There is no current or recent heart failure decompensation, orthopnea, PND, or edema. He uses CPAP nightly for obstructive sleep apnea.

He had an episode of acute appendicitis requiring hospitalization and laparoscopic appendectomy in the past year, complicated by a transient acute kidney injury that resolved. There have been no other recent infections or hospitalizations.

CURRENT MEDICATIONS  
- Amiodarone 400 mg orally 6x/week (none Sundays)  
- Carvedilol 37.5 mg orally twice daily  
- Lisinopril 10 mg orally twice daily  
- Spironolactone 25 mg orally daily  
- Aspirin 81 mg orally daily  
- Warfarin 5 mg most days, 7.5 mg on Fridays (INR monitored)  
- Capmatinib 400 mg orally twice daily  
- Cholecalciferol 5,000 units orally daily  
- Docusate 100 mg orally three times daily  
- Multivitamin daily  
- Acetaminophen 650 mg as needed  
- Pravastatin 40 mg orally at bedtime

ALLERGIES  
No known drug allergies.

SOCIAL HISTORY  
Former smoker (cessation >12 years), ~30 pack-years; no tobacco or vaping use since. Alcohol intake minimal to none. No illicit drug use. Lives with supportive spouse in a single-family home. Has three adult children and several grandchildren. Occupation: retired. No concerning occupational or environmental exposures. No recent travel.

FAMILY HISTORY  
No notable family history of lung cancer. Multiple paternal cousins and a grandson have cardiomyopathy or arrhythmia syndromes; no known hereditary cancer syndromes.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS  
General: No fever, weight loss, or night sweats.  
Pulmonary: Mild chronic cough, no hemoptysis or increased SOB.  
Cardiac: No chest pain, palpitations, orthopnea, PND, or edema.  
GI: Appetite intact, regular bowel habits, no current abdominal pain.  
GU: No dysuria, hematuria, or new symptoms.  
Neuro: No headaches, vision change, or focal deficit.  
Psych: Mood generally stable, happy to be at home, some ongoing adjustment to diagnosis noted in spouse.

PHYSICAL EXAM  
Vitals: BP 102/60, HR 68, Temp 98.1 °F, SpO₂ 96% (RA), RR 16. Height 1.80 m, Weight 114.8 kg, BMI 35.3.  
General: Alert, well appearing, no acute distress.  
Skin: Warm, dry, no rashes, incisions from prior thoracoscopy well healed.  
HEENT: Sclerae anicteric, oropharynx clear.  
Neck: No lymphadenopathy, JVP not elevated.  
Chest: Symmetric expansion, breath sounds clear, no crackles/wheezes.  
Cardiac: Regular S1/S2, no murmurs/rubs/gallops.  
Abdomen: Soft, non-tender, non-distended, healed laparoscopic scars.  
Extremities: No clubbing, cyanosis, or edema.  
Neuro: CN II-XII intact, strength and sensation preserved, gait normal.  
Psych: Appropriate mood and affect, good insight and judgment.

LABS/IMAGING  
- Recent PET/CT: Stable or mildly progressive pulmonary and mediastinal nodal disease, new small hepatic lesion consistent with progression (see prior imaging for baseline). No brain metastases on MRI.  
- Molecular: MET exon 14 skipping mutation confirmed; negative for EGFR, ALK, ROS1, BRAF, KRAS. PD-L1 <1%.  
- Recent CBC, CMP, and INR: within goal range for chronic conditions, creatinine baseline 1.3–1.4.
- Recent echo: LVEF 30–35%, no interval change; mild global hypokinesis.
- ICD device check: Normal function, ~11 years battery life, no recent therapies delivered.

FUNCTIONAL STATUS  
Independent in activities of daily living. Ambulates without assistance. Mild limitations in exertion attributed to baseline cardiac and pulmonary function; able to walk several blocks and manage stairs. Tolerates daily activities well, continues to socialize with friends and family.

NUTRITION  
Tolerating regular diet. Weight stable; BMI remains elevated. No cachexia. No difficulty chewing or swallowing.

PSYCHOSOCIAL  
Maintains positive outlook, reports acceptance of cancer diagnosis and treatment plan. Support system remains strong. Spouse adjusting to diagnosis; anticipatory counseling/support provided. Both report open communication with children and family.

ADDITIONAL NOTES  
- No acute symptoms related to progressive disease.  
- No new neurologic or constitutional symptoms.  
- Continues regular follow-up with Oncology, Cardiology, and Primary Care.  
- Monitored closely for side effects of MET inhibitor, anticoagulation, and cardiac therapy.

---
[End of note]

He was initially diagnosed with NSCLC of the left hilum approximately 12 months ago, with mediastinal involvement and evidence of limited extrapulmonary metastases at presentation. He experienced mild, non-limiting nausea controlled with as-needed ondansetron and prochlorperazine, and ongoing chronic back pain responsive to intermittent dilaudid.

He denied hemoptysis, fever, chills, or night sweats. He reported mild right-sided chest discomfort at times associated with cough, resolved with expectorant and albuterol inhaler. No recent episodes of confusion or focal neurologic deficits. Cognitively intact, oriented to person, place, and date. He denies headache, visual changes, or seizures.

He lives at home with his wife; they jointly owned a sporting goods store prior to retirement. Former smoker (33.75 pack-years), quit ~9 months ago, no tobacco use since. Mother: heart disease (CABG in 70s), deceased  
Father: MI in 60s, deceased  
Sister: cervical cancer, deceased

GI: Occasional heartburn, controlled with omeprazole. No emesis, hematemesis, or melena.  
GU: No dysuria, hematuria, or change in urine output.

- Tiotropium (Spiriva) 18 mcg daily  
- Aspirin 81 mg daily  
- Atorvastatin 40 mg M/W/F  
- Omeprazole 20 mg daily  
- Cetirizine 10 mg daily prn  
- HydroMORphone 2 mg q4h prn  
- Torsemide 20 mg daily  
- Magnesium oxide 500 mg daily  
- Nitroglycerin 0.4 mg SL prn  
- Benzonatate 100 mg tid prn  
- Cholecalciferol 1000 IU daily  
- Oxygen 4 L/min via nasal cannula, continuous  
- Dronabinol 2.5 mg bid (for appetite)  
- Warfarin (recently switched to rivaroxaban for atrial fibrillation)  
- Amiodarone 200 mg bid  
- Prednisone 20 mg daily (on slow taper for post-radiation pneumonitis, per pulmonology)

NECK: No lymphadenopathy, no jugular venous distension.  
LUNGS: Mild kyphosis; breath sounds decreased throughout bilaterally, more pronounced at lung bases. Occasional coarse inspiratory crackles at left base. No wheezes. No dullness to percussion.  
CV: Irregularly irregular rhythm. S1/S2 present, no gallop or rub. Soft systolic murmur at right upper sternal border.  
ABD: Soft, nontender, no masses, no hepatosplenomegaly, positive bowel sounds.  
EXT: No clubbing or cyanosis, trace edema at ankles.

— Recent chest CT: Interval increase in nodular consolidation in left upper lobe along the hilum, highly suspicious for disease recurrence versus infection. Stable mediastinal adenopathy and left lower lobe nodular consolidation. Severe centrilobular emphysema. Small bilateral pleural effusions.

FUNCTIONAL STATUS  
ECOG performance status: 2 (limited self-care; spends >50% of day in chair, gets short of breath with minimal exertion, independent in most ADLs but needs assistance for some activities).

SUBJECTIVE SUMMARY  
The patient is a 71-year-old man with advanced non-squamous NSCLC (oligometastatic at diagnosis, now with radiographic limited progression at the left hilum), severe COPD, HFrEF, atrial fibrillation, and ongoing tobacco-related comorbidities. He is on maintenance pemetrexed, home O2, and supportive therapies. He reports progressive fatigue, decreased exercise tolerance, and chronic cough. Appetite and mood are fair. He denies acute infectious symptoms or active bleeding.

NEUROSURGERY PROGRESS NOTE

[Deid: Name]  NEUROSURGERY AND SPINE

SUBJECTIVE

The patient is a 74-year-old female who was initially diagnosed with Stage IA peripheral non–small cell lung cancer (large cell carcinoma, right upper lobe) in 2019. She underwent right upper lobectomy with mediastinal lymph node sampling and has been followed in oncology clinic since, with no evidence of recurrence until her recent presentation. She presented with three weeks of progressive dizziness, severe vertigo, intermittent frontal headaches, and gradually worsening nausea and vomiting. Her symptoms became so pronounced that she was unable to ambulate without becoming violently ill, and her oral intake decreased substantially. She denied chest pain, shortness of breath, fevers, or chills. No new focal neurological symptoms reported. She also denied any bowel or bladder dysfunction.

Following admission, the patient underwent further work-up including CT and MRI, which revealed multiple supratentorial and infratentorial enhancing lesions, most prominently a right cerebellar mass (3.4 x 3.6 x 2.5 cm) and a left frontal lesion (2.1 x 1.7 x 2 cm), concerning for brain metastases. She underwent stereotactically guided suboccipital craniectomy for resection of the right cerebellar mass with placement of a right occipital ventriculostomy. Postoperative course notable for moderate hemorrhage at resection site and interval increase in size and hemorrhagic component of the left frontal lesion, for which she subsequently underwent stereotactically guided left frontal craniotomy for resection. Foley catheter was required for transient postoperative urinary retention, but was able to be removed, and she is now voiding on her own.

The patient has generally felt improvement in her vertigo and nausea since surgery, though remains easily fatigued. Headaches are much improved and incisional pain controlled with oral medication. She has been actively participating in physical and occupational therapy. No complaints of limb weakness or numbness. No further vomiting; appetite is slowly improving. She is able to ambulate short distances with assistance. She and her husband are aware of her diagnosis and recent interventions and have been updated daily; they continue to express gratitude for the care provided. No new neurological complaints or other medical concerns voiced at this time.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS

General: Denies fever, chills, or weight loss.
HEENT: No visual changes, no diplopia, no new dysphagia. Oropharynx clear.
Cardiac: Denies chest pain, palpitations, syncope.
Respiratory: No shortness of breath, cough, hemoptysis or wheezing.
GI: Denies abdominal pain, constipation, diarrhea, melena. Appetite slowly improving.
GU: Now voiding independently, no dysuria or hematuria, no incontinence.
Neuro: No new weakness, numbness, or seizures. Continued mild expressive dysphasia, which is improving.
Musculoskeletal: No joint pain, no edema.
Skin: No rashes or lesions.

HR: 86 bpm

BMI: 27.8

Eyes: Pupils equal, round, reactive to light. EOMI. No papilledema.
Neck: Supple, no lymphadenopathy or thyromegaly. No JVD.

Respiratory: Clear to auscultation bilaterally, non-labored breathing.
Abdomen: Soft, non-distended, non-tender, normoactive bowel sounds.
GU: Voiding spontaneously. Foley previously in place, now removed.
Extremities: No edema, pulses intact. Moves all extremities spontaneously. No deformity.
Neuro: Awake, alert, oriented. Follows commands. Speech mildly slowed but improving (expressive dysphasia). Cranial nerves II–XII grossly intact. Motor: 5/5 throughout. Sensory: grossly intact. No pronator drift. Gait not directly assessed at bedside, but ambulates with assistance.
Skin: Warm, dry, no rashes or ulcerations.
Psych: Mood appropriate, engaging in conversation.

LABS & DATA REVIEW

Most recent labs notable for mild anemia (Hgb 9.1 g/dL), stable leukocytosis attributed to post-surgical changes (WBC 18.9 x10³/µL), and normal renal function (Cr 0.63 mg/dL). Electrolyte panel stable, with potassium in low-normal range (4.0 mmol/L). Sodium mildly low but stable (135 mmol/L). BUN elevated (34 mg/dL), attributed to perioperative status, diuretic use, and oral intake, improved with IV fluids and diet advancement. Glucose mildly elevated (127 mg/dL), consistent with steroid use. LFTs within normal limits except for mild hyperbilirubinemia (1.1 mg/dL). Urinalysis and culture negative; post-void residual improved, now voiding spontaneously.

Neuroimaging: Most recent postoperative CT (left frontal craniotomy and right cerebellar resection) demonstrates expected post-surgical changes, no new hemorrhage, evolving resolution of prior hematoma, and no hydrocephalus. No new lesions identified.

Biaxin (oral ulcers, throat closing, nausea/vomiting)

Penicillin (nausea and vomiting)
Sulfa drugs (nausea and vomiting)
Codeine (nausea/vomiting)
Corticosteroids (jittery)
Iodine-containing compounds (nausea and vomiting)
Contrast media (nausea and vomiting)

Past medical history: Non–small-cell lung cancer (large cell carcinoma, right upper lobe, pathologic stage IA, 2019), COPD, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, hypothyroidism, osteoarthritis of right hip, fatty liver, GERD.

Immunizations: Pneumococcal vaccine administered.

Patient progressing appropriately in postoperative course, with ongoing improvement in neurologic status and independence. Home health services and close follow-up with primary oncologist and neurosurgery scheduled. Additional details in care plan.

raw_note:
**Clinical Note**

**SUBJECTIVE:**
The patient is a 78-year-old female presenting for follow-up of metastatic non-small cell lung cancer with known MET exon 14 skipping mutation. She was previously diagnosed with stage IVB lung adenocarcinoma and has a history of left upper lobe wedge resection for stage IA disease several years prior; no recurrence at the surgical site since. Over the past year, she has had progression of disease, now with evidence of disseminated pulmonary and extrathoracic metastases (including new nodules seen on most recent chest and abdominal imaging).

The patient recalls a lengthy diagnostic process, with molecular profiling revealing MET exon 14 skipping. She reports completing targeted therapy with capmatinib for over 9 months but recently developed radiographic and clinical progression. She experienced increasing fatigue, anorexia, and mild cough in the preceding weeks. She denies hemoptysis or pleuritic chest pain. No dyspnea at rest, but she is more easily winded with activities of daily living. She denies orthopnea or peripheral edema. She notes mild, intermittent right hip pain, suspicious for bony metastasis but no neurologic deficit or severe localized pain.

She continues to struggle with chronic fatigue, weight loss, and sarcopenia. Decreased appetite persists despite dietary interventions and use of marinol. She has been adherent to current medications, including scheduled omeprazole, iron, oxybutynin, and escitalopram. She has not required narcotic pain medication in the past week. She uses Miralax occasionally for constipation and reports sleep maintenance insomnia but fair response to Lunesta as needed.

Socially, the patient lives at home with her significant other, who assists with meals and mobility. She ambulates with a cane and spends much of her time reading or watching television. She denies tobacco use since 1981; alcohol rarely, no illicit drug use. She has a robust social support system and maintains regular contact with friends and family.

Review of systems is otherwise negative except as detailed above. She denies hematuria, melena, or focal neurologic symptoms. She endorses chronic numbness in her feet. No dysphagia presently. Urinary urgency is stable.

**OBJECTIVE:**
General: Elderly female in no acute distress, alert and conversational.
Vital Signs: BP 132/70 mmHg, Pulse 74, Temp 98.1 °F, SpO2 97% (RA), Weight 54.1 kg (previous 55.2 kg), BMI 21.1 kg/m^2.
HEENT: Normocephalic, atraumatic. Mucous membranes moist. No icterus.
Neck: Supple, no lymphadenopathy or JVD.
Lungs: Breath sounds clear bilaterally, no rales, wheezes, or rhonchi. No increased work of breathing.
Cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm. No murmurs or gallops. No peripheral edema.
Abdomen: Soft, non-tender, no organomegaly or masses. Bowel sounds present.
Musculoskeletal: Ambulates with cane. No focal bony tenderness to palpation of spine or hips. No gross joint effusions. Chronic mild kyphosis.
Skin: No new rashes. Well-healed scar L chest. No ulcers, no jaundice.
Neurologic: Alert. Cranial nerves II-XII grossly intact. Strength 5/5 throughout. Distal sensation decreased in bilateral feet.
Psychiatric: Pleasant and cooperative. Affect appropriate.
Extremities: No clubbing or cyanosis. 1+ pitting edema bilateral ankles (chronic).

Labs:
- CBC: Hgb 10.4 g/dL, WBC 6.8, Platelets 235.
- CMP: Na 138, K 3.9, Cl 104, CO2 23, BUN 28, Cr 0.98.
- LFTs: Within normal limits.
- Calcium: 8.9 mg/dL.
- Vitamin D (previous): Low, on supplementation.
- Recent ALK, EGFR, KRAS, ROS1, BRAF, and RET testing: Negative.
- MET exon 14 skipping: Positive (confirmed on prior broad panel).

Imaging:
- Chest/Abdomen/Pelvis CT (last week): Multiple bilateral pulmonary nodules, new 1.2 cm hepatic lesion, new sclerotic lesion in right iliac crest, stable post-surgical LUL changes. No new pleural effusion.
- Brain MRI (2 months ago): No intracranial metastases.

Current Medications:
- Capmatinib (discontinued after progression)
- Escitalopram 10 mg daily
- Eszopiclone 3 mg nightly PRN
- Omeprazole 20 mg BID
- Oxybutynin 5 mg BID PRN
- Iron gluconate 325 mg daily
- Vitamin D3 4000 IU daily
- Miralax PRN
- Marinol 2.5 mg BID (appetite)
- Acetaminophen 500 mg q4h PRN pain

Allergies: Gabapentin (angioedema), Oxycodone (GI upset).

Wound: No open wounds; chronic venous stasis changes bilateral lower extremities.

Functional Status: Walks with cane. No new falls. Needs assistance with meals and some ADLs.

**[End of Note]**

[Deid: Name]  Age: 79 y.o.  Encounter Date: [DATE: 28972]  
Chief Complaint:  
Patient presents for follow-up after recent diagnosis and treatment for right upper lobe lung adenocarcinoma and subsequent management of mediastinal lymph node involvement.  

HPI:  
[Deid: Name] is a 79-year-old male with a significant past medical history notable for stage IB (pT2aN0M0) right upper lobe adenocarcinoma, status post right upper lobectomy and mediastinal lymph node dissection in 2015. Final pathology showed 2.6 cm acinar adenocarcinoma with pleural invasion and negative margins; all sampled nodes were negative for metastatic disease at the time of resection. He has a remote history of significant tobacco use (approximately 49 years), COPD with prior exacerbations, and multiple other comorbidities including chronic diastolic heart failure, peripheral vascular disease, aortic insufficiency with severe calcific stenosis (recently treated with TAVR), recurrent right pleural effusion, and gallstones.

Several months after resection, surveillance imaging detected new mediastinal lymphadenopathy. PET-CT revealed FDG-avid right paratracheal and subcarinal nodes. EBUS-TBNA confirmed metastatic adenocarcinoma (N2). No distant metastases were identified on PET-CT or brain MRI. Multidisciplinary tumor conference consensus was for non-surgical management of mediastinal disease given comorbidity burden, prior lobectomy, and patient/family preference.

He received definitive concurrent chemoradiation with weekly carboplatin/paclitaxel and IMRT to the mediastinum. Radiation was completed without major interruption. He developed moderate esophagitis and mild fatigue but no hospitalizations. There was no gross disease progression or new extrathoracic involvement during therapy. Post-treatment imaging showed decreased nodal volume, no evidence of new disease, and no radiographic or clinical progression.

Following completion of concurrent chemoradiation, he started on consolidative durvalumab. He tolerated immunotherapy reasonably well; he experienced mild infusion-related fatigue but no significant immune-mediated adverse events. He completed the planned course of durvalumab. Serial imaging (chest CT and PET) after completion of consolidation have continued to show stable post-radiation changes, absent metabolic activity in previously involved nodes, and no interval development of new or recurrent pulmonary lesions or distant metastatic disease.

He now presents as an active cardiac rehab participant after recent successful TAVR. He continues outpatient management for heart failure and COPD. He is able to ambulate independently at home and with supervision at cardiac rehab, although he describes some baseline exertional dyspnea similar to his previous functional status. He denies chest pain, palpitations, orthopnea, or paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea. He continues to smoke 2-3 cigarettes a day and has declined to set a definitive quit date despite ongoing counseling. He is not interested in additional treatment at this time.

Current Medications:  
- albuterol HFA inhaler: 2 puffs every 4 hours as needed  
- fluticasone-salmeterol (ADVAIR) 250-50: 1 puff twice daily  
- tiotropium (SPIRIVA): 2 puffs daily  
- torsemide (DEMADEX): 20 mg twice daily  
- aspirin 325 mg daily  
- Breo Ellipta 200/25 mcg: 1 puff daily  
- Nebulizer as needed  
- Additional cardiac and symptom-directed medications as per cardiology.

Allergies:  
No known drug allergies.

Social History:  
- Former creamery worker, now retired.  
- Lives independently in a single-family home.  
- Widowed, children are nearby and supportive.  
- Smoking: 2-3 cigarettes daily, past exposure >49 years, slow reduction strategy.  
- Alcohol: none.  
- Denies illicit drug use.

Family History:  
- Father: cancer  
- Mother: depression

Review of Systems:  
- General: Denies weight loss, fever, chills, night sweats, or fatigue beyond baseline.  
- Cardiac: No chest pain, PND, orthopnea, palpitations, or syncope.  
- Respiratory: Stable baseline exertional dyspnea, no acute increase. No cough or hemoptysis.  
- GI: Denies new dysphagia, heartburn, nausea, vomiting, or abdominal pain.  
- GU: No dysuria or hematuria.  
- Neuro: No headache, focal weakness, numbness, or new cognitive changes.  
- Psych: Denies depression or anxiety, maintains positive outlook.  
- Skin: No rashes, ulcers, or new lesions.

Physical Exam:  
General: Pleasant, alert, comfortable elderly male in no acute distress.  
Vital Signs: BP 104/60 mmHg | Pulse 79 | Wt 98.4 kg (217 lb) | SpO2 97% | BMI: 29.43 kg/m²  
HEENT: Normocephalic, atraumatic. No scleral icterus. Mucous membranes moist.  
Neck: No lymphadenopathy or JVD.  
Respiratory: Chest wall symmetric, clear to auscultation bilaterally, end-expiratory wheeze and prolonged expiratory phase. No crackles or rales. No increased work of breathing.  
Cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm. Normal S1/S2. No murmurs, rubs, or gallops. Peripheral pulses 1+ bilaterally, no JVD.  
Abdomen: Soft, nontender, nondistended, normoactive bowel sounds. No hepatosplenomegaly.  
Extremities: No clubbing, cyanosis, or digital edema. Mild bilateral pitting edema, stable.  
Skin: Healed surgical scars on chest, no active skin lesions.  
Neuro: Alert, oriented, normal strength and sensation.  
Psychiatric: Appropriate affect.

Laboratory and Imaging Findings:  
- Most recent CBC and basic metabolic panel: stable, within acceptable ranges for age and comorbidity.  
- Surveillance chest CT: stable post-radiation changes, no suspicious nodularity or lymphadenopathy.  
- PET/CT: no FDG-avid disease.  
- Most recent echocardiogram: normal function of prosthetic aortic valve, no evidence of new cardiac dysfunction.  
- Pulmonary function testing: consistent with known moderate-severe obstructive defect, stable from prior.  
- No evidence of locoregional or distant recurrence on recent imaging.

Current Outpatient Medications:  
- See above comprehensive list; reviewed and reconciled for accuracy.

Summary:  
Patient is over 1 year out from concurrent chemoradiation and immunotherapy for pN2 mediastinal node-positive adenocarcinoma of the right lung. He has remained on scheduled surveillance with clinical and radiographic stability. Continues to be followed closely for comorbid cardiac and pulmonary disease, as well as for ongoing tobacco cessation efforts. No evidence of disease recurrence to date. 

[End of Note]

Follow-up for lung cancer.  

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS  
[Deid: Name] is a 73-year-old woman with a history of poorly differentiated squamous cell carcinoma of the right lung (clinical stage cT3N1M0, PD-L1 negative, MRI brain negative for osseous or parenchymal metastases) and MALT lymphoma of the nasopharynx, who presents today for routine post-treatment surveillance.

She was originally diagnosed three years ago after presenting with persistent cough and intermittent exertional dyspnea. Initial PET/CT demonstrated a hypermetabolic mass in the right upper lobe with additional small nodules in the right apex and left upper lobe, as well as a midline nasopharyngeal lesion. Further workup included bronchoscopic biopsies confirming squamous cell carcinoma, and nasopharyngeal tissue consistent with low-volume MALT lymphoma. Mediastinal node biopsies were negative for malignancy.

Her initial management involved multidisciplinary review. She received concurrent chemoradiation with weekly paclitaxel and carboplatin and a total radiation dose of 60 Gy to the chest, completed without major complications. Subsequently, she received two cycles of full-dose paclitaxel/carboplatin. Follow-up imaging demonstrated partial response with significant reduction of the right upper lobe and hilar mass, but new small nodules in the right upper and left upper lobes, radiographically equivocal for tumor versus treatment-related pneumonitis. These nodules were not PET-avid and were monitored with serial CT scans. 

Post-chemoradiation, she was initiated on consolidation durvalumab, which she completed one year ago. Of note, she experienced right-sided shingles during therapy that resolved with antivirals, leaving residual hyperpigmentation and mild neuropathy, managed currently with gabapentin.

Since the completion of systemic therapy, she has remained clinically stable. She reports no fevers, chills, hemoptysis, or new bone pain. Her cough is only intermittent and nonproductive, and she denies chest pain, hematuria, headache, or significant change in dyspnea. raw_note:
NURSING SHIFT CARE PLAN SUMMARY NOTE

Pain/Comfort: 
Patient continues to report significant discomfort primarily in the back, neck, and at abdominal incision site. Describes ongoing chest pain with deep breaths as well as persistent back pain and tenderness at the incisional area—pain is intermittently rated 6–7/10. Tylenol offered but refused; PRN hydroxyzine administered per provider order with moderate relief. Dilaudid provided for breakthrough pain, with resultant improvement but ongoing requests for additional doses. Patient is also experiencing overall discomfort with mobility and is often reluctant to participate in repositioning or self-care activities due to pain.

Precautions: 
Patient remains on fall precautions given history of debilitation, recent surgery, and reported episodes of lightheadedness and fatigue. Bed in lowest position, bed alarm engaged, and call light within reach at all times.

ASSESSMENT FINDING/INTERVENTION/EVALUATION FOR ACTIVE PROBLEMS DURING THIS HOSPITALIZATION:

Active Problems: 
Pain (chronic and acute post-op), open midline abdominal incision with dehiscence at inferior aspect, ostomy with recent stoma color changes, wound infection (E. coli ESBL positive), and acute on chronic hypoxia. Also has history of atrial fibrillation with variable control, and advanced COPD contributing to respiratory symptoms and oxygen desaturations. 

Assessment/Interventions:
Patient is alert and oriented but becomes irritable and anxious when in pain; forgetfulness noted at times. She is afebrile, but required escalation of oxygen overnight due to desaturations (SpO2 dropped to 86% on room air, improved to 94% on 2L NC; currently ranging 89–94% on 2–3L). Lungs with diminished breath sounds and expiratory wheezes bilaterally, worse with activity. Staff continues to encourage use of incentive spirometer and deep-breathing exercises, though patient frequently refuses citing discomfort. 

Abdominal exam: midline incision remains partially open at distal end, with purulent and sometimes yellow/green drainage noted. Wound packing and ABD dressings changed at least twice per shift according to wound care protocol; tissue culture positive for ESBL E. coli, now on meropenem per ID recommendations. Wound and ostomy team continue to monitor and guide care. Ostomy stoma is dusky/maroon with the area of superficial mucosal slough; patent with moderate output, emptied three times this shift, but patient consistently refuses education or participation in ostomy management. JP drain present, draining minimal serous fluid.

Patient is incontinent of urine and requests ongoing use of Purewick device, which is kept in place with regular assessments for skin integrity. No rashes noted. Briefs changed as needed for incontinence; patient is encouraged to participate with hygiene but has minimal engagement.

Activity: Patient remains bedfast; requires assist of 2 and sometimes a mechanical lift for repositioning due to weakness and pain. She continues to refuse ambulation or attempts to transfer to chair despite repeated education on benefits for wound healing and pulmonary status.

Nutrition: Recently advanced to regular diet, but intake variable due to poor appetite and intermittent nausea. Tolerating sips and small meals; Ensure supplement offered. Oral cavity tender—nystatin ordered for oral mucosal changes.

raw_note:
---
**CLINICAL NOTE**

**Subjective / History of Present Illness:**

This is a 53-year-old male with a known history of stage IIIB (T1-2, N3) squamous cell carcinoma of the left upper lobe, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), hyperlipidemia, and paranoid schizophrenia. The patient was initially diagnosed after presenting for evaluation of palpitations and shortness of breath; workup revealed a large hilar mass and complete collapse of the left upper lobe.

He is currently undergoing concurrent chemoradiation with carboplatin and paclitaxel along with daily thoracic radiation therapy. BNP 171 (no acute CHF), troponin <0.01  
INR 1.0 (holding warfarin peri-op)

ECG: AF with RVR, incomplete RBBB, ventricular response rate variable

- After lobectomy, developed severe respiratory failure (acute on chronic) with hypercapnia, requiring BiPAP and ICU transfer for pulmonary support.  
- Weaned gradually, transitioned to high-flow O2, then to nasal cannula; now maintained on 4–6L NC.  
- Multiple episodes atrial fibrillation with RVR; rate control with diltiazem (increased) and sotalol (held), now on metoprolol.  
- Diuresed with IV/PO furosemide; mild pitting edema currently.  
- Recent swallow evaluation recommended (pending).  
- Ongoing PT/OT; deconditioned, mild improvement in strength and stamina.  
- Ongoing broncho-pulmonary hygiene with RT support; suctioning as needed, incentive spirometry in use, regular nebs and inhalers administered.  
- No current infection; afebrile, down-trending WBC.  
- Daughter updated regularly; goals of care and advanced directives reviewed.  
- Awaiting multidisciplinary consensus for management of multiple synchronous lung nodules and mediastinal involvement; pending MRI brain for staging.

NURSING/ANCILLARY  
- Respiratory: BiPAP as needed, O2 titrated per SpO2, RT support, suctioning as indicated; chest physiotherapy, upright positioning, pulmonary toilet encouraged.  
- Pain: IV dilaudid PRN, transitioned oral as tolerated; pain ball at incision site.  
- Nutrition: Adequate oral intake; swallow study pending.  
- Mobility: Up to chair with assist; PT/OT daily.  
- Continence: Foley d/c’d, independent voiding.  
- Incision: Clean, dry, well approximated.  
- Communication: Oriented, able to answer questions, demonstrates understanding.

SUMMARY  
Status post-lobectomy for Stage IB lung adenocarcinoma with acute post-op respiratory failure, now improving. Notable for multifocal lung nodules and new mediastinal lymphadenopathy; EBUS positive for small cell carcinoma in right interlobar node, other sites negative. Functional status impaired but improving with supportive care. Multiple comorbidities including severe COPD, AF, CAD, DM2, and history of breast cancer. Close respiratory, cardiac, and oncologic monitoring ongoing. Daughter updated on all results; advanced care planning discussions ongoing in setting of new metastatic findings.

CHIEF COMPLAINT: 
Follow up after recent surgical resection of left lower lobe lung cancer.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS:
[Deid: Name] is a 70-year-old male with a new diagnosis of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), adenocarcinoma, left lower lobe. He initially presented with a lung mass found on imaging obtained during a hospital admission for back pain. Further work-up included chest CT which revealed a 1.3 cm left lower lobe mass with suspicious features. PET-CT demonstrated mild uptake in the left lower lobe nodule; no evidence of metastatic disease. No additional suspicious lesions were identified in the skeleton.

The patient underwent a complete surgical workup, including pulmonary function testing and cardiology clearance, and was deemed an appropriate surgical candidate (good performance status, ECOG 0-1). 

He proceeded to flexible bronchoscopy, left video-assisted thoracoscopic (VAT) left lower lobe wedge resection, and completion left lower lobectomy with thoracic lymphadenectomy on [DATE: 25892]. Intraoperative frozen section confirmed adenocarcinoma. Mediastinal and hilar nodal sampling were performed, and no gross nodal involvement was seen intraoperatively.

POSTOPERATIVE COURSE:
Immediate postoperative recovery was uncomplicated. He was transferred to surgical floor, with respiratory and hemodynamic stability throughout. Pain was well-controlled on multimodal analgesia (acetaminophen, gabapentin, as needed oxycodone). Incentive spirometry and early ambulation initiated on POD1.

The patient was able to ambulate independently and tolerate oral intake. Incentive spirometry volumes improved from 1000 to 1250 cc by POD2, and he required no supplemental oxygen. Chest tube was removed on POD1 after clamping trial and confirmation of no air leak or pneumothorax on CXR. Surgical incisions were clean, dry, and intact on serial examinations. 

He experienced postoperative urinary retention, requiring one straight catheterization overnight with 800 mL returned. PVRs were persistently elevated (>400 mL), although he was able to void small amounts spontaneously. He was started on tamsulosin, with some improvement noted in volume of spontaneous voids, but ultimately required short-term indwelling catheter at discharge for comfort and to prevent recurrence. Plans were made for urology follow up and voiding trial outpatient.

He had one episode of emesis after consuming a large hamburger on POD3, attributed to dietary indiscretion; otherwise, he tolerated diet well and resumed normal bowel function with medical management for constipation.

The discharge plan included resumption of home medications, wound care, activity as tolerated, and close follow-up with surgery, oncology, and urology. He was discharged home with support from his co-op community.

SOCIAL HISTORY:
Lives alone in a senior co-op, strong network of friends and supportive siblings nearby. Quit smoking over 20 years ago (35 pack-year history). Rare alcohol use.

FAMILY HISTORY:
Mother: heart disease and alcoholism. Father: psychiatric illness. Siblings: hypertension. Brother with history of melanoma.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS:
– Denied chest pain, shortness of breath, palpitations, cough, or hemoptysis perioperatively.
– No fevers or chills. Denied calf pain or swelling.
– Denied current wound issues, rashes, or new skin lesions.
– Neuropathy symptoms in feet present but stable.
– Denied headaches, dizziness, or syncope.

MEDICATIONS:
- Acetaminophen 1000 mg q6h PRN
- Oxycodone 5 mg q4h PRN
- Gabapentin 300 mg TID
- Lovastatin 40 mg QHS
- Allopurinol 300 mg QD
- Aspirin 81 mg QD
- Tamsulosin 0.4 mg QD (recently started)
- Multivitamin QD
- Ammonium lactate cream PRN for dry skin

ALLERGIES:
- Naproxen (hives)
- Lisinopril-hydrochlorothiazide (angioedema)

VITAL SIGNS: [POD2]
BP 138/60 mmHg | Pulse 76 | Temp 96.8°F (36°C) | Resp 18 | Ht 1.73 m (5'8") | Wt 110 kg (242 lb) | BMI 36.9 kg/m² | SpO2 99% on room air.

PHYSICAL EXAM:
General: Alert, well-nourished, in no acute distress, sitting comfortably in chair.
Cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm, normal S1/S2, no murmurs.
Pulmonary: Clear to auscultation bilaterally. Incentive spirometry volumes to 1250 mL.
Abdomen: Soft, non-tender, normal bowel sounds. Passing flatus, normal bowel movements resumed.
Genitourinary: Indwelling foley catheter in place at time of discharge for persistent retention.
Extremities: No edema, no calf tenderness.
Wound: Thoracoscopy incisions well-approximated, steri-strips intact, no erythema, no drainage. Chest tube site clean and dry.
Skin: No rashes or lesions noted.

LABS/IMAGING:
Preop:
- PET-CT negative for distant disease.
- Pulmonary function tests WNL for surgery.

Postop:
- Pathology: Confirmed adenocarcinoma of left lower lobe, completely resected (stage IB, pathologic). Margins negative (R0). No evidence of nodal metastases (N0).
- CBC and BMP stable throughout perioperative course.

FUNCTIONAL / PSYCHOSOCIAL:
Ambulating independently. Physical therapy cleared for home without additional therapy. Patient is alert, oriented, and motivated for recovery. Some anxiety related to final pathology, addressed by surgical and nursing teams.

DISCHARGE INSTRUCTIONS (summarized, not plan):
– Wound care instructions given; okay to shower after chest tube site dressing removed.
– Use incentive spirometer hourly while awake.
– Ambulate as tolerated.
– Foley catheter to remain until voiding trial with urology.
– Continue bowel regimen as needed.
– Resume all home medications including tamsulosin for BPH.
– Follow up with surgery and oncology as scheduled.
– Monitor for fever, increased pain, wound changes, signs of infection or DVT.

**Clinical Nutrition / Initial Assessment**

**Reason for Assessment:**  
Physician order for nutrition support and assessment for weight loss.

**Nutrition Assessment:**

**Client History:**  
The patient is a 61-year-old female with a history of non-small cell lung cancer (status post-pneumonectomy), chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), alcohol use disorder, and generalized weakness. She presented to the emergency department with progressive weakness over the past two weeks, reporting episodes of severe weakness so profound that she needed to crawl on the floor at home. She lives alone, with her daughter intermittently checking in, and her husband has recently come to stay with her for additional support. She reports poor appetite and significant difficulty preparing meals due to low energy; typically, she is able to eat only one or two meals daily, with better intake in the morning. Occasionally, friends or family prepare food for her. She has recently started consuming Ensure/Boost supplements at home.

**Diet Order:**  
Regular diet.

**Energy Intake:**  
No intakes documented prior to assessment; patient described chronically poor intake, generally only eating 1–2 meals per day and often skipping meals for lack of strength and appetite. On some occasions, she has required assistance to obtain or prepare food. She has recently started oral nutrition supplements (Ensure/Boost).

**Supplement Intake:**  
Recently started commercial nutrition supplements as able.

**Food Allergies/Intolerances:**  
No known food allergies.

**Anthropometrics:**  
- Height: 1.6 m (5'3")  
- Weight (recent):  
  - [DATE: 22477]: 105 lbs 14.4 oz (48.0 kg)  
  - [DATE: 22476]: 120 lbs (54.4 kg, estimated)  
  - [DATE: 22102]: 122 lbs (55.3 kg)  
  - [DATE: 22096]: 115 lb 6.4 oz (52.34 kg)  
  - [DATE: 21762]: 117 lb 1.6 oz (53.1 kg)  
- Body Mass Index: 18.76 kg/m²  
- Weight history notable for ~14% loss over the past year, with a reported acute loss of ~10 lbs in the week prior to admission.

**Medications:**  
Folic acid, multivitamin, thiamine, and reviewed others.

**Biochemical Data/Medical Tests:**  
Labs notable for Na 146, BUN 4; others reviewed.

**Physical Exam / Nutrition-Focused Physical Findings:**  
- General appearance: Thin, frail, with visible loss of muscle mass; notably in the calves.
- Skin: Intact.
- Digestive: No bowel movement at time of assessment.

**Nutrition Education:**  
Nutrition education anticipated as appropriate; will be tailored to patient and family as needs arise.

**Malnutrition Criteria (per AND Clinical Characteristics):**  
- Chronic severe reduced energy intake for at least one month.
- Documented significant weight loss (unable to quantify precisely due to limited records, but patient and EMR indicate >10% over past year, with acute further loss).
- Mild acute muscle mass loss on exam.

**Recommended Nutrition Diagnosis:**  
Moderate malnutrition in the context of chronic illness (non-small cell lung cancer, COPD, and alcohol use disorder).

**Interventions:**

1. **Meals and Snacks:**  
   - Continue regular diet as tolerated.  
   - Strongly encouraged to consume small, frequent meals throughout the day.  
   - Strategies discussed include preparing larger meals when able and saving leftovers, as well as utilizing meal delivery or Meals on Wheels-type services.  
   - Advised to choose high calorie and high protein foods as much as possible.  
   - Husband provided with a list of high-calorie, high-protein foods/snacks and basic recipes.  
   - Encouraged consistent daily multivitamin use.  
   - Comfort menu made available to maximize oral intake.

2. **Medical Food Supplement:**  
   - Commercial beverage supplements (Ensure Enlive) recommended three times daily between meals/snacks. Each bottle provides 350 kcal and 20 grams of protein with HMB for lean body mass maintenance.

**Monitoring and Evaluation:**  
Plan for reassessment by Registered Dietitian within 1–5 days or sooner as clinically indicated.

**Nutrition Discharge Planning:**  
To be determined. Will coordinate with care team and social work regarding home support, food security, and supplement access.

**Registered Dietitian Signature:**  
[Deid: Name], LD, Clinical Dietitian  
[DATE: 22477]

SUBJECTIVE

History of Present Illness:
Mr. [Deid: Name] is a 57-year-old Black male with a history of poorly differentiated right lower lobe lung adenocarcinoma (6.5 cm, 2/9 lymph nodes positive, PD-L1 negative) diagnosed in [DATE: 20204]. He underwent right lower and middle lobectomy with mediastinal lymphadenectomy ([DATE: 20259]) followed by adjuvant chemotherapy with carboplatin and paclitaxel, completed [DATE: 20366]. Initial follow-up PET and brain MRI showed no evidence of residual or metastatic disease. He was monitored with serial imaging, and had chronic stable mild COPD and hypertension.

In [DATE: 20551], he presented with approximately two weeks of progressively debilitating right-sided headaches, dizziness, unsteadiness, and blurred vision, particularly on the left side. Neurologic review revealed mild confusion, gait instability, and some difficulty with left peripheral vision. He denied fevers, chills, weight loss, or recent sick contacts. There was no numbness or focal weakness.

A CT scan of the head revealed a right parietal/occipital mass (5.5 x 3.9 x 4.1 cm) with significant vasogenic edema and a leftward midline shift of 9 mm. MRI confirmed a peripherally enhancing cystic lesion in the same location. There was no evidence of other metastatic disease on CT chest/abdomen/pelvis or PET scan. He was admitted and started on IV dexamethasone.

After discussion in a multidisciplinary setting, the patient, his wife, and family agreed to proceed with a right parietal craniotomy for tumor excision. The procedure was performed successfully on [DATE: 20562], and the postoperative course was notable for improvement in headaches and neurological function. Pathology confirmed metastatic adenocarcinoma of lung origin. He subsequently completed stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS) to the resection cavity per recommendations from radiation oncology.

Over subsequent weeks, the patient recovered well, gradually weaning off steroids with no recurrence of severe neurologic symptoms. He reported transient mild post-operative confusion and imbalance, which improved steadily. He remained functional at home with his wife, ambulating independently with a cane.

About 2–3 months later, the patient experienced new onset of seizure activity, characterized by a witnessed tonic-clonic seizure at home with post-ictal confusion and transient left arm weakness. He was brought to the emergency department by his wife. He had been prescribed levetiracetam (Keppra) for seizure prophylaxis but admitted to occasionally missing doses. Examination in the ED was notable for full orientation and no focal deficits, though he reported mild persistent left arm paresthesia. Repeat MRI demonstrated three new right parietal-temporal enhancing lesions measuring up to 3.5 cm, all within or adjacent to the previous surgical site, again associated with vasogenic edema and 7 mm midline shift. No new extracranial disease was found on PET imaging.

The patient was admitted and started on IV dexamethasone and levetiracetam, with a plan for further local therapy. After further multidisciplinary discussion involving neurosurgery, oncology, and radiation oncology, he underwent repeat craniotomy with tumor resection and SRS to new lesions. Postoperative course was notable for mild hyponatremia, managed with temporary fluid restriction and salt tablets, and brief urinary retention managed with tamsulosin and short-term Foley catheterization. There was also transient postoperative confusion that resolved with correction of sodium.

Currently, the patient is at his neurologic baseline. He continues to reside at home with his spouse, performing personal ADLs with some assistance. His wife is his primary caretaker. He ambles with a cane and climbs stairs with supervision. Mild residual cognitive changes and left hand numbness persist but do not impair function.

- COPD (moderate, not on home O2)
- Hypertension
- Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (diet-controlled)
- Arthritis, Depression, PTSD

Surgical History:

- Stereotactic radiosurgery to brain ([DATE: 20618], [DATE: 20742])

- Sertraline 200 mg daily
- Tiotropium and budesonide-formoterol inhalers daily
- PRN acetaminophen, Zofran, tamsulosin
- Gabapentin, mirtazapine, prazosin for pain/arthropathy and PTSD

Allergies: No known drug allergies

Social History:

- No current tobacco, alcohol, or illicit drugs
- Married, lives in a multilevel home with spouse; ambulates with cane
- Retired, limited physical activity due to prior surgeries/illnesses

Family History:
- Hypertension: mother and father
- Diabetes: mother

Review of Systems:
- Constitutional: No fever, chills, or weight loss.
- HEENT/Eyes: Mild blurry vision, no new changes.
- Neuro: No new headache; left hand numbness persists. No weakness.
- Respiratory: No cough or shortness of breath.

He underwent right lower and middle lobectomy with mediastinal lymphadenectomy ([DATE: 20259]) followed by adjuvant chemotherapy with carboplatin and paclitaxel, completed [DATE: 20366]. Initial follow-up PET and brain MRI showed no evidence of residual or metastatic disease. He was monitored with serial imaging, and had chronic stable mild COPD and hypertension.

In [DATE: 20551], he presented with approximately two weeks of progressively debilitating right-sided headaches, dizziness, unsteadiness, and blurred vision, particularly on the left side. Neurologic review revealed mild confusion, gait instability, and some difficulty with left peripheral vision. He denied fevers, chills, weight loss, or recent sick contacts. There was no numbness or focal weakness.

A CT scan of the head revealed a right parietal/occipital mass (5.5 x 3.9 x 4.1 cm) with significant vasogenic edema and a leftward midline shift of 9 mm. MRI confirmed a peripherally enhancing cystic lesion in the same location. There was no evidence of other metastatic disease on CT chest/abdomen/pelvis or PET scan. He was admitted and started on IV dexamethasone.

After discussion in a multidisciplinary setting, the patient, his wife, and family agreed to proceed with a right parietal craniotomy for tumor excision. The procedure was performed successfully on [DATE: 20562], and the postoperative course was notable for improvement in headaches and neurological function. Pathology confirmed metastatic adenocarcinoma of lung origin. He subsequently completed stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS) to the resection cavity per recommendations from radiation oncology.

Over subsequent weeks, the patient recovered well, gradually weaning off steroids with no recurrence of severe neurologic symptoms. He reported transient mild post-operative confusion and imbalance, which improved steadily. He remained functional at home with his wife, ambulating independently with a cane.

About 2–3 months later, the patient experienced new onset of seizure activity, characterized by a witnessed tonic-clonic seizure at home with post-ictal confusion and transient left arm weakness. He was brought to the emergency department by his wife. He had been prescribed levetiracetam (Keppra) for seizure prophylaxis but admitted to occasionally missing doses. Examination in the ED was notable for full orientation and no focal deficits, though he reported mild persistent left arm paresthesia. Repeat MRI demonstrated three new right parietal-temporal enhancing lesions measuring up to 3.5 cm, all within or adjacent to the previous surgical site, again associated with vasogenic edema and 7 mm midline shift. No new extracranial disease was found on PET imaging.

The patient was admitted and started on IV dexamethasone and levetiracetam, with a plan for further local therapy. After further multidisciplinary discussion involving neurosurgery, oncology, and radiation oncology, he underwent repeat craniotomy with tumor resection and SRS to new lesions. Postoperative course was notable for mild hyponatremia, managed with temporary fluid restriction and salt tablets, and brief urinary retention managed with tamsulosin and short-term Foley catheterization. There was also transient postoperative confusion that resolved with correction of sodium.

Currently, the patient is at his neurologic baseline. He continues to reside at home with his spouse, performing personal ADLs with some assistance. His wife is his primary caretaker. He ambles with a cane and climbs stairs with supervision. Mild residual cognitive changes and left hand numbness persist but do not impair function.

Mr. [Deid: Name] is a 57-year-old man with metastatic lung adenocarcinoma (initial T3N1, PD-L1 negative) with isolated brain metastases, status post brain surgery and SRS, now with further limited brain recurrence managed with repeat local therapy.
